Always exclude active TB first with a chest X-ray and symptom review, because treating active disease with one drug causes resistance.
cards.q: A patient has a positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) for TB, a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms. What is this and how is it treated?

cards.a: Dexamethasone (a corticosteroid). Steroids reduce the inflammation and swelling around the brain and meninges, and they reduce mortality and neurological disability in TB meningitis. They are also used in TB pericarditis with effusion. Give steroids alongside the anti-tuberculous drugs, not instead of them.
cards.q: A patient with TB meningitis is started on anti-tuberculous therapy. What additional drug should be given and why?

cards.a: Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). It must be managed by a specialist TB service with drug-susceptibility testing, using a longer regimen (usually 9 to 18 months) built from second-line drugs such as bedaquiline, linezolid, fluoroquinolones and clofazimine. Never add a single drug to a failing regimen — that creates further resistance.
cards.q: A patient's TB is resistant to both rifampicin and isoniazid. What is this called and how is it managed?

cards.a: Ethambutol-induced optic neuritis. Ethambutol can damage the optic nerve, causing loss of visual acuity and colour vision. Stop the drug immediately and refer urgently to ophthalmology. Check vision and colour vision at baseline and at every visit while a patient is on ethambutol, and warn them to report any visual change at once.
cards.q: A patient on ethambutol for TB reports blurred vision and difficulty telling red from green. What is happening and what should you do?

cards.a: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy (prevented with pyridoxine, vitamin B6) and hepatitis. Give pyridoxine with isoniazid to all patients at risk — diabetics, alcohol users, pregnant patients and those with HIV. If liver enzymes rise above 5 times the upper limit of normal, or above 3 times with symptoms, stop isoniazid and the other hepatotoxic drugs and seek specialist advice.
cards.q: A patient on isoniazid develops numbness and tingling in their hands and feet, and their liver tests are rising. What is the cause and management?

cards.a: Rifampicin turns body fluids orange-red — this is harmless and expected, and contact lens wearers should be warned. It also strongly induces liver enzymes (CYP450), so it speeds up the breakdown of many drugs including warfarin, oral contraceptives, antiretrovirals and transplant drugs. Doses of these drugs often need increasing, and alternative contraception is needed.
cards.q: A patient on rifampicin notices their urine and tears have turned orange, and their warfarin dose is no longer working. Why?

cards.a: Start ART within 2 weeks of starting TB treatment (within 8 weeks if the CD4 count is above 50). Early ART improves survival in TB-HIV co-infection. Warn the patient about immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) — a paradoxical worsening of TB symptoms as the immune system recovers — which is treated with steroids, not by stopping ART.
cards.q: A patient has TB and HIV with a CD4 count of 80. When should antiretroviral therapy (ART) be started?

cards.a: TB lymphadenitis (scrofula) — painless, slowly enlarging neck nodes — is the most common extrapulmonary form. TB of the spine (Pott disease) is the other classic site: it causes back pain, a gibbus deformity and can compress the spinal cord, causing paraplegia. Extrapulmonary TB is treated with the same RIPE regimen, usually for 6 months, though bone and meningeal disease may need longer.
cards.q: What is the most common form of extrapulmonary TB, and what other site is important to know about?

cards.a: Small cell lung cancer is usually central, grows rapidly, spreads early, and is strongly linked to smoking. It often causes paraneoplastic syndromes — SIADH (low sodium) and ectopic ACTH (Cushing syndrome). It responds well to chemotherapy but surgery is rarely possible because it has usually spread by diagnosis. Non-small cell lung cancer is more often resectable and is managed by stage, with surgery, targeted therapy or immunotherapy.
cards.q: How does small cell lung cancer differ from non-small cell lung cancer in presentation and management?

cards.a: A PET-CT scan to look for distant spread, a contrast CT of the chest and abdomen, and an MRI of the brain, because lung cancer commonly spreads to the brain. Mediastinal lymph nodes are sampled with EBUS (endobronchial ultrasound) to determine the N stage. Accurate staging decides whether the cancer is operable, needs chemoradiation, or needs systemic therapy.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer. What staging investigations are needed before deciding treatment?

cards.a: Test for EGFR mutations, ALK rearrangements, ROS1 and PD-L1 expression. Adenocarcinoma in a non-smoker is often driven by one of these mutations, and if present it can be treated with a targeted tablet (for example an EGFR inhibitor) that works far better than chemotherapy. Molecular testing is now standard for all advanced non-small cell lung cancer — never start chemotherapy before the results are back.
cards.q: A non-smoking woman has a peripheral lung adenocarcinoma. What molecular tests should be done and why?

cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma. It is usually central, often cavitates, and secretes parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), which raises calcium. Treat the hypercalcaemia with IV fluids and a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid, and treat the cancer itself. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is a medical emergency when severe.
cards.q: A patient with lung cancer has a central cavitating mass and a high calcium level. What cell type is likely and what causes the hypercalcaemia?

cards.a: Superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction — the tumour or nodes compress the SVC, blocking blood return from the head and arms. It is usually not an immediate emergency unless there is airway compromise. Manage by treating the cancer (chemotherapy or radiotherapy), and consider an SVC stent for rapid symptom relief. Give steroids only if there is airway oedema.
cards.q: A patient with lung cancer develops facial swelling, dilated neck veins and breathlessness when lying flat. What is this and how is it managed?

cards.a: A Pancoast tumour — an apical lung cancer invading the brachial plexus (causing arm pain and hand wasting) and the cervical sympathetic chain (causing Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis). It is usually a squamous cell carcinoma. It needs staging with MRI of the brachial plexus, and treatment is usually chemoradiation followed by surgery if resectable.
cards.q: A smoker has shoulder pain radiating down the arm, wasting of the hand muscles and a drooping eyelid with a small pupil on the same side. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: SIADH from ectopic ADH secretion by the tumour. The excess ADH retains water and dilutes the sodium. Treat with fluid restriction, and treat the underlying cancer — chemotherapy often corrects the sodium. For severe or symptomatic hyponatraemia, give hypertonic saline. Do not give large volumes of IV fluids, which will worsen the dilution.
cards.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer has a sodium of 122 mmol/L, is euvolaemic and has a high urine osmolality. What is the cause and how is it treated?

cards.a: Adults aged 50 to 80 with a smoking history of at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the last 15 years, using annual low-dose CT scanning. Screening detects cancers earlier, when they are still curable, and reduces lung cancer mortality. A chest X-ray is not a screening test — it misses early cancers.
cards.q: Who should be offered lung cancer screening, and with what test?

cards.a: Brain metastases — lung cancer is the commonest cause. Get an urgent MRI of the brain with contrast, give dexamethasone to reduce the swelling around the metastases, and involve oncology and neurosurgery. Treatment may be whole-brain radiotherapy, stereotactic radiosurgery for a few lesions, or systemic therapy depending on the tumour type.
cards.q: A patient with lung cancer develops a headache, vomiting and weakness on one side. What is the most likely cause and the immediate management?

cards.a: Risk-stratify and investigate — a nodule of this size in a smoker is suspicious. Get a PET-CT to assess metabolic activity, compare with any old imaging for growth, and refer for tissue diagnosis (CT-guided biopsy or bronchoscopy) if it looks malignant. Small nodules under 6 mm in low-risk patients can be watched with serial CT, but a 12 mm nodule in a smoker should not just be observed.
cards.q: A chest CT shows a solitary 12 mm lung nodule in a 65-year-old smoker. What is the next step?

cards.a: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern. Treat with an antifibrotic — pirfenidone or nintedanib — which slows the decline in lung function. Do NOT give long-term steroids or immunosuppression: they do not help in IPF and they increase mortality. Also give oxygen if hypoxic, offer pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinate, and refer early for transplant assessment.
cards.q: A patient has progressive breathlessness, dry cough and basal crackles. High-resolution CT shows subpleural honeycombing at the bases. What is the diagnosis and what treatment should be avoided?

cards.a: An acute exacerbation of IPF. It is a rapid, unexplained deterioration with new ground-glass change on CT, and it carries a very high mortality. Exclude infection, heart failure and pulmonary embolism first. Treatment is supportive — high-dose steroids are often given but the evidence is weak, and many patients need intensive care. Discuss goals of care and transplant status early.
cards.q: A patient with known IPF suddenly worsens with new bilateral infiltrates and hypoxia, with no infection found. What is this and what is the outlook?

cards.a: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis). Repeated inhalation of an antigen (bird droppings, mouldy hay, hot tub water) triggers an immune reaction in the lungs. The key treatment is removing the antigen — avoid the exposure completely. Steroids help in the acute phase, but continued exposure leads to irreversible fibrosis, so antigen avoidance matters more than drugs.
cards.q: A bird keeper develops breathlessness, cough and fever a few hours after cleaning the aviary, with symptoms improving when away from home. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Treat the underlying connective tissue disease and the lung disease together — usually with immunosuppression such as mycophenolate or rituximab, guided by rheumatology and respiratory teams. Unlike IPF, connective tissue disease-associated ILD often responds to immunosuppression. Also stop any drug that could be causing it, give oxygen if needed, and monitor lung function regularly.
cards.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops progressive interstitial lung disease. How should it be managed?

cards.a: Stop the amiodarone — this is drug-induced interstitial lung disease. Amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin and some chemotherapy drugs can all cause ILD. Stopping the drug early can allow recovery; continuing it leads to progressive fibrosis. Steroids may help in severe cases. Always ask about new drugs in any patient with new interstitial lung disease.
cards.q: A patient develops progressive breathlessness and interstitial changes after starting amiodarone. What should you do?

cards.a: UIP (the pattern of IPF) has a poor prognosis, does not respond to steroids, and is treated with antifibrotics. NSIP has a better prognosis, often responds to steroids and immunosuppression, and is commonly linked to connective tissue disease. The pattern on high-resolution CT and the clinical context decide the treatment — so getting the pattern right matters.
cards.q: What is the difference between usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) and non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) in prognosis and treatment?

cards.a: Refer early — as soon as the disease is progressive despite treatment, or the patient needs increasing oxygen, or lung function is falling. Transplant assessment takes time, and patients can deteriorate quickly or become too unwell to transplant. Early referral does not commit the patient to transplant; it keeps the option open. Also discuss advance care planning and palliative care in parallel.
cards.q: A patient with advanced interstitial lung disease is breathless on minimal exertion despite oxygen. When should lung transplantation be considered?

cards.a: A falling DLCO means gas transfer across the alveolar membrane is worsening — the fibrosis is progressing or there is a new complication. Check for an acute exacerbation, infection, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension or heart failure. DLCO is often the most sensitive marker of progression in ILD, falling before the FVC does.
cards.q: A patient with interstitial lung disease has worsening breathlessness and a falling DLCO (diffusing capacity). What does a falling DLCO mean and what should you check?

cards.a: Group 1 is pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH, including idiopathic and connective tissue disease). Group 2 is due to left heart disease. Group 3 is due to lung disease and hypoxia. Group 4 is chronic thromboembolic. Group 5 is miscellaneous. The group matters because treatment is completely different — PAH drugs help Group 1 but can harm Group 2, and Group 4 may be curable with surgery.
cards.q: What are the five groups of pulmonary hypertension, and why does the group matter?

cards.a: Treat with a combination of a PDE5 inhibitor (such as sildenafil), an endothelin receptor antagonist (such as bosentan) and, in severe disease, a prostacyclin. Calcium channel blockers are used only in the small minority who are vasoreactive on right heart catheterisation — giving them to non-responders is ineffective and can cause hypotension. All patients need a specialist pulmonary hypertension centre.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. What is the treatment, and which drug class is only used in some patients?

cards.a: No — this is Group 2 pulmonary hypertension from left heart disease, and the treatment is to treat the heart failure (diuretics, guideline-directed therapy, valve repair if indicated). PAH-specific drugs such as sildenafil or bosentan do not help in left heart disease and can cause harm by increasing pulmonary blood flow into a failing left ventricle.
cards.q: A patient with heart failure and a high pulmonary artery pressure on echo is found to have pulmonary hypertension. Should you start a PAH-specific drug?

cards.a: Treat the COPD and the hypoxia — optimise inhalers, give long-term oxygen if indicated, and treat exacerbations promptly. This is Group 3 pulmonary hypertension, caused by lung disease and low oxygen. PAH-specific drugs are not indicated and do not improve outcomes in COPD-related pulmonary hypertension; correcting the hypoxia is what lowers the pressures.
cards.q: A patient with severe COPD develops pulmonary hypertension. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Right heart catheterisation. It directly measures the mean pulmonary artery pressure (25 mmHg or higher at rest defines pulmonary hypertension), the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (to distinguish pre-capillary from post-capillary disease) and the cardiac output. Echocardiography estimates the pressure and is the screening test, but it cannot confirm the diagnosis or classify it.
cards.q: What is the gold standard test to diagnose pulmonary hypertension, and what does it measure?

cards.a: Admit to intensive care, treat the trigger (infection, arrhythmia, missed medication), give cautious fluids only if clearly volume depleted, and support the right ventricle with inotropes such as dobutamine and a vasopressor such as norepinephrine to maintain coronary perfusion. Avoid overloading with fluids — a failing right ventricle cannot cope with volume. Involve the pulmonary hypertension team urgently and consider IV prostacyclin.
cards.q: A patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension presents with acute right heart failure — low blood pressure, raised JVP and worsening breathlessness. What is the management?

cards.a: This is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. A small, stable pneumothorax can be managed with observation and high-flow oxygen, which speeds reabsorption of the air. A large or symptomatic pneumothorax needs needle aspiration first; if that fails or the pneumothorax is large, insert a chest drain. Admit for observation either way.
cards.q: A tall, thin 22-year-old man develops sudden left-sided chest pain and breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows a 3 cm pneumothorax with no mediastinal shift. What is the management?

cards.a: A secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in COPD is more dangerous and less likely to resolve on its own, because the underlying lung is diseased. These patients usually need a chest drain rather than simple aspiration, and they need admission and close monitoring. They also have a higher risk of recurrence and of a persistent air leak, so involve the respiratory team early.
cards.q: A patient with COPD develops a pneumothorax. How does management differ from a primary spontaneous pneumothorax?

cards.a: This is an iatrogenic pneumothorax. Assess the size and the patient's symptoms: a small, asymptomatic pneumothorax can be observed with oxygen and a repeat chest X-ray, while a large or symptomatic one needs a chest drain. Also review the procedure — ultrasound guidance reduces the risk. Do not discharge the patient without a repeat X-ray showing the pneumothorax is stable or improving.
cards.q: A patient develops a pneumothorax after a central line insertion. What should you do?

cards.a: Definitive prevention — video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with pleurodesis, or chemical pleurodesis. After a second pneumothorax the recurrence risk is high (over 50%), so observation alone is not enough. Surgery also allows the surgeon to staple any blebs or bullae. Advise the patient to stop smoking, which reduces recurrence.
cards.q: A patient has had a second spontaneous pneumothorax on the same side. What should you offer to prevent recurrence?

cards.a: Do not fly until the pneumothorax has fully resolved and a chest X-ray confirms it — usually at least 1 to 2 weeks after resolution, and longer after surgery. Cabin pressure falls at altitude, so trapped air expands and a small pneumothorax can become a tension pneumothorax mid-flight. The same applies to scuba diving, which is generally advised against after a pneumothorax.
cards.q: A patient with a pneumothorax is due to fly in 2 days. What should you advise?

cards.a: This is a tension pneumothorax — air is trapped under pressure and is compressing the heart and the good lung. It is a clinical diagnosis: do NOT wait for a chest X-ray. Decompress immediately with a large-bore needle in the second intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line (or the fifth space at the anterior axillary line), then insert a chest drain. Waiting for imaging can be fatal.
cards.q: A patient with a pneumothorax suddenly becomes hypotensive with a distended neck veins and the trachea pushed to the other side. What has happened and what must you do?

cards.a: Massive haemoptysis is an airway emergency. Protect the airway first — intubate if needed, position the patient with the bleeding side down (lateral decubitus) so blood does not flood the good lung, and give IV access and blood. The definitive treatment is usually bronchial artery embolisation by interventional radiology, or bronchoscopy to localise the bleed. Do not give a cough suppressant as the only treatment.
cards.q: A patient is coughing up large volumes of blood — over 600 mL in 24 hours. What is the immediate management?

cards.a: Bronchiectasis is the most common cause overall, followed by tuberculosis and lung cancer. Get a chest X-ray and a CT of the chest, check clotting and blood count, and arrange bronchoscopy if the cause is unclear or cancer is suspected. A CT is better than a plain X-ray at finding bronchiectasis, a tumour or a cavitating lesion.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of haemoptysis, and what investigations should you do?

cards.a: ANCA-associated vasculitis (such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis) causing diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis — a pulmonary-renal syndrome. This is life-threatening. Give high-dose IV steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide urgently, and consider plasma exchange in severe alveolar haemorrhage. Do not delay immunosuppression while waiting for a biopsy.
cards.q: A patient has haemoptysis, a rising creatinine, blood in the urine and a positive ANCA. What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?

cards.a: Sarcoidosis. But non-caseating granulomas are not specific — you must exclude tuberculosis (which causes caseating granulomas, but can look similar), lymphoma, fungal infection and foreign-body reactions before calling it sarcoidosis. Send TB cultures, check for lymphoma, and review the drug history. The classic chest X-ray finding is bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, often with lung infiltrates.
cards.q: A patient has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray, a dry cough and a raised ACE level. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. What is the diagnosis, and what must you exclude first?

cards.a: No — many patients with sarcoidosis need no treatment at all, and the disease often resolves on its own. Steroids are reserved for symptomatic disease, progressive lung involvement, eye disease (uveitis), cardiac or neurological involvement, or hypercalcaemia. Monitor with regular lung function tests, chest imaging and eye checks instead.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with sarcoidosis but has only mild hilar lymphadenopathy and no symptoms. Should you start steroids?

cards.a: Cardiac sarcoidosis — granulomas in the heart cause heart block, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death. Treat with steroids and immunosuppression, and consider an ICD, because the risk of a lethal arrhythmia is high and the scarred heart can cause VT even after the inflammation settles. Arrange a cardiology referral and rhythm monitoring urgently.
cards.q: A patient with sarcoidosis develops palpitations and syncope, and cardiac MRI shows scarring in the heart. What is the management?

cards.a: Lofgren syndrome — an acute presentation of sarcoidosis with erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar adenopathy, ankle arthritis and fever. It has an excellent prognosis and usually resolves on its own within months. Treat with NSAIDs and reassurance; steroids are rarely needed. It is one of the few forms of sarcoidosis where the outcome is almost always good.
cards.q: A young woman has painful red nodules on her shins, swollen ankles, fever and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is this and what is the prognosis?

cards.a: The normal squamous lining of the lower oesophagus is replaced by intestinal-type lining, after years of acid reflux (GERD). It matters because it can progress to oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Patients need surveillance endoscopy.
cards.q: What is Barrett's oesophagus, and why does it matter?

cards.a: The two main causes are H. pylori infection and NSAIDs. H. pylori is treated with triple therapy: a PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole if allergic to penicillin) for 14 days. Then re-test to confirm the infection is gone.
cards.q: What causes a peptic ulcer, and how is H. pylori treated?

cards.a: Ulcerative colitis: continuous inflammation starting in the rectum, only the colon, bloody diarrhoea, no skip areas. Crohn's: skip lesions anywhere from mouth to anus, often the terminal ileum, non-bloody diarrhoea, strictures and fistulas, granulomas on biopsy. Both are inflammatory bowel disease.
cards.q: How do you tell ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease?

cards.a: It grades how severe liver failure is, using bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy. Class A = mild, B = moderate, C = severe. A higher score means worse liver function and higher risk of death — it helps decide about transplant.
cards.q: What is the Child-Pugh score used for in cirrhosis?

cards.a: Infection of ascitic fluid in a patient with cirrhosis, without an obvious source. Diagnose by ascitic fluid neutrophil count (PMN) of 250 cells/mm3 or more. Treat with cefotaxime plus albumin. SAAG (serum-ascites albumin gradient) of 1.1 g/dL or more points to portal hypertension as the cause of the ascites.
cards.q: What is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), and how is it diagnosed?

cards.a: Gallstones and alcohol — together they cause most cases. Diagnosis needs 2 of 3: typical upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, lipase or amylase more than 3 times the upper limit, and imaging showing pancreatitis. Treatment is IV fluids, pain control, and nothing by mouth initially.
cards.q: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?

cards.a: Charcot's triad = fever + right upper quadrant pain + jaundice. It means cholangitis — infection of the bile ducts, usually from a gallstone blocking the duct. Reynolds' pentad adds confusion and low blood pressure (shock) — that is severe cholangitis and needs urgent antibiotics and bile duct drainage (ERCP).
cards.q: What is Charcot's triad, and what does Reynolds' pentad add?

cards.a: IV octreotide (or terlipressin) plus IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone), plus urgent endoscopy with band ligation. Give blood transfusion carefully — aim for haemoglobin around 7 g/dL, not normal, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens bleeding.
cards.q: What is the first treatment for a variceal bleed in cirrhosis?

cards.a: HBsAg positive = current infection. Anti-HBs positive = immunity (after vaccine or past infection). Anti-HBc IgM = acute infection. HBeAg positive = high infectivity. If HBsAg is positive for more than 6 months, it is chronic hepatitis B.
cards.q: How do you interpret hepatitis B serology?

cards.a: Stop the triggering antibiotic if possible. First-line treatment is fidaxomicin, or oral vancomycin. Do NOT use metronidazole as first line anymore. For severe or recurrent cases, faecal microbiota transplant is used. C. difficile causes watery diarrhoea after antibiotics.
cards.q: What is the treatment for Clostridioides difficile infection?

cards.a: Resuscitate first: secure two large-bore IV lines, give IV fluids and transfuse red cells to a target haemoglobin of 7 g/dL, and correct coagulopathy. Endoscopy is done once the patient is stabilised, ideally within 24 hours. Scoping an unstable, under-resuscitated patient risks further collapse and a poor view because blood fills the stomach.
cards.q: A patient vomits blood and is hypotensive with a haemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL. What is the first step before endoscopy?

cards.a: Hold the warfarin and reverse the coagulopathy, usually with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate if bleeding is severe. Restarting anticoagulation is decided later with cardiology once bleeding is controlled. Continuing warfarin during an active bleed makes haemostasis impossible, while a short hold rarely causes a clot.
cards.q: A patient with an upper GI bleed is on warfarin with an INR of 4. What do you do about the anticoagulation?

cards.a: Apply endoscopic haemostasis, such as a clip or thermal coagulation, plus adrenaline injection, and start a high-dose IV proton pump inhibitor. A visible vessel means a high risk of rebleeding without treatment. After endoscopy, keep the PPI going and test for H. pylori.
cards.q: A patient with a bleeding peptic ulcer has a visible vessel seen on endoscopy. What is the next step?

cards.a: They can be considered for outpatient management with urgent outpatient endoscopy, because a score of 0 predicts a very low risk of needing transfusion, endoscopic therapy or surgery. A low score means no concerning features such as low blood pressure, low haemoglobin or melaena with instability. Admitting every low-risk bleeder wastes beds and exposes them to hospital risks.
cards.q: A patient with an upper GI bleed has a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0. What is the management?

cards.a: Place a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) — it decompresses the portal system and stops variceal bleeding when endoscopic therapy fails. A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is only a temporary bridge to TIPS because it controls bleeding by pressure but risks aspiration and oesophageal injury. Definitive control needs portal pressure reduction.
cards.q: A patient with a variceal bleed keeps bleeding despite band ligation and octreotide. What is the next step?

cards.a: Start a non-selective beta-blocker such as nadolol or carvedilol, which lowers portal pressure by reducing cardiac output and splanchnic blood flow. Alternatively, endoscopic band ligation is used if beta-blockers are not tolerated. Preventing the first bleed matters because a variceal bleed carries high mortality.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis has small oesophageal varices and has never bled. What prevents a first bleed?

cards.a: Do a colonoscopy after bowel preparation, usually within 24 hours. In a stable patient, colonoscopy both finds the source, often diverticular bleeding, and allows treatment such as clipping. CT angiography is reserved for brisk, unstable bleeding where the source cannot be found endoscopically.
cards.q: A patient with a lower GI bleed is haemodynamically stable with bright red blood per rectum. What is the first investigation?

cards.a: Get a CT angiogram, which can localise active bleeding and guide embolisation by interventional radiology. It needs a brisk bleed to show contrast extravasation. Surgery is a last resort when embolisation fails or the patient deteriorates.
cards.q: A patient with brisk rectal bleeding is unstable despite resuscitation and colonoscopy cannot find the source. What is the next test?

cards.a: Hold it during the acute bleed, but restart it as soon as haemostasis is achieved, usually within 1 to 3 days, because the risk of a heart attack or stent thrombosis from stopping aspirin is higher than the risk of rebleeding. Add a PPI for gastroprotection. Stopping aspirin permanently after a bleed is a common error that causes cardiac events.
cards.q: A patient on aspirin for a previous heart attack has a GI bleed. Should the aspirin be stopped permanently?

cards.a: Most tears stop bleeding on their own, so management is supportive: IV fluids, antiemetics and a PPI, with endoscopic clipping only if bleeding continues. The tear comes from forceful vomiting raising pressure at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Surgery is almost never needed.
cards.q: A patient with an upper GI bleed is found to have a Mallory-Weiss tear. What is the management?

cards.a: Do a capsule endoscopy to look at the small bowel, which is the usual source when upper and lower endoscopy are negative. Small bowel sources include angiodysplasia and small bowel tumours. A capsule is non-invasive and visualises the whole small bowel.
cards.q: A patient with melena and a normal upper endoscopy has ongoing bleeding. What is the next investigation?

cards.a: Antibiotics reduce bacterial infections and rebleeding and improve survival in acute variceal bleeding, because bacterial translocation from the gut is common in advanced cirrhosis. This is prophylaxis, not treatment of a known infection. Every variceal bleeder should receive a short course.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis and a variceal bleed is given ceftriaxone. Why give antibiotics when there is no proven infection?

cards.a: A restrictive transfusion strategy improves outcomes in upper GI bleeding. Over-transfusion raises portal pressure and can worsen bleeding, especially in variceal bleeding, and adds transfusion risks. Transfuse to 7 g/dL, or 8 g/dL if there is cardiac disease.
cards.q: A patient with an upper GI bleed needs transfusion. Why is the target haemoglobin 7 g/dL rather than normal?

cards.a: Stop the NSAID if possible, start a PPI, and test for and treat H. pylori. If the NSAID cannot be stopped, continue the PPI and switch to a COX-2 selective agent such as celecoxib, which is gentler on the stomach. NSAIDs block prostaglandins that protect the gastric mucosa, so the ulcer will not heal while the drug continues.
cards.q: A patient takes an NSAID daily and develops a gastric ulcer. What is the management?

cards.a: Do a test of cure with a urea breath test or stool antigen test at least 4 weeks after finishing antibiotics, and after stopping the PPI for at least 2 weeks. Testing too early gives false negatives because the PPI suppresses the bacteria without clearing it. Serology is useless for cure because antibodies stay positive for life.
cards.q: A patient treated for H. pylori asks when to check if it is gone. What test and when?

cards.a: Use bismuth-based quadruple therapy: PPI plus bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole for 14 days. Failure is usually due to clarithromycin resistance, so repeating the same regimen will fail again. Always confirm cure afterwards with a urea breath test or stool antigen.
cards.q: A patient fails first-line triple therapy for H. pylori. What is the next regimen?

cards.a: This is a surgical emergency: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and a PPI, and take them for an urgent operation to close the perforation. Free air means the ulcer has burst through the stomach or duodenal wall, spilling contents into the abdomen. Conservative management is only for a tiny, sealed perforation in a stable patient.
cards.q: A patient with a duodenal ulcer has a perforation with free air under the diaphragm. What is the management?

cards.a: Gastric ulcers can be malignant, unlike duodenal ulcers which are almost never cancer. Biopsy the ulcer edge and repeat endoscopy after 8 to 12 weeks to confirm healing. An ulcer that does not heal is cancer until proven otherwise.
cards.q: A patient with a gastric ulcer is treated with a PPI. Why must the ulcer be biopsied and re-scoped?

cards.a: Measure a fasting serum gastrin level. A very high gastrin with low gastric pH confirms a gastrinoma, a gastrin-secreting tumour usually in the pancreas or duodenum. Gastrin drives massive acid production, which is why ordinary ulcer treatment fails. Stop the PPI for a week before testing if safe, because PPIs raise gastrin falsely.
cards.q: A patient with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome has severe refractory peptic ulcers and diarrhoea. What is the first test?

cards.a: A COX-2 selective NSAID such as celecoxib, plus a PPI, is the safest combination. COX-2 drugs spare the COX-1 enzyme that protects the stomach lining. Paracetamol is even safer for the stomach but may not control inflammatory pain.
cards.q: A patient with peptic ulcer disease keeps taking NSAIDs for arthritis. Which painkiller is safest for the stomach?

cards.a: Check adherence and timing — the PPI must be taken 30 to 60 minutes before the first meal of the day — then consider endoscopy and pH monitoring. Refractory reflux may be due to poor compliance, non-acid reflux, functional heartburn or eosinophilic oesophagitis. Increasing the dose blindly without checking why it failed misses the real diagnosis.
cards.q: A patient has heartburn that does not improve on a PPI. What is the next step?

cards.a: Confirm the dysplasia with an expert pathology review, then offer endoscopic ablation such as radiofrequency ablation, or close surveillance endoscopy. Low-grade dysplasia raises the risk of progression to cancer, so it cannot simply be watched casually. High-dose PPI is continued to reduce acid exposure.
cards.q: A patient with Barrett's oesophagus has low-grade dysplasia on biopsy. What is the management?

cards.a: Refer for endoscopic eradication therapy, usually endoscopic mucosal resection of visible lesions followed by radiofrequency ablation of the remaining Barrett's segment. High-grade dysplasia is one step from adenocarcinoma, so it needs treatment, not just surveillance. Oesophagectomy is reserved for cases where endoscopic therapy fails or cancer is found.
cards.q: A patient with Barrett's oesophagus has high-grade dysplasia. What is the next step?

cards.a: Achalasia: the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax and the oesophagus loses peristalsis. Treatment is pneumatic balloon dilatation, Heller myotomy, or per-oral endoscopic myotomy (POEM). Botulinum toxin injection is only for patients too frail for these, because its effect wears off. Manometry confirms the diagnosis.
cards.q: A patient has difficulty swallowing solids and liquids, with regurgitation and weight loss. Barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus with a tapered 'bird's beak'. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Eosinophilic oesophagitis: an allergic inflammation of the oesophagus, confirmed by eosinophils on biopsy. Treat with a swallowed topical steroid such as fluticasone or budesonide slurry, a PPI, and dietary elimination of triggers. Dilatation is needed only if there is a fixed stricture.
cards.q: A young man with atopy has difficulty swallowing solids and food getting stuck. Endoscopy shows rings and furrows in the oesophagus. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: At least 8 weeks for healing of erosive oesophagitis, then step down to the lowest effective dose or on-demand therapy for maintenance. Stopping after a few days leaves the oesophagus unhealed and symptoms return. Long-term PPI is safe for most patients and is needed in severe disease.
cards.q: A patient with severe oesophagitis from reflux is started on a PPI. How long should treatment continue?

cards.a: Lose weight, stop smoking, avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime, and raise the head of the bed. These reduce acid exposure by lowering abdominal pressure and keeping acid out of the oesophagus at night. Lifestyle change alone rarely cures severe reflux but makes drug treatment work better.
cards.q: A patient with GERD is overweight, smokes and eats late at night. What lifestyle advice matters most?

cards.a: Laparoscopic fundoplication, usually a Nissen wrap, which tightens the lower oesophageal sphincter by wrapping the top of the stomach around the oesophagus. Surgery is reserved for patients who fail medical therapy, cannot tolerate PPIs, or have a large paraoesophageal hernia. It is not first-line treatment for ordinary heartburn.
cards.q: A patient with a large hiatus hernia and severe reflux fails medical therapy. What is the surgical option?

cards.a: It means the stomach lining is congested from portal hypertension and can bleed, so continue portal pressure reduction with a non-selective beta-blocker. It is not the same as gastritis and does not respond to PPIs alone. Severe bleeding may need TIPS.
cards.q: A patient with oesophageal varices is found to have portal hypertensive gastropathy. What does this mean for management?

cards.a: IV methylprednisolone. Severe ulcerative colitis means more than 6 bloody stools a day with systemic features such as fever, tachycardia, anaemia or a raised ESR. Oral steroids are not absorbed or effective enough in severe disease, and delaying IV treatment risks toxic megacolon and perforation.
cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis has 8 bloody stools a day, fever and a CRP of 80 mg/L. What is the first treatment?

cards.a: Give IV ciclosporin or infliximab as rescue therapy. Failure to respond to IV steroids after 3 to 5 days means the colon will not recover on steroids alone, and rescue therapy can avoid colectomy. If rescue therapy also fails, surgery (colectomy) is needed.
cards.q: A patient with severe ulcerative colitis has not improved after 3 days of IV steroids. What is the next step?

cards.a: Toxic megacolon: the colon dilates and loses muscle tone, risking perforation and sepsis. Stop antidiarrhoeal drugs and opioids, keep the patient nil by mouth, give IV fluids, steroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and get an urgent surgical review. A plain abdominal X-ray showing colonic dilatation above 6 cm confirms it.
cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops a distended abdomen, fever and a dilated colon on X-ray. What is this and what is the management?

cards.a: Mesalazine (5-ASA) is the maintenance drug for ulcerative colitis and reduces relapse, while also lowering colorectal cancer risk with long-term use. Sulfasalazine is an older alternative that causes more side effects. Steroids induce remission but do not maintain it and should never be used long term.
cards.q: A patient with mild ulcerative colitis is in remission. What is the maintenance treatment?

cards.a: Use a biologic such as infliximab or adalimumab, usually combined with an immunomodulator such as azathioprine. Moderate to severe Crohn's disease needs treatment that heals the bowel wall, not just symptom control. Steroids are only a short-term bridge because they do not heal the mucosa.
cards.q: A patient with moderate to severe Crohn's disease affecting the ileum fails mesalazine. What is the next treatment?

cards.a: Start with an anti-TNF agent such as infliximab. Fistulising Crohn's disease needs a drug proven to close fistulas, and infliximab has the best evidence. Antibiotics such as metronidazole and ciprofloxacin help drain sepsis but do not close fistulas alone, and a seton drain is placed if there is an abscess.
cards.q: A patient with Crohn's disease develops a perianal fistula. What is the drug of choice?

cards.a: Screen for tuberculosis with an interferon-gamma release assay and a chest X-ray, and screen for hepatitis B, before starting. Anti-TNF drugs suppress immunity and can reactivate latent tuberculosis or hepatitis B, which can be fatal. Vaccination should also be brought up to date before starting.
cards.q: A patient with Crohn's disease is about to start infliximab. What screening must be done first?

cards.a: Stop the biologic and start broad-spectrum antibiotics. Immunosuppressed patients with Crohn's disease can develop an intra-abdominal abscess, and continuing the biologic worsens infection. Drainage by interventional radiology is often needed alongside antibiotics.
cards.q: A patient with Crohn's disease on infliximab develops fever and right lower quadrant pain. What do you do first?

cards.a: An ileocolonic resection of the diseased segment. Fibrotic strictures do not respond to drugs because the bowel wall is scarred, not inflamed. Endoscopic balloon dilatation is an option for short strictures, but long or multiple strictures need surgery.
cards.q: A patient with longstanding ileal Crohn's disease has a fibrotic stricture causing obstruction. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Yes, and it should be used even if there is no diarrhoea. Smoking worsens Crohn's disease, increases flares, strictures and the need for surgery, and reduces the effectiveness of treatment. Interestingly, smoking protects against ulcerative colitis, but that is never a reason to smoke.
cards.q: A patient with Crohn's disease smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Does smoking cessation matter for their disease?

cards.a: Treat with IV fluids, correct electrolytes, and give antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, then drain the abscess with a percutaneous drain if it is large. A small abscess may settle with antibiotics alone. Surgery is deferred until the infection settles, because operating on an infected abdomen is riskier.
cards.q: A patient with Crohn's disease has an intra-abdominal abscess on CT. What is the management?

cards.a: Use a topical mesalazine suppository or enema, which delivers the drug directly to the rectum. Topical therapy works better than oral drugs for proctitis because the disease is limited to the rectum. Oral mesalazine alone often does not reach the rectum in high enough concentration.
cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum has bloody stools. What is the first treatment?

cards.a: Yes, because ulcerative colitis raises the risk of colorectal cancer, and the risk rises with disease duration and extent. Surveillance colonoscopy with biopsies starts 8 years after diagnosis and is repeated every 1 to 3 years. Primary sclerosing cholangitis raises the risk further and needs yearly surveillance.
cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis for 10 years asks about colon cancer screening. What do you advise?

cards.a: Stop the mesalazine and check a stool test for C. difficile. Mesalazine intolerance can mimic a flare with diarrhoea and abdominal pain, but C. difficile infection is also common in IBD and must be excluded before escalating steroids. Treating a C. difficile infection as a flare with steroids makes it worse.
cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis on mesalazine develops worsening diarrhoea. Before escalating treatment, what must be excluded?

cards.a: Azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, which are steroid-sparing immunomodulators that maintain remission. Check thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity first, because low TPMT means a high risk of severe bone marrow suppression. Monitor the full blood count and liver function regularly.
cards.q: A patient with Crohn's disease keeps relapsing when steroids are tapered. What is the steroid-sparing maintenance drug?

cards.a: Vedolizumab, an anti-integrin antibody that blocks white cells from entering the gut. It is gut-selective, so it causes less systemic immunosuppression than anti-TNF drugs. It works more slowly, so it is better for maintenance than for rapid rescue of severe disease.
cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis has failed anti-TNF therapy and has recurrent infections. Which biologic is the most gut-selective option?

cards.a: A large-volume paracentesis with albumin cover, 6 to 8 g of albumin per litre of fluid removed. Albumin prevents circulatory dysfunction and kidney injury after removing large volumes of fluid. Diuretics alone are too slow for tense ascites causing breathlessness.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis has tense ascites causing severe breathlessness. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Restrict sodium to about 2 g per day and start spironolactone with furosemide in a ratio of 100 mg to 40 mg. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone, which drives sodium retention in cirrhosis. Monitor potassium and kidney function, because over-diuresis causes kidney injury and low sodium.
cards.q: A patient with new ascites from cirrhosis is stable and not breathless. What is the first treatment?

cards.a: Do a diagnostic paracentesis and calculate the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG). A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more means portal hypertension, usually cirrhosis. A low SAAG points to other causes such as peritoneal tuberculosis or cancer. The fluid neutrophil count is checked at the same time to exclude SBP.
cards.q: A patient has new ascites. What is the first test, and what result points to cirrhosis?

cards.a: Give albumin, 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3, together with cefotaxime. Albumin expands the circulation and reduces the risk of kidney failure and death in SBP. Antibiotics alone are not enough in these patients.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis is diagnosed with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. What is given alongside the antibiotic, and why?

cards.a: Start long-term norfloxacin prophylaxis after the first episode of SBP, because recurrence is common and often fatal. Also consider referral for liver transplantation. Secondary prophylaxis is continued until transplant or death.
cards.q: A patient recovers from spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. What prevents it coming back?

cards.a: Lactulose, titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day. Lactulose acidifies the colon and traps ammonia, reducing the amount absorbed into the blood. Rifaximin is added if encephalopathy recurs despite lactulose. Sedatives must be avoided because they worsen confusion.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis is confused and asterixis is present. What is the first treatment for hepatic encephalopathy?

cards.a: A serum ammonia level does not diagnose or grade encephalopathy reliably — the diagnosis is clinical, based on confusion, asterixis and a history of liver disease. Ammonia can be high in patients without encephalopathy and normal in some with it. Do not delay treatment waiting for the level.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis is confused. Should you check a serum ammonia level to diagnose hepatic encephalopathy?

cards.a: Restrict dietary protein only briefly during an acute episode, then return to a normal protein intake of about 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg per day. Long-term protein restriction worsens muscle wasting and does not help encephalopathy. Malnutrition is a major problem in cirrhosis and must be avoided.
cards.q: A patient with hepatic encephalopathy is on a low-protein diet. Should protein restriction continue long term?

cards.a: This is hepatorenal syndrome, a functional kidney failure caused by severe portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilatation. Treat with albumin plus a vasoconstrictor such as terlipressin, and refer urgently for liver transplantation, which is the definitive treatment. Dialysis is only a bridge.
cards.q: A patient with advanced cirrhosis develops rising creatinine and very low urine output, with no protein in the urine and normal kidneys on ultrasound. What is this and what is the treatment?

cards.a: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS), which lowers portal pressure and reduces ascites formation. It is used when ascites no longer responds to diuretics or needs repeated paracentesis. TIPS can worsen encephalopathy, so patients are selected carefully.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis has ascites that no longer responds to maximum diuretics. What is the next step?

cards.a: Refer for liver transplantation assessment. A MELD score of 15 or more, or decompensated cirrhosis with complications such as refractory ascites, recurrent variceal bleeding or encephalopathy, means transplant should be considered. Transplant is the only treatment that reverses advanced cirrhosis.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis has a MELD score of 18 and recurrent variceal bleeding. What is the definitive management?

cards.a: Screen with an ultrasound of the liver every 6 months, with or without alpha-fetoprotein. Regular screening catches hepatocellular carcinoma early, when it can be treated with resection, ablation or transplant. Screening every year is too infrequent because these tumours can grow quickly.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis asks how to screen for liver cancer. What test and how often?

cards.a: Stop the diuretic and give albumin, because over-diuresis and infection are the commonest triggers. Also check for bleeding, infection and constipation, which precipitate encephalopathy. Identifying and treating the trigger is as important as giving lactulose.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis on diuretics becomes acutely confused. What is the most likely trigger and what do you do?

cards.a: An abdominal ultrasound with Doppler to look for portal vein thrombosis, which is a common cause of sudden decompensation in cirrhosis. Portal vein thrombosis raises portal pressure and worsens ascites and variceal bleeding. Anticoagulation is considered if the clot is acute and there is no active bleeding.
cards.q: A patient with stable cirrhosis suddenly develops worsening ascites and variceal bleeding. What imaging is needed?

cards.a: Give IV albumin and hold diuretics, because the kidney injury is usually due to low effective circulating volume. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs and contrast. Most acute kidney injury in cirrhosis is pre-renal, not hepatorenal syndrome, and it is reversible if treated early.
cards.q: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops a rising creatinine after a large paracentesis without albumin. What is the management?

cards.a: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer's solution, aiming for a good urine output. Early fluids restore perfusion to the pancreas and reduce the risk of necrosis. Over-resuscitation is harmful, so monitor urine output and breathing, but under-resuscitation in the first 24 hours is the commonest error.
cards.q: A patient with acute pancreatitis is hypotensive and tachycardic. What is the most important treatment in the first 24 hours?

cards.a: Do not start antibiotics routinely. Antibiotics are only given if there is proven infected necrosis or another infection such as cholangitis. Sterile pancreatic necrosis does not need antibiotics, and unnecessary use breeds resistance. If infection is suspected, do a CT-guided fine needle aspiration or start broad-spectrum antibiotics.
cards.q: A patient with acute pancreatitis has pancreatic necrosis on CT but no fever. Should antibiotics be started?

cards.a: The BISAP score or Ranson criteria, which predict severity and mortality using features such as age, white cell count, blood urea, mental status and pleural effusion. A high score means the patient needs close monitoring, often in intensive care. Early identification of severe pancreatitis saves lives.
cards.q: A patient with acute pancreatitis is admitted. What scoring system predicts severity and the need for intensive care?

cards.a: Feed them early, within 24 to 48 hours, starting with a low-fat oral diet once pain settles. Early feeding reduces infection and organ failure compared with prolonged fasting. Total parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate enteral feeding after several days.
cards.q: A patient with mild acute pancreatitis is improving. When should feeding start?

cards.a: Urgent ERCP within 24 hours to remove the stone. Cholangitis with pancreatitis is a biliary emergency because the blocked duct is infected. Antibiotics alone cannot clear an obstructed, infected duct. Delaying drainage increases mortality.
cards.q: A patient with gallstone pancreatitis develops fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. What is the next step?

cards.a: Cholecystectomy during the same admission, once the pancreatitis has settled. Removing the gallbladder prevents another attack, which can be more severe. Discharging the patient and booking surgery later risks a recurrent attack before the operation.
cards.q: A patient recovers from gallstone pancreatitis. When should the gallbladder be removed?

cards.a: Advise complete alcohol abstinence, give pancreatic enzyme replacement if there is malabsorption, and treat diabetes if it develops. Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive, irreversible disease, and continued drinking accelerates destruction of the pancreas. Pain control and nutritional support are central to care.
cards.q: A patient with chronic pancreatitis from alcohol has weight loss and greasy stools. What is the management?

cards.a: Pancreatic cancer, which can present as painless jaundice from a tumour in the head of the pancreas blocking the bile duct, with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign). CT of the abdomen with contrast is the first imaging test. Refer urgently to a hepatobiliary team.
cards.q: An older patient has painless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable gallbladder. What is the most likely diagnosis and first test?

cards.a: It means the necrosis is infected, which is the most dangerous complication of severe pancreatitis. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics and arrange drainage, usually by a minimally invasive necrosectomy after 4 weeks when the collection has walled off. Early open surgery has high mortality.
cards.q: A patient with severe pancreatitis develops fever and gas in the pancreatic necrosis on CT. What does this mean and what is the management?

cards.a: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the treatment of choice for symptomatic gallstones, because it removes the source of pain and prevents complications such as cholecystitis and pancreatitis. Asymptomatic gallstones found by chance do not need surgery. Medical dissolution with ursodiol is slow and rarely used.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent biliary colic from gallstones. What is the definitive treatment?

cards.a: Cholecystectomy within 72 hours of symptom onset. Early surgery reduces complications and shortens the hospital stay compared with waiting for the inflammation to settle. Delayed surgery risks recurrent attacks and a more difficult operation.
cards.q: A patient has acute cholecystitis confirmed on ultrasound. When should surgery be done?

cards.a: This is Mirizzi syndrome, where a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct compresses the common hepatic duct and causes jaundice. It is a surgical problem, and cholecystectomy is difficult because the anatomy is distorted, so referral to a hepatobiliary surgeon is needed. ERCP may be used to place a stent first.
cards.q: A patient with gallstones develops jaundice and a stone impacted in the cystic duct compressing the hepatic duct. What is this called?

cards.a: Get an MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound, which show stones in the common bile duct that ultrasound often misses. If a stone is found, ERCP removes it. Ultrasound is good for the gallbladder but poor for the bile duct, so a normal ultrasound does not exclude choledocholithiasis.
cards.q: A patient has gallstones, jaundice and a raised alkaline phosphatase, but ultrasound shows no bile duct stone. What is the next test?

cards.a: ERCP to drain the bile duct, plus broad-spectrum antibiotics. Antibiotics alone cannot sterilise an obstructed duct, so drainage is the life-saving step. Urgent drainage within 24 hours is needed in severe cholangitis with shock or confusion.
cards.q: A patient has cholangitis with fever, jaundice and low blood pressure. What is the definitive treatment?

cards.a: The bile duct is blocked, so bile cannot drain, causing jaundice, itching and pale stools. Ursodiol improves bile flow in primary biliary cholangitis, an autoimmune disease of the small bile ducts that mainly affects middle-aged women. Refer to hepatology, because the disease progresses to cirrhosis.
cards.q: A middle-aged woman has itching, jaundice, pale stools and a very high alkaline phosphatase. What is the likely cause and treatment?

cards.a: Acalculous cholecystitis: inflammation of the gallbladder without stones, seen in critically ill patients after major surgery or trauma. Treat with antibiotics and percutaneous cholecystostomy drainage if the patient is too unwell for surgery. It is easily missed because there are no stones on ultrasound.
cards.q: A critically ill patient in intensive care develops fever and right upper quadrant pain, but ultrasound shows no gallstones. What is the likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Endoscopic sphincterotomy during ERCP, which cuts the sphincter of Oddi to allow the stone to pass or be removed. This treats the obstruction without open surgery. A stent is placed if the stone cannot be removed immediately.
cards.q: A patient has a stone stuck in the common bile duct causing jaundice. What is the endoscopic treatment?

cards.a: A HIDA scan, which shows whether the gallbladder fills and empties normally. In acalculous cholecystitis or biliary dyskinesia, the gallbladder does not fill. Ultrasound may be normal, so a functional test is needed when the diagnosis is suspected but stones are absent.
cards.q: A patient has suspected cholecystitis but ultrasound is normal. What is the next test?

cards.a: There is no specific drug treatment for hepatitis A — it is self-limiting and managed supportively with rest, fluids and avoiding alcohol. Vaccination prevents it, and post-exposure prophylaxis with vaccine or immunoglobulin is given to close contacts. Hepatitis A never becomes chronic.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with acute hepatitis A. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Start antiviral treatment with tenofovir or entecavir. Treatment is indicated when there is active viral replication with raised ALT and significant liver inflammation or fibrosis. Antivirals suppress the virus and reduce the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer, but they rarely cure it, so treatment is usually long term.
cards.q: A patient with chronic hepatitis B has a high viral load and raised ALT. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Interferon-free direct-acting antivirals, such as sofosbuvir with velpatasvir, which cure more than 95% of patients in 8 to 12 weeks. Hepatitis C is now a curable infection. Screen for hepatitis B before treatment, because hepatitis C treatment can reactivate hepatitis B.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C. What is the treatment and the expected outcome?

cards.a: Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B, advise complete alcohol abstinence, and give nutritional support with thiamine. Alcoholic hepatitis is driven by continued drinking, so abstinence is the single most effective treatment. Steroids are used only in severe cases with a high Maddrey discriminant function score.
cards.q: A patient with alcoholic hepatitis is admitted. What are the key management steps?

cards.a: The Maddrey discriminant function, calculated from bilirubin and prothrombin time. A score of 32 or more means severe alcoholic hepatitis with high short-term mortality, and prednisolone is considered. A low score is managed supportively without steroids.
cards.q: A patient with alcoholic hepatitis has a bilirubin of 12 mg/dL and a prolonged prothrombin time. What score decides whether steroids are given?

cards.a: Prednisolone, which suppresses the autoimmune attack on the liver. Autoimmune hepatitis is diagnosed by raised IgG, positive autoantibodies such as anti-smooth muscle antibody, and liver biopsy showing interface hepatitis. Azathioprine is added as a steroid-sparing agent for maintenance.
cards.q: A young woman has raised transaminases, positive anti-smooth muscle antibodies and raised IgG. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for decompensated Wilson's disease, because the underlying defect is a faulty copper transporter in the liver. Chelation with penicillamine or trientine removes copper in milder disease. Kayser-Fleischer rings in the cornea support the diagnosis.
cards.q: A young patient with Wilson's disease has decompensated cirrhosis despite chelation. What is the definitive treatment?

cards.a: Weight loss, exercise and control of diabetes and lipids. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is driven by metabolic syndrome, so lifestyle change is the main treatment. There is no approved drug that cures it. Vitamin E and pioglitazone are sometimes used in selected patients with steatohepatitis.
cards.q: A patient with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and diabetes asks about treatment. What is the mainstay?

cards.a: Check a hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-HBc before starting immunosuppression, and give antiviral prophylaxis if positive. Immunosuppression can reactivate hepatitis B and cause fulminant liver failure. This applies to chemotherapy, biologics and high-dose steroids.
cards.q: A patient needs chemotherapy and has a history of hepatitis B. What must be done first?

cards.a: Liver transplantation, because acute liver failure from paracetamol overdose is often fatal without it. Give N-acetylcysteine early, which replenishes glutathione and detoxifies the paracetamol metabolite. The King's College criteria help decide who needs transplant listing.
cards.q: A patient with a paracetamol overdose develops acute liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy. What is the definitive treatment?

cards.a: Start colorectal cancer screening at age 45 with a colonoscopy every 10 years, or a faecal immunochemical test yearly, until age 75. Screening finds polyps before they become cancer and finds cancer early when it is curable. People with a family history of colorectal cancer start earlier.
cards.q: A healthy 45-year-old asks about colorectal cancer screening. What do you advise?

cards.a: Remove the polyp during colonoscopy and send it for histology. Adenomatous polyps are precancerous, and removing them prevents cancer. The interval for the next colonoscopy depends on the number, size and type of polyps found.
cards.q: A polyp is found during a screening colonoscopy. What is the management?

cards.a: An iron deficiency anaemia in an older adult is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise, so do a colonoscopy. Right-sided colon cancers bleed slowly and silently, causing anaemia and weight loss without visible blood. Upper endoscopy is also done if colonoscopy is normal.
cards.q: An older man has iron deficiency anaemia and weight loss, with no visible blood in the stool. What is the next investigation?

cards.a: Refer urgently for surgery, usually a hemicolectomy with removal of the affected bowel and lymph nodes. Localised colon cancer is treated surgically, and chemotherapy is added if lymph nodes are involved. Delaying surgery allows the cancer to spread.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with localised colon cancer. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Familial adenomatous polyposis, caused by a mutation in the APC gene, which produces hundreds of polyps and almost certain colorectal cancer by age 40. Management is prophylactic colectomy and screening of family members. Genetic counselling is essential.
cards.q: A young patient has hundreds of colonic polyps and a family history of colon cancer in their 30s. What is the syndrome and management?

cards.a: Lynch syndrome, a hereditary mismatch repair defect that raises the risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer. These patients need colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years starting at age 20 to 25, and screening for other cancers. Family members should be offered genetic testing.
cards.q: A patient has colorectal cancer at age 35 with a strong family history of colon and endometrial cancer. What is the syndrome and what screening is needed?

cards.a: A faecal immunochemical test (FIT) every year, which detects blood in the stool and is more sensitive than the old guaiac test. A positive FIT needs a colonoscopy. FIT is a good option for patients who decline colonoscopy, but it does not find polyps as well as colonoscopy.
cards.q: A patient declines colonoscopy for colorectal cancer screening. What is the alternative test?

cards.a: Send a stool test for C. difficile toxin, stop the offending antibiotic if possible, and start oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Do not give anti-diarrhoeal drugs, because they trap the toxin in the colon. Test only patients with diarrhoea, because many people carry the bacteria without disease.
cards.q: A patient develops watery diarrhoea three days after starting clindamycin. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Fulminant C. difficile infection with toxic megacolon is a surgical emergency. Give high-dose oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole, and get an urgent surgical review for possible colectomy. The colon is at risk of perforation, and medical treatment alone may be too slow.
cards.q: A patient with C. difficile infection develops a distended abdomen, very high white cell count and a lactate of 4 mmol/L. What is the management?

cards.a: Faecal microbiota transplant, which restores normal gut bacteria and cures most cases. It is recommended after two or more recurrences. Antibiotics alone often fail because they do not restore the normal gut flora that keeps C. difficile in check.
cards.q: A patient has had three episodes of C. difficile infection, each treated with vancomycin. What is the next step?

cards.a: Admit for IV fluids and antibiotics, usually a fluoroquinolone or cephalosporin with metronidazole, and keep the patient nil by mouth. Uncomplicated diverticulitis can be treated as an outpatient with oral antibiotics, but perforation, abscess or sepsis needs admission. A CT scan confirms the diagnosis and shows complications.
cards.q: A patient has left lower quadrant pain, fever and a CT showing diverticulitis with a small abscess. What is the management?

cards.a: Sigmoid volvulus: the sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, causing obstruction. Treat with endoscopic detorsion using a flexible sigmoidoscope and a rectal tube, then plan elective sigmoid resection, because it recurs in most patients. Emergency surgery is needed if there is ischaemia or perforation.
cards.q: An older patient has a massively distended abdomen and an X-ray showing a 'coffee bean' sign. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Amoebic liver abscess, caused by Entamoeba histolytica spreading from the bowel to the liver. Treat with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin to clear bowel cysts. Drainage is only needed for a large abscess or one at risk of rupture.
cards.q: A traveller returns from an endemic area with fever, right upper quadrant pain and a liver abscess on imaging. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Start oral rehydration solution and replace fluids and electrolytes, and give antibiotics such as azithromycin if there is dysentery with blood or fever. Most traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting, so antibiotics are not needed for mild watery diarrhoea. Loperamide can be used for mild cases but not if there is blood or fever.
cards.q: A traveller has watery diarrhoea after eating street food abroad. What is the management?

cards.a: A strict gluten-free diet for life, which allows the small bowel to heal and reverses malabsorption. Diagnosis is confirmed by positive tissue transglutaminase antibodies and a duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, taken while still eating gluten. Even small amounts of gluten damage the bowel.
cards.q: A patient has diarrhoea, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia, with positive tissue transglutaminase antibodies. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Irritable bowel syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion, so first exclude coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease and thyroid disease, and check for alarm features such as weight loss, blood in the stool or a family history of cancer. If red flags are absent, manage with dietary advice, a low-FODMAP diet and antispasmodics. IBS does not cause weight loss, fever or blood.
cards.q: A young patient has cramping abdominal pain relieved by passing stool, with alternating diarrhoea and constipation. What must be excluded before diagnosing IBS?

cards.a: Urgent CT angiography of the abdomen to confirm the diagnosis and look for bowel ischaemia. Mesenteric ischaemia is a surgical emergency because the bowel dies quickly without blood flow. Atrial fibrillation is the commonest cause, throwing an embolus to the superior mesenteric artery.
cards.q: An older patient with atrial fibrillation has severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination findings, with a raised lactate. What is the next test?

cards.a: Stop the NSAID or aspirin, give a PPI, and consider endoscopic therapy if bleeding continues. Dieulafoy lesions, angiodysplasia and NSAID ulcers are common causes in older adults. A CT angiogram or capsule endoscopy is used if endoscopy cannot find the source.
cards.q: An older patient on NSAIDs has melaena but upper endoscopy is normal. What is the next step?

cards.a: The superior mesenteric artery, usually from an embolus in atrial fibrillation or thrombosis on atherosclerosis. Treatment is urgent revascularisation, often with embolectomy or endovascular stenting, plus anticoagulation. Delayed treatment leads to bowel infarction and death.
cards.q: A patient with acute mesenteric ischaemia needs surgery. Which artery is most commonly affected and what is the treatment?

cards.a: A nasogastric tube for decompression, IV fluids, and nil by mouth, with surgery if there is ischaemia, perforation or the obstruction does not resolve. Adhesions from previous surgery are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction. A contrast CT confirms the diagnosis and shows complications.
cards.q: A patient with previous abdominal surgery has vomiting, distension and no flatus. What is the first management step?

cards.a: A strangulated hernia, where the blood supply to the trapped bowel is cut off. This is a surgical emergency — resuscitate and operate urgently, because the bowel will infarct within hours. An incarcerated hernia that is not strangulated can sometimes be reduced, but a strangulated one must not be forced back.
cards.q: A patient has a painful, tender inguinal hernia that cannot be reduced, with vomiting and fever. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Appendicectomy, usually laparoscopically, within 24 hours. Appendicitis is diagnosed clinically with migratory right lower quadrant pain, fever and a raised white cell count, confirmed by CT or ultrasound. Antibiotics alone can treat uncomplicated appendicitis but have a high recurrence rate, so surgery remains standard.
cards.q: A patient has migratory abdominal pain settling in the right lower quadrant, with fever and a raised white cell count. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-). Normal is 8-12 mEq/L. Example: Na 140, Cl 100, HCO3 24 gives 140 - 124 = 16, which is high. A high anion gap means metabolic acidosis from acids like lactate, ketones (DKA), renal failure or toxins.
cards.q: What is the anion gap formula?

cards.a: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3- + 8, plus or minus 2. It is used in metabolic acidosis to check if the lungs are compensating correctly. Example: HCO3- 12 gives expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26 mmHg. If the actual PaCO2 is much higher, there is also a respiratory acidosis.
cards.q: What is Winter's formula, and what is it used for?

cards.a: pH = 6.1 + log [ HCO3- / (0.03 x PaCO2) ]. HCO3- is bicarbonate, PaCO2 is carbon dioxide pressure. If HCO3- falls, pH falls (metabolic acidosis). If PaCO2 rises, pH falls (respiratory acidosis). Normal pH is 7.35-7.45.
cards.q: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for blood pH?

cards.a: FeNa = fractional excretion of sodium. FeNa below 1% means pre-renal AKI — the kidneys are holding on to sodium because blood flow is low (dehydration, heart failure). FeNa above 2% means ATN — the tubules are damaged and cannot reabsorb sodium. FeNa is not reliable if the patient is on diuretics.
cards.q: How does FeNa separate pre-renal AKI from acute tubular necrosis (ATN)?

cards.a: 1. Calcium gluconate IV — protects the heart, does not lower potassium. 2. Insulin + glucose IV — moves potassium into cells. 3. Salbutamol nebuliser and sodium bicarbonate — also shift potassium in. 4. Dialysis if severe or not responding. Always do an ECG first — look for peaked T waves and wide QRS.
cards.q: What is the emergency treatment for high potassium (hyperkalaemia)?

cards.a: No faster than 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours (even slower, 4-6, if high risk). Correcting too fast can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome — permanent brain damage. If the patient has seizures from very low sodium, correct faster at first, then slow down.
cards.q: How fast can you safely correct low sodium (hyponatraemia)?

cards.a: Stage 1: GFR 90 or more, with kidney damage. Stage 2: 60-89. Stage 3a: 45-59, 3b: 30-44. Stage 4: 15-29. Stage 5: below 15, or on dialysis — kidney failure. GFR is measured in mL/min/1.73 m2. Lower GFR means worse kidney function.
cards.q: What are the stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD) by GFR?

cards.a: Nephrotic: heavy protein in urine (more than 3.5 g per day), low albumin, swelling (oedema), high cholesterol, frothy urine. Nephritic: blood in urine (red cell casts), high blood pressure, raised creatinine, less protein. Nephrotic loses protein, nephritic is inflamed and bleeds.
cards.q: How do you tell nephrotic from nephritic syndrome?

cards.a: Osmolality = 2 x Na+ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8. All in mg/dL for glucose and BUN, Na+ in mEq/L. Normal is 275-295 mOsm/kg. Example: Na 140, glucose 180, BUN 14 gives 280 + 10 + 5 = 295. A high osmolality with low sodium suggests pseudohyponatraemia or added osmoles like mannitol.
cards.q: What is the formula for serum osmolality?

cards.a: Corrected calcium = measured calcium + 0.8 x (4.0 - albumin). Albumin in g/dL, calcium in mg/dL. Example: calcium 8.0, albumin 2.0 gives 8.0 + 0.8 x 2 = 9.6 mg/dL — actually normal. Use this because calcium binds to albumin, so low albumin makes total calcium look falsely low.
cards.q: What is the corrected calcium formula?

cards.a: Give intravenous isotonic fluids, such as normal saline, and stop any drugs that harm the kidneys, like NSAIDs. Dehydration reduces blood flow to the kidneys, so restoring volume restores perfusion and often reverses the injury before permanent damage sets in. Reassess urine output and creatinine after fluids.
cards.q: A patient with acute kidney injury (AKI) from dehydration has a creatinine of 2.0 and very low urine output. What is the first step in management?

cards.a: Check for obstruction with a bladder scan or renal ultrasound, and assess whether they need vasopressors to support blood pressure. Fluids only help if the problem is low volume; obstruction or persistent low blood pressure needs a different fix, and ongoing hypotension will keep damaging the kidneys.
cards.q: A patient with AKI remains hypotensive and oliguric after 2 litres of intravenous fluids. What should you check next?

cards.a: NSAIDs block prostaglandins that keep the kidney's blood vessels open, so kidney perfusion falls, especially when heart failure already limits flow. Stop the NSAID and use paracetamol instead. Kidney function usually recovers once the drug is removed, because the injury is from reduced flow, not structural damage.
cards.q: An elderly patient with heart failure develops AKI a week after starting ibuprofen. What is the most likely mechanism, and what should you do?

cards.a: Continue the ACE inhibitor and recheck bloods in a week. A rise in creatinine of up to 30% is expected because ACE inhibitors lower pressure inside the glomerulus, which is part of how they protect the kidney. Stop the drug only if creatinine rises more than 30%, potassium goes above 5.5, or the patient becomes symptomatic.
cards.q: A patient starts an ACE inhibitor and their creatinine rises by 20% with potassium of 5.0. What is the next step?

cards.a: Supportive care: restore blood pressure and volume, stop nephrotoxic drugs, and wait for the tubules to recover over days to weeks. There is no drug that heals ATN directly. Diuretics do not improve outcomes or speed recovery, even if they increase urine output, so do not give them to try to convert oliguria.
cards.q: A patient develops acute tubular necrosis (ATN) after a period of very low blood pressure in intensive care. What is the mainstay of treatment?

cards.a: Use the fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea). A FeUrea below 35% suggests pre-renal AKI, because the kidneys are still reabsorbing urea avidly when blood flow is low. FeNa is misleading on diuretics because the drug forces sodium into the urine, but urea handling is less affected.
cards.q: A patient on a diuretic has AKI and you need to tell pre-renal from ATN, but the fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) is unreliable on diuretics. What should you use instead?

cards.a: Acute tubular necrosis. Muddy brown granular casts are dead tubular cells shed into the urine after ischaemic or toxic injury to the tubules. It confirms structural tubular damage rather than simple low blood flow, so recovery takes days to weeks and management is supportive.
cards.q: A patient with AKI has muddy brown casts in the urine. What is the diagnosis, and what does it mean?

cards.a: Acute interstitial nephritis, an allergic reaction in the kidney. Stop the penicillin immediately, because continued exposure worsens the inflammation.
