cards.a: 21-hydroxylase deficiency — the adrenal glands cannot make cortisol, so ACTH rises and drives androgen production. Girls may be virilised at birth; salt-wasting forms lose sodium and become hypotensive. Treat with hydrocortisone (and fludrocortisone in salt-wasters) and monitor growth.
cards.q: A newborn girl has ambiguous genitalia, low sodium, high potassium and low cortisol. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome — adrenal haemorrhage from meningococcal sepsis. It presents as septic shock with a purpuric rash. Give antibiotics immediately, IV fluids, and hydrocortisone for the adrenal failure — this is a resuscitation emergency, not a diagnostic puzzle.
cards.q: A patient with meningococcal sepsis develops a purpuric rash, shock and low cortisol. What is the syndrome and the management?

cards.a: Give IV isotonic fluids first — usually 2 to 3 litres in the first 24 hours — then a bisphosphonate such as zoledronate. Fluids lower calcium by diluting it and increasing urinary excretion. Calcitonin works within hours but only briefly, so it bridges until the bisphosphonate takes effect in 2 to 4 days.
cards.q: A patient has confusion and a calcium of 14 mg/dL. What is the first treatment, and what do you give next?

cards.a: Stop thiazide diuretics and lithium, both of which raise calcium, and give IV fluids. Check PTH: high PTH points to hyperparathyroidism, low PTH with high calcium points to cancer (PTH-related peptide) or other causes. Treating the calcium first protects the kidneys while you find the cause.
cards.q: A patient on a thiazide diuretic has a calcium of 12 mg/dL. What should you stop first and what test finds the cause?

cards.a: Surgery (parathyroidectomy) is indicated if the patient is symptomatic, calcium is more than 1 mg/dL above normal, there is kidney involvement (stones or reduced function), osteoporosis, or the patient is under 50. Asymptomatic older patients with mild disease can be monitored instead.
cards.q: A patient has primary hyperparathyroidism with kidney stones and a calcium of 12 mg/dL. Should they have surgery?

cards.a: Give IV calcium gluconate — it stabilises the heart and treats the symptoms. Look for Chvostek sign (facial twitch on tapping the cheek) and Trousseau sign (hand spasm with a blood pressure cuff). Check magnesium too, because low magnesium prevents calcium from correcting.
cards.q: A patient after thyroid surgery has tingling around the mouth, muscle cramps and a calcium of 7.0 mg/dL. What is the treatment and what signs support the diagnosis?

cards.a: Hypoparathyroidism from parathyroid gland injury or removal during surgery, or hungry bone syndrome where bones rapidly take up calcium after the overactive parathyroid is removed. Give calcium and vitamin D (calcitriol), monitor calcium closely, and check magnesium.
cards.q: A patient develops low calcium two days after thyroidectomy. What is the most likely cause and how do you treat it?

cards.a: Correct magnesium first. Low magnesium impairs PTH release and makes the kidneys waste potassium and calcium, so potassium and calcium will not correct until magnesium is replaced. Give IV magnesium sulfate, then recheck potassium and calcium.
cards.q: A patient has low potassium and low calcium that do not improve despite replacement. What should you check and correct first?

cards.a: Replace vitamin D (cholecalciferol) and recheck calcium, phosphate and PTH. Vitamin D deficiency causes low calcium, raised PTH and bone pain, and is a common cause of a high PTH with normal calcium. Treat the deficiency before considering parathyroid surgery.
cards.q: A patient has a high PTH, a normal calcium and low vitamin D. What should you do before considering parathyroid surgery?

cards.a: Order a DEXA scan in women aged 65 and over, and in younger postmenopausal women with risk factors (steroids, low weight, prior fracture). Start a bisphosphonate such as alendronate as first-line treatment, plus calcium and vitamin D if deficient. Also review fall risk and stop smoking.
cards.q: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has a wrist fracture after a minor fall. What test and treatment are indicated?

cards.a: Take it first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, stay upright for 30 minutes, and do not eat or take other medicines during that time. This prevents oesophagitis and ensures absorption. Check dental health first — bisphosphonates rarely cause jaw bone death, especially after dental extraction.
cards.q: How should a patient take oral alendronate, and what should you check before starting it?

cards.a: Do not stop denosumab abruptly — rebound bone loss causes multiple vertebral fractures within months. If denosumab must be stopped, switch to a bisphosphonate to protect the bone. Denosumab is an injection given every 6 months and is an alternative when bisphosphonates are not tolerated.
cards.q: A patient on denosumab for osteoporosis wants to stop treatment. What is the danger and what should you do instead?

cards.a: Alendronate or another bisphosphonate. Paget disease of bone causes a raised alkaline phosphatase with bone pain and deformity, from disorganised bone turnover. Bisphosphonates slow the abnormal bone breakdown and relieve pain.
cards.q: A patient has bone pain, an enlarged skull and a very high alkaline phosphatase. What is the diagnosis and the treatment?

cards.a: Give IV fluids and a bisphosphonate (zoledronate). Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is usually driven by PTH-related peptide from the tumour. Treat the calcium urgently while arranging cancer treatment — the calcium itself can cause confusion, kidney failure and arrhythmia.
cards.q: A patient with lung cancer has a calcium of 13.5 mg/dL and is confused. What is the cause and the treatment?

cards.a: Give hypertonic (3%) saline, slowly and carefully, with frequent sodium checks. Severe symptoms (seizures, coma) mean the brain is swelling, and hypertonic saline is the only treatment that raises sodium fast enough. Admit to ICU and monitor the rate of correction.
cards.q: A patient has a sodium of 115 mmol/L with seizures. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Correct sodium by no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours (slower in chronic hyponatraemia). Correcting too fast causes osmotic demyelination syndrome — permanent brain damage with quadriparesis and locked-in syndrome. Slow correction is safer than fast correction except in seizures.
cards.q: How fast may you correct hyponatraemia, and what happens if you correct it too fast?

cards.a: Fluid restriction is first-line for SIADH — limit water intake and treat the cause (drugs, pneumonia, brain injury). For severe symptomatic hyponatraemia, give hypertonic saline. Salt tablets and loop diuretics can help; tolvaptan blocks ADH and is used when fluid restriction fails.
cards.q: A patient with SIADH has a sodium of 128 mmol/L and is clinically euvolaemic. What is the first-line treatment?

cards.a: Do NOT give IV fluids — the patient is euvolaemic, not dehydrated. SIADH is treated by restricting water, not giving it. Giving isotonic fluids worsens the hyponatraemia, because the kidneys excrete the salt and keep the water.
cards.q: A patient with SIADH and hyponatraemia is euvolaemic. Why must you not give them IV normal saline?

cards.a: Central diabetes insipidus: give desmopressin (an ADH analogue). Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: the kidneys ignore ADH, so desmopressin does not work — use a thiazide diuretic with a low-salt diet, which paradoxically reduces urine output, and stop the cause such as lithium.
cards.q: How does treatment differ between central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

cards.a: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — lithium damages the kidney's ability to respond to ADH. Stop lithium if possible (with psychiatry advice), encourage fluids, and use a thiazide diuretic with a low-salt diet. Monitor lithium levels and kidney function.
cards.q: A patient on long-term lithium is passing large volumes of dilute urine and is very thirsty. What is the diagnosis and the management?

cards.a: Replace free water slowly — correct sodium by no more than 10 to 12 mmol/L per day — using oral water or IV dextrose 5% (which becomes free water). Calculate the water deficit from body weight and sodium. Rapid correction of hypernatraemia causes cerebral oedema.
cards.q: A patient has a sodium of 160 mmol/L from dehydration. How do you correct it and how fast?

cards.a: Use the water deprivation test: in psychogenic polydipsia the kidneys concentrate urine once water is withheld; in central DI they cannot, but urine concentrates after desmopressin; in nephrogenic DI urine stays dilute even after desmopressin. This test distinguishes the three causes of large-volume dilute urine.
cards.q: How do you distinguish psychogenic polydipsia from central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

cards.a: Beer potomania — drinking large volumes of beer with almost no salt or protein leaves the kidneys unable to excrete free water, so sodium falls. Treat by restricting fluid and giving salt and protein; correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
cards.q: A patient who drinks large amounts of beer daily has a sodium of 122 mmol/L. What is the cause and the management?

cards.a: Give isotonic saline — this is true volume depletion, and the body is retaining water because ADH is appropriately high. Replacing the volume switches off ADH and the sodium corrects itself. This is the opposite of SIADH, where the patient is euvolaemic and fluids make things worse.
cards.q: A patient with vomiting and diarrhoea has a sodium of 128 mmol/L and is clinically dry. What is the cause and the treatment?

cards.a: A dopamine agonist — cabergoline is first-line. It shrinks the prolactinoma and normalises prolactin, restoring periods and fertility. Surgery is reserved for tumours that do not respond or cause visual loss. Do not operate first on a prolactinoma that would shrink with a tablet.
cards.q: A woman has a prolactinoma, raised prolactin, amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. What is the first-line treatment — surgery or medicine?

cards.a: Check IGF-1 — it is the screening test for acromegaly (excess growth hormone). Confirm with an oral glucose tolerance test (growth hormone should suppress and does not). Treatment is transsphenoidal surgery first, with octreotide (a somatostatin analogue) if surgery does not cure it.
cards.q: A patient has enlarged hands, jaw and tongue, with headaches and visual field loss. What test screens for acromegaly and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Replace cortisol FIRST, then thyroid hormone. Giving thyroid hormone before cortisol increases cortisol clearance and can precipitate an adrenal crisis in a patient with both deficiencies. This order applies whenever both axes are low.
cards.q: A patient with hypopituitarism has low cortisol and low thyroid hormone. Which hormone do you replace first and why?

cards.a: Sheehan syndrome — pituitary necrosis after severe postpartum haemorrhage and low blood pressure. The pituitary loses its blood supply, causing failure to lactate and later hypopituitarism. Replace the missing hormones (cortisol first, then thyroid, then sex hormones).
cards.q: A woman fails to lactate after a delivery complicated by severe haemorrhage and later develops fatigue and low blood pressure. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Pituitary apoplexy — sudden bleeding into a pituitary tumour, causing severe headache, visual loss and low cortisol. Give IV hydrocortisone immediately, get urgent MRI and neurosurgical review — decompression surgery is often needed to save vision.
cards.q: A patient with a known pituitary tumour develops sudden severe headache, visual loss and hypotension. What is the diagnosis and the immediate management?

cards.a: Watch for diabetes insipidus in the first days after pituitary surgery — large volumes of dilute urine with rising sodium. Treat with desmopressin and monitor fluids and sodium closely. It may be temporary, permanent, or follow a triphasic pattern, so daily sodium checks are essential.
cards.q: After transsphenoidal pituitary surgery, a patient passes 6 litres of dilute urine in a day with a rising sodium. What is the diagnosis and the management?

cards.a: A non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm — it causes bitemporal hemianopia (loss of the outer visual fields). Refer urgently for transsphenoidal surgery to decompress the optic chiasm; medical treatment cannot fix the compression.
cards.q: A patient has headaches and loss of the outer visual fields on both sides. What is the likely cause and the treatment?

cards.a: MEN 1 — parathyroid hyperplasia (high calcium), pituitary tumours (often prolactinoma) and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (such as gastrinoma or insulinoma). Screen family members, because it is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
cards.q: A patient has hyperparathyroidism, a prolactinoma and a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour. What syndrome is this and what should you do for the family?

cards.a: MEN 2A (medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism) and MEN 2B (medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas). Always screen for and remove the phaeochromocytoma BEFORE thyroid surgery, or the operation can trigger a hypertensive crisis.
cards.q: A patient with medullary thyroid cancer is found to have MEN 2. What other tumour must be excluded before thyroid surgery and why?

cards.a: Carcinoid syndrome — flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze and right-sided heart valve disease from serotonin released by a neuroendocrine tumour (usually with liver metastases). Check urinary 5-HIAA and treat with octreotide (a somatostatin analogue), which controls the flushing and diarrhoea.
cards.q: A patient with a small bowel neuroendocrine tumour has flushing, watery diarrhoea and wheeze. What is the syndrome, what test confirms it, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Screen for and treat the complications: diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis (DEXA scan), muscle weakness, infections and depression. Cushing syndrome damages the whole body, so controlling cortisol alone is not enough — blood pressure, glucose and bone health must be managed in parallel while awaiting definitive surgery.
cards.q: A patient with Cushing syndrome is awaiting pituitary surgery. What complications should you screen for and manage in the meantime?

cards.a: Screen at 24 to 28 weeks with an oral glucose tolerance test. Treat with diet and exercise first, then insulin if targets are not met — insulin does not cross the placenta. After delivery, recheck glucose, because gestational diabetes predicts future type 2 diabetes.
cards.q: When and how do you screen for gestational diabetes, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Check morning testosterone twice (low on both), plus LH, FSH and prolactin to find the cause. Testosterone replacement can help symptoms but is contraindicated in prostate cancer, breast cancer and untreated severe sleep apnoea, and it raises haematocrit — so check PSA and haematocrit before and during treatment.
cards.q: A man has fatigue, low libido and a low morning testosterone. How do you confirm hypogonadism and when must you not give testosterone?

cards.a: Low ferritin is the most reliable test — ferritin below 30 ng/mL confirms iron deficiency in most patients. Also: low haemoglobin, low MCV (small red cells), low iron, high TIBC. Causes: blood loss (especially GI in adults), poor diet, malabsorption. Treat the cause plus oral iron.
cards.q: What lab finding confirms iron deficiency anaemia?

cards.a: B12 deficiency: large red cells (high MCV), low B12, neurological symptoms — numbness, tingling, loss of vibration sense, and dorsal column problems. Folate deficiency: same blood picture, but NO neurological symptoms. Treat B12 with B12 injections or high-dose oral B12; treat folate with folate — but check B12 first, because giving folate alone can worsen B12 nerve damage.
cards.q: How do you tell B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?

cards.a: HbS is abnormal haemoglobin that sickles red cells when oxygen is low. Crises: painful vaso-occlusive crisis, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19). Hydroxyurea increases fetal haemoglobin and reduces crises. Patients need vaccinations and penicillin prophylaxis in childhood.
cards.q: What is sickle cell disease, and what does hydroxyurea do?

cards.a: AML is usually in adults, with Auer rods in the blood/bone marrow, and blasts in the blood. ALL is usually in children, with lymphoblasts, and often presents with bone pain and fever. Both present with anaemia, low platelets, low white cells, and infections from bone marrow failure.
cards.q: How do you tell AML from ALL?

cards.a: Hodgkin lymphoma: Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy, often young adults, painless lymph nodes, B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), spreads in a predictable pattern. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: more varied, often extranodal, no Reed-Sternberg cells. Both need biopsy, not just imaging.
cards.q: What is the key cell in Hodgkin lymphoma?

cards.a: Prolonged PT and aPTT, low platelets, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, and schistocytes (fragmented red cells) on the blood film. It is caused by widespread clotting and bleeding at the same time, often from sepsis, trauma or obstetric catastrophe. Treat the cause, give platelets, plasma and cryoprecipitate as needed.
cards.q: What labs are seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)?

cards.a: TTP: fever, low platelets, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, neurological symptoms, and kidney failure — the pentad. It is due to low ADAMTS13, which normally cuts von Willebrand factor. Treatment is urgent plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) plus steroids. Do NOT give platelets unless there is life-threatening bleeding — they worsen clotting.
cards.q: What is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and what is the treatment?

cards.a: CRAB: C = hyperCalcaemia, R = Renal failure, A = Anaemia, B = Bone lesions (lytic, punched-out lesions on X-ray). It is a plasma cell cancer with monoclonal protein (M-spike) on electrophoresis and Bence Jones protein in urine. Back pain and kidney failure are common presentations.
cards.q: What is the CRAB acronym in multiple myeloma?

cards.a: Warfarin is monitored by INR (target usually 2-3), and reversed with vitamin K or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Heparin is monitored by aPTT, reversed with protamine. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) do not need routine monitoring; apixaban is reversed with andexanet alfa, dabigatran with idarucizumab.
cards.q: How do you monitor and reverse warfarin, heparin and DOACs?

cards.a: Stop the transfusion immediately, check the patient, and send blood samples. Fever alone may be a febrile reaction; fever + low blood pressure + flank pain + dark urine suggests acute haemolytic reaction from ABO mismatch — this is an emergency. TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) causes breathlessness and low oxygen within 6 hours of transfusion.
cards.q: What do you do first in a transfusion reaction, and what is TRALI?

cards.a: Check ferritin and the red cell count. Iron deficiency has a low ferritin and a low red cell count; thalassaemia trait has a normal or high ferritin with a high red cell count and a very low MCV. Getting this right matters because thalassaemia trait does not need iron — giving iron will not help and can cause iron overload.
cards.q: A patient has a low MCV anaemia. How do you tell iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait?

cards.a: Look for gastrointestinal blood loss with upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. In adults, iron deficiency usually means chronic blood loss, and colon cancer is the cause you must not miss. Iron tablets treat the anaemia but not the source of the bleeding.
cards.q: An adult man or a postmenopausal woman is found to have iron deficiency anaemia. What is the next step after starting iron?

cards.a: First check adherence and how they take it — iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach, and tea, coffee, calcium and antacids block absorption. If they are taking it correctly and still not responding, or they cannot tolerate it, switch to intravenous iron, which bypasses the gut.
cards.q: A patient on oral iron for iron deficiency anaemia has no improvement after a month. What should you check, and what is the next step?

cards.a: In anaemia of chronic disease, ferritin is normal or high because ferritin rises with inflammation, while iron and transferrin saturation are low and TIBC is low or normal. In true iron deficiency, ferritin is low and TIBC is high. Treat the underlying disease in anaemia of chronic disease; iron only helps if there is true iron deficiency as well.
cards.q: How do you tell anaemia of chronic disease from iron deficiency anaemia?

cards.a: Check B12 and folate levels, a reticulocyte count, thyroid function, liver function and a medication review — alcohol, methotrexate, hydroxyurea and zidovudine all cause macrocytosis. A high reticulocyte count points to haemolysis or blood loss instead of a vitamin deficiency.
cards.q: A patient has a macrocytic anaemia with a high MCV. What is the workup?

cards.a: Treat immediately — do not wait for confirmatory test results. Nerve damage from B12 deficiency can become permanent if treatment is delayed, even though the anaemia itself recovers. Give B12 by injection or high-dose oral B12, and recheck the level later.
cards.q: A patient with B12 deficiency has numbness, tingling and loss of vibration sense. What is the urgency of treatment?

cards.a: It is autoimmune destruction of the stomach cells that make intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed — anti-intrinsic factor antibodies confirm it. Treatment is lifelong B12 replacement, because the stomach will never make intrinsic factor again. These patients also need surveillance for stomach cancer.
cards.q: What is pernicious anaemia, and how is it treated long term?

cards.a: High LDH, low haptoglobin, high indirect bilirubin and a high reticulocyte count. The blood film may show spherocytes or schistocytes. Then order a direct Coombs test: a positive Coombs points to immune haemolysis, while a negative one points to a non-immune cause such as a mechanical valve or G6PD deficiency.
cards.q: What labs suggest haemolysis as the cause of anaemia?

cards.a: Corticosteroids such as prednisolone. They suppress the immune attack on the red cells. Transfusion is only for severe symptomatic anaemia, because transfused red cells are destroyed just as fast. If steroids fail, rituximab or splenectomy is the next step.
cards.q: A patient has warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia with a positive Coombs test. What is the first-line treatment?

cards.a: Cold agglutinin disease is caused by IgM antibodies that attack red cells in the cold, often after Mycoplasma or EBV infection, or with lymphoma. Steroids work poorly here. The main treatment is keeping the patient warm and treating the underlying cause, with rituximab for persistent cases.
cards.q: How is cold agglutinin disease different from warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, and how is it treated?

cards.a: G6PD deficiency — the red cells cannot handle oxidative stress, so they break down, and the blood film shows Heinz bodies and bite cells. Avoid the triggers: fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides and nitrofurantoin. The haemolysis is usually self-limited once the trigger is removed.
cards.q: A patient develops sudden haemolysis after eating fava beans or taking an oxidant drug. What is the diagnosis and what must you avoid?

cards.a: Do a bone marrow biopsy: aplastic anaemia shows an empty, hypocellular marrow. In a young patient with a matched sibling donor, bone marrow transplant is curative. In older patients or those without a donor, treatment is antithymocyte globulin (ATG) plus ciclosporin to suppress the immune attack on the marrow.
cards.q: A patient has pancytopenia — low red cells, white cells and platelets. What is the next step, and how is aplastic anaemia treated?

cards.a: Regular red cell transfusions to keep haemoglobin high enough for growth and to suppress the marrow, plus iron chelation therapy such as deferasirox, because every transfusion adds iron that damages the heart and liver. Monitor ferritin and liver and heart iron, and give folic acid.
cards.q: How is beta-thalassaemia major managed long term?

cards.a: Check iron studies first — iron deficiency is common and must be corrected before erythropoietin will work. If iron is adequate and the anaemia is from low erythropoietin production by the failing kidneys, give an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent. Do not aim for a normal haemoglobin, because overcorrection raises the risk of clots and stroke.
cards.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease has anaemia. What do you check first, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Use a restrictive threshold: transfuse when haemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL in a stable patient, or below 8 g/dL if they have heart disease or ongoing ischaemia. Transfusing at higher levels does not improve outcomes and adds the risks of transfusion reactions, lung injury and volume overload.
cards.q: When should you transfuse red blood cells in a stable hospitalised patient?

cards.a: A high reticulocyte count means the marrow is working hard to replace lost or destroyed red cells — think haemolysis or acute bleeding. A low reticulocyte count means the marrow is failing — think iron, B12 or folate deficiency, aplastic anaemia, or marrow infiltration by cancer.
cards.q: How does the reticulocyte count help you work out the cause of anaemia?

cards.a: Lead poisoning. Lead blocks haem synthesis, causing a microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling, and also causes abdominal pain, constipation and neurological damage in children. Remove the source of lead exposure and treat with chelation if the lead level is high.
cards.q: A child has anaemia with basophilic stippling on the blood film, abdominal pain and developmental delay. What is the cause?

cards.a: It is anaemia where iron is trapped in the mitochondria of red cell precursors, forming ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow examination. Causes include alcohol, isoniazid, lead and myelodysplastic syndrome. Treat by removing the cause, and give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) because it is a cofactor in haem synthesis.
cards.q: What is sideroblastic anaemia, and what causes it?

cards.a: Give oxygen if saturations are low, intravenous fluids, strong pain relief, and encourage incentive spirometry to prevent chest complications. Also check for infection, dehydration or another trigger. Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of crises long term by raising fetal haemoglobin.
cards.q: A patient with sickle cell disease has severe bone pain in a vaso-occlusive crisis. What is the management?

cards.a: Acute chest syndrome — a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease. Treat with oxygen, antibiotics covering pneumonia, fluids and pain control, plus incentive spirometry. If it is severe, with falling oxygen or worsening anaemia, give a simple or exchange blood transfusion.
cards.q: A sickle cell patient develops fever, chest pain and a new infiltrate on chest X-ray. What is this and how is it treated?

cards.a: Splenic sequestration crisis — blood is trapped in the spleen, so haemoglobin falls fast and the child goes into shock. Give an urgent red cell transfusion, which usually shrinks the spleen and restores the blood count. After repeated episodes, splenectomy is considered.
cards.q: A child with sickle cell disease suddenly becomes pale and shocked with a rapidly enlarging spleen. What has happened and what do you do?

cards.a: Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 infection, which temporarily shuts down red cell production in the marrow. The reticulocyte count is near zero, which is the clue. Treat with a red cell transfusion and supportive care until the marrow recovers.
cards.q: A sickle cell patient has a sudden fall in haemoglobin with almost no reticulocytes. What is the cause?

cards.a: Screen with transcranial Doppler ultrasound of the brain vessels; a high blood flow velocity predicts stroke risk. Children at high risk are put on a chronic transfusion programme to keep the sickle haemoglobin low. Hydroxyurea is an alternative for some children who cannot continue transfusions.
cards.q: How do you prevent stroke in a child with sickle cell disease?

cards.a: This is priapism — a urological emergency. Treat it within hours with hydration, pain relief and urgent urology involvement, because prolonged priapism causes permanent erectile damage. Do not dismiss it as a minor complaint.
cards.q: A man with sickle cell disease has a painful erection lasting more than 4 hours. What is the management?

cards.a: It is a diagnosis of exclusion: isolated low platelets with an otherwise normal blood count and blood film, and no other cause such as drugs, infection, liver disease or marrow disease. Antibody tests are not reliable. A bone marrow biopsy is only needed if there are other abnormal cells or the patient does not respond to treatment.
cards.q: How is immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) diagnosed?

cards.a: Treat if the platelet count is below 30,000, or if there is active bleeding, regardless of the count. First-line treatment is corticosteroids such as prednisone, with IV immunoglobulin added if bleeding is severe or a rapid rise is needed. A patient with platelets above 30,000 and no bleeding can simply be observed.
cards.q: When do you treat ITP, and what is the first-line treatment?

cards.a: Rituximab, thrombopoietin receptor agonists such as eltrombopag or romiplostim, or splenectomy. Splenectomy removes the main site where platelets are destroyed, but it is usually delayed because many patients respond to medical therapy and splenectomy carries a lifelong infection risk.
cards.q: A patient with ITP does not respond to steroids. What are the next options?

cards.a: Use the 4Ts score: Timing (5 to 10 days after heparin), Thrombocytopenia (platelet fall of more than 50 percent), Thrombosis (a new clot), and no oTher cause. A high score means HIT is likely — send a PF4 antibody test, but do not wait for the result to act.
cards.q: A patient on heparin develops a falling platelet count 5 to 10 days after starting it. How do you assess for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?

cards.a: Stop ALL heparin immediately, including heparin flushes and low-molecular-weight heparin, and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban. Do NOT transfuse platelets — it feeds the clotting — and do NOT start warfarin until the platelet count has recovered, because warfarin can worsen clotting in HIT.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with HIT and has a new clot. What is the immediate management?

cards.a: Both cause low platelets, but they behave oppositely: HIT causes clots because the antibodies activate platelets, while ITP causes bleeding because platelets are destroyed. HIT is treated by stopping heparin and anticoagulating; ITP is treated with steroids. Confusing the two is dangerous — giving heparin to HIT or platelets to HIT worsens the clotting.
cards.q: How do you tell HIT apart from ITP, and why does the difference matter?

cards.a: Transfuse platelets prophylactically when the count is below 10,000, below 50,000 before most surgery or invasive procedures, and below 100,000 before brain or eye surgery. Above these levels, transfusion is usually not needed unless there is active bleeding or platelet dysfunction.
cards.q: What are the platelet transfusion thresholds?

cards.a: Stop the drug. Common culprits include quinine, heparin, sulfonamides, vancomycin and some diuretics. The platelet count usually recovers within a week of stopping the drug. Do not start steroids — this is not ITP, and removing the cause is the treatment.
cards.q: A patient develops a sudden fall in platelets after starting a new drug, with no other cause found. What is the management?

cards.a: Use the Wells score to estimate risk, then a D-dimer if the risk is low, and a duplex ultrasound of the leg veins if the risk is high or the D-dimer is positive. Start anticoagulation as soon as DVT is suspected if there is no major bleeding risk — do not wait for the scan if the patient is high risk.
cards.q: A patient has a swollen, painful calf after a long flight. How do you work up suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?

cards.a: Risk-stratify: a massive PE causes low blood pressure and needs thrombolysis or embolectomy, because anticoagulation alone is too slow. A submassive PE has right heart strain on echo or raised troponin but normal blood pressure — these patients get anticoagulation and close monitoring, with thrombolysis only if they deteriorate.
cards.q: A patient with a pulmonary embolism is hypotensive. Is anticoagulation alone enough?

cards.a: Treat for at least 3 months. If the clot was provoked by a temporary cause such as surgery or immobility, 3 months is enough. If it was unprovoked, or there is a recurrent clot or ongoing risk such as active cancer, consider indefinite anticoagulation after weighing the bleeding risk.
cards.q: How long should anticoagulation continue after a first DVT or PE?

cards.a: Mechanical heart valves, moderate to severe mitral stenosis, pregnancy, severe kidney failure, and triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome. In these situations warfarin or heparin is used instead, because DOACs have not been shown to be safe or effective there.
cards.q: In which patients should you NOT use a DOAC for anticoagulation?

cards.a: Warfarin is teratogenic, especially in the first trimester, causing birth defects. Use low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) instead during pregnancy, because it does not cross the placenta. Warfarin is safe during breastfeeding, so it can be restarted after delivery.
cards.q: A pregnant patient needs anticoagulation. Which drug do you use, and which must you avoid?

cards.a: Low-molecular-weight heparin is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta, so it does not affect the baby. It is given by injection and monitored by anti-Xa levels if needed. Warfarin and DOACs are avoided in pregnancy.
cards.q: Why is low-molecular-weight heparin preferred over warfarin in pregnancy?

cards.a: Antiphospholipid syndrome causes recurrent clots or miscarriages with positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti-beta2-glycoprotein antibodies. Treatment is lifelong warfarin with an INR of 2 to 3. DOACs are not recommended for triple-positive patients because they have higher clot rates than warfarin in this group.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent clots and miscarriages with positive antiphospholipid antibodies. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Hold warfarin and recheck the INR. If the INR is above 10, give low-dose oral vitamin K. If there is no bleeding, do not give prothrombin complex concentrate — that is reserved for major bleeding. Also check for interacting drugs, alcohol use and liver disease, which all raise the INR.
cards.q: A patient on warfarin has an INR of 8 with no bleeding. What do you do?

cards.a: Give 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) plus intravenous vitamin K immediately. 4F-PCC replaces the clotting factors quickly, while vitamin K restarts the liver making them. Do not rely on fresh frozen plasma — it is slower and needs a large volume.
cards.q: A patient on warfarin has life-threatening bleeding. How do you reverse it?

cards.a: Give protamine sulfate, which binds and neutralises heparin. Protamine works well for unfractionated heparin but only partly reverses low-molecular-weight heparin. Watch for low blood pressure and allergic reactions during the infusion.
cards.q: A patient is bleeding from too much unfractionated heparin. What is the reversal agent?

cards.a: Idarucizumab — a specific antibody fragment that binds dabigatran and reverses it within minutes. It is the reversal agent of choice for life-threatening bleeding or emergency surgery in a patient on dabigatran.
cards.q: A patient on dabigatran has major bleeding. What is the specific reversal agent?

cards.a: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban, but it is expensive and not always available. 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is the practical alternative used in most hospitals for life-threatening bleeding on these drugs.
cards.q: A patient on apixaban has major bleeding. How do you reverse it?

cards.a: Give pharmacological prophylaxis — low-molecular-weight heparin or low-dose unfractionated heparin — to all medical and surgical inpatients who are at risk of clots and not bleeding. If the bleeding risk is high, use mechanical prophylaxis such as compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression until drugs are safe.
cards.q: How do you prevent VTE in a hospitalised patient?

cards.a: Use low-molecular-weight heparin or a DOAC such as apixaban or rivaroxaban. Warfarin is less convenient and interacts with chemotherapy and diet. Treat for at least 6 months, and longer while the cancer is active, because the clot risk stays high.
cards.q: A patient with active cancer develops a DVT. Which anticoagulant is preferred?

cards.a: Treat the underlying cause — that is the only thing that stops DIC. Give platelets, plasma and cryoprecipitate if there is bleeding and the labs are low. Heparin is only used in the rare situation where clotting dominates, such as a clot in a large vessel or purpura fulminans.
cards.q: What is the treatment of DIC?

cards.a: Both cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes and low platelets, but TTP is mainly neurological — confusion, seizures — and is due to very low ADAMTS13, while HUS is mainly renal failure and usually follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga-toxin E. coli. TTP needs urgent plasma exchange; HUS is mostly supportive care.
cards.q: How do you tell TTP from haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)?

cards.a: Supportive care with intravenous fluids and dialysis if needed. Do NOT give antibiotics or anti-diarrhoea drugs — they increase the risk of HUS by releasing more Shiga toxin from the bacteria. The kidney failure is usually temporary and most children recover.
cards.q: A child develops bloody diarrhoea from E. coli O157:H7 and then kidney failure with low platelets. How is this managed?

cards.a: Atypical HUS is caused by uncontrolled activation of the complement system, not by infection. It is treated with eculizumab, a drug that blocks complement, plus supportive care. Unlike typical HUS it often recurs and can cause permanent kidney failure without treatment.
cards.q: What causes atypical HUS, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Look for schistocytes on the blood film, a high LDH, a low haptoglobin and a negative Coombs test — that combination means microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. Then work out the cause: TTP, HUS, DIC, malignant hypertension or a mechanical heart valve. A positive Coombs would point to immune haemolysis instead.
cards.q: A patient has anaemia with fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the blood film. What is the workup?

cards.a: Refer urgently to haematology and do a bone marrow biopsy — AML is a medical emergency because the marrow is failing. Check for DIC, infections and bleeding first, and do not delay referral for more blood tests. Treatment is induction chemotherapy, sometimes with a bone marrow transplant.
cards.q: An adult has pancytopenia with blasts in the blood and Auer rods. What is the next step?

cards.a: Start all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) immediately — do not wait for genetic confirmation of the PML-RARA translocation. APL carries a very high risk of fatal bleeding from DIC, and ATRA makes the leukaemia cells mature and reduces that risk. Add arsenic trioxide as part of the treatment.
cards.q: A patient is suspected to have acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL). What treatment must not be delayed?

cards.a: Differentiation syndrome — the ATRA-treated leukaemia cells mature and cause fever, breathlessness, weight gain, low blood pressure and lung infiltrates. Give dexamethasone immediately, and hold ATRA if the syndrome is severe. Do not stop ATRA permanently for a mild case — steroids usually control it.
cards.q: A patient on ATRA for APL develops fever, breathlessness and weight gain. What is this and how is it treated?

cards.a: Give aggressive intravenous hydration and allopurinol before chemotherapy to prevent uric acid building up. In high-risk patients — a large tumour burden or already raised uric acid — use rasburicase instead, which breaks down uric acid directly. Also monitor potassium, phosphate and calcium closely.
cards.q: How do you prevent tumour lysis syndrome before starting chemotherapy for a bulky leukaemia or lymphoma?

cards.a: ALL is the most common cancer of childhood. It typically presents with fever, bone pain, pallor and easy bruising from marrow failure, with lymphoblasts in the blood. Treatment is multi-drug chemotherapy over 2 to 3 years, and the cure rate in children is high.
cards.q: What is the most common leukaemia in children, and how does it present?

cards.a: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is driven by the Philadelphia chromosome, which makes the BCR-ABL fusion protein. Treatment is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib, taken as a daily tablet. Monitor the BCR-ABL level to check the response — a deep molecular response means the treatment is working.
cards.q: What is the Philadelphia chromosome, and how is chronic myeloid leukaemia treated?

cards.a: Watch and wait. CLL is a slow-growing cancer of older adults, recognised by a high lymphocyte count with smudge cells on the blood film. If the patient has no symptoms, no bulky nodes and no cytopenias, treatment is not started — it does not improve survival to treat early.
cards.q: An older adult is found to have chronic lymphocytic leukaemia with no symptoms. Should you start treatment?

cards.a: Start treatment when there are B symptoms, progressive anaemia or low platelets, bulky lymph nodes or spleen, or a rapidly rising lymphocyte count. Treatment is usually a combination of chemotherapy and an antibody such as rituximab, or targeted drugs such as ibrutinib in high-risk disease.
cards.q: When should you start treatment in CLL?

cards.a: Leukostasis — the very high white cell count makes the blood thick, so it cannot flow through small vessels in the lungs and brain. Give hydroxyurea and leukapheresis to lower the white count fast, with hydration and tumour lysis prophylaxis. Do NOT transfuse red cells — it makes the blood even thicker and worsens the problem.
cards.q: A patient with leukaemia has a white cell count over 100,000 with breathlessness and confusion. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: An excisional biopsy of the whole lymph node. A fine-needle aspirate is not enough — lymphoma diagnosis needs the node architecture, which only a larger sample shows. Also send the node for flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry and cytogenetics.
cards.q: A patient has a painless, enlarged lymph node that does not go away. What biopsy should you do?

cards.a: ABVD chemotherapy — doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine. Bleomycin can cause lung fibrosis, so check lung function before and during treatment and avoid giving too much oxygen. Most patients with Hodgkin lymphoma are cured with this regimen.
cards.q: What is the standard treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma, and what toxicity must you monitor?

cards.a: B symptoms are fever above 38 degrees, drenching night sweats, and weight loss of more than 10 percent of body weight over 6 months. They matter for staging — a patient with B symptoms is stage B, not A — and they predict a worse prognosis.
cards.q: What are B symptoms in lymphoma, and why do they matter?

cards.a: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma — the most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Treatment is R-CHOP chemotherapy (rituximab plus cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone). It is aggressive but potentially curable, so treatment should start promptly.
cards.q: What is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Burkitt lymphoma — a very fast-growing B-cell lymphoma with a starry-sky appearance on biopsy and a c-myc gene translocation. It often presents as a jaw mass in children or abdominal disease in adults. Because the cells divide so fast, tumour lysis syndrome is a major risk and prophylaxis must be given before chemotherapy.
cards.q: What is Burkitt lymphoma, and what complication must you prevent before treatment?

cards.a: Watch and wait. Follicular lymphoma is an indolent, slow-growing lymphoma that is usually incurable but compatible with a long life. Treatment is only started when there are symptoms, bulky disease or cytopenias — treating early does not improve survival.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with follicular lymphoma and has no symptoms. What is the management?

cards.a: MGUS is a small monoclonal protein (M-spike under 3 g/dL) with fewer than 10 percent plasma cells in the marrow and NO end-organ damage. Myeloma has a larger M-spike or more plasma cells PLUS end-organ damage (CRAB). MGUS is monitored, not treated, because most patients never develop myeloma.
cards.q: How do you tell MGUS from multiple myeloma?

cards.a: Smouldering myeloma has a larger M-spike or more plasma cells than MGUS but still no end-organ damage. It is not treated yet, but it is monitored closely because the risk of progressing to myeloma is much higher than with MGUS.
cards.q: What is smouldering myeloma, and how is it managed?

cards.a: Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, a bone marrow biopsy, and imaging of the bones (skeletal survey or PET-CT) to look for lytic lesions. Also check calcium, kidney function and haemoglobin for the CRAB features. A tissue diagnosis is needed — the M-spike alone is not enough.
cards.q: What is the workup for suspected multiple myeloma?

cards.a: A triplet regimen of bortezomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone, followed by autologous stem cell transplant in eligible patients. Maintenance lenalidomide is then given long term. Treatment aims to control the disease and protect the kidneys and bones, not to cure it.
cards.q: What is the standard treatment for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma?

cards.a: Light chain cast nephropathy — the excess light chains form casts that block the kidney tubules. Give aggressive intravenous fluids, stop nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs, and avoid contrast dye. Starting myeloma treatment quickly to reduce the light chains is the key to saving the kidneys.
cards.q: A myeloma patient develops acute kidney failure. What is the cause and the management?

cards.a: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia is a lymphoma that makes large amounts of IgM, which thickens the blood and causes hyperviscosity — blurred vision, nosebleeds, headache and confusion. Urgent plasmapheresis removes the IgM and relieves the symptoms, while chemotherapy treats the underlying lymphoma.
cards.q: A patient with an IgM paraprotein has blurred vision, nosebleeds and confusion. What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?

cards.a: AL amyloidosis — misfolded light chains deposit in tissues, including the heart. It is diagnosed by Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Cardiac amyloid causes a thick heart wall on echo but low voltage on ECG, and it carries a poor prognosis.
cards.q: A patient with myeloma has a thick heart wall on echo but low voltage on ECG. What is the diagnosis and how is it confirmed?

cards.a: Polycythaemia vera — a JAK2 mutation drives overproduction of red cells, causing headache, itching after a hot shower, gout and clots. Treatment is regular phlebotomy to keep the haematocrit below 45 percent, plus low-dose aspirin. High-risk patients also get hydroxyurea to suppress the marrow.
cards.q: A patient has a high haemoglobin, itching after a hot shower, and a JAK2 mutation. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Essential thrombocythaemia — a JAK2 or CALR mutation causes the marrow to make too many platelets, raising the risk of clots and bleeding. Low-risk patients get low-dose aspirin alone; high-risk patients (older than 60, or with a previous clot) also get hydroxyurea to lower the platelet count.
cards.q: A patient has a persistently high platelet count with a JAK2 mutation and no other cause. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Primary myelofibrosis — the marrow becomes scarred and fibrotic, so blood is made in the spleen and liver instead. The blood film shows teardrop-shaped red cells and immature white cells, and the bone marrow biopsy is often a dry tap. The spleen becomes very large, and treatment is mainly supportive, with JAK inhibitors such as ruxolitinib for symptoms.
cards.q: A patient has a huge spleen, teardrop cells on the blood film, and a dry tap on bone marrow biopsy. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Myelodysplastic syndrome — the marrow makes abnormal, dysplastic blood cells in an older adult, causing cytopenias and a risk of transforming into AML. A bone marrow biopsy confirms it. Low-risk patients are managed supportively with transfusions; high-risk patients may get hypomethylating drugs or a transplant.
cards.q: An older adult has unexplained cytopenias with dysplastic cells on the blood film. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Iron overload from repeated transfusions damages the heart, liver and endocrine glands. Monitor ferritin and liver and heart iron, and start iron chelation therapy such as deferasirox or deferoxamine when the iron burden is high. Chelation removes the excess iron and prevents organ damage.
cards.q: A patient receiving regular blood transfusions develops a rising ferritin. What is the risk and the treatment?

cards.a: Febrile neutropenia is a single temperature of 38.3 degrees or higher, or 38.0 degrees lasting over an hour, in a patient with an absolute neutrophil count below 500. It is an emergency in a cancer patient because they have no white cells to fight infection.
cards.q: What is the definition of febrile neutropenia?

cards.a: Take blood cultures and start broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour — do not wait for the culture results. Cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam is the usual first choice. Also examine the patient carefully for a source: lungs, urine, skin, mouth and central line.
cards.q: A chemotherapy patient with an ANC of 300 develops a fever of 38.5 degrees. What is the immediate management?

cards.a: Add vancomycin when there is a suspected catheter infection, skin or soft tissue infection, severe mucositis, hypotension, or known MRSA colonisation. Vancomycin is not needed routinely — adding it to every febrile neutropenia patient does not improve outcomes and increases kidney injury.
cards.q: In febrile neutropenia, when should you add vancomycin?

cards.a: G-CSF (such as filgrastim) is used as prophylaxis when the chemotherapy regimen carries a high risk of febrile neutropenia, to keep the white count up. It is NOT routinely given as treatment once febrile neutropenia has already started, because it does not shorten the fever or improve survival in most patients.
cards.q: When should G-CSF be used in febrile neutropenia, and when should it not?

cards.a: Add an antifungal drug, such as an echinocandin or voriconazole. A fever that persists for 4 to 7 days on broad-spectrum antibiotics suggests a fungal infection, which bacteria do not explain. Also look for fungal sources with a CT chest and check galactomannan.
cards.q: A neutropenic patient still has a fever after 5 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics. What should you add?

cards.a: High potassium, high phosphate, low calcium and high uric acid, with acute kidney failure. It happens when cancer cells break down rapidly after chemotherapy. Give aggressive intravenous fluids, rasburicase to break down uric acid, and correct the potassium urgently — high potassium can stop the heart.
cards.q: What are the lab findings of tumour lysis syndrome, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Give intravenous fluids first — large volumes of normal saline — because hypercalcaemia causes dehydration and the kidneys need fluid to excrete calcium. Then give a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid, which stops bone breakdown; calcitonin can be used as a short-term bridge because it works within hours.
cards.q: A cancer patient has a calcium of 14 mg/dL with confusion. What is the treatment order?

cards.a: Superior vena cava syndrome — a tumour, usually lung cancer or lymphoma, compresses the vein draining the head and arms, causing facial swelling, distended neck veins and breathlessness. First secure the airway if needed, then give steroids and arrange urgent radiotherapy or a stent to relieve the obstruction. A tissue diagnosis is still needed but must not delay relieving the obstruction.
cards.q: A patient with lung cancer develops facial swelling, distended neck veins and breathlessness. What is this and how is it managed?

cards.a: Give high-dose dexamethasone immediately — do not wait for the MRI. Steroids reduce the swelling around the cord and protect the remaining nerve function. Then get an urgent MRI of the whole spine and arrange urgent surgery or radiotherapy. The longer the delay, the more likely the weakness becomes permanent.
cards.q: A cancer patient develops back pain, leg weakness and urinary retention. What is the first treatment, and what must you not delay it for?

cards.a: Give dexamethasone to reduce the swelling around the metastases, which relieves headache and neurological symptoms. Seizure prophylaxis with levetiracetam is only given if the patient has had a seizure — it is not given routinely. Definitive treatment is whole-brain radiation or stereotactic radiosurgery.
cards.q: A patient with lung cancer has brain metastases with headache and weakness. What is the management?

cards.a: Squamous cell lung cancer causes hypercalcaemia from PTH-related peptide; small cell lung cancer causes SIADH with low sodium and ectopic ACTH causing Cushing syndrome; renal cell cancer causes high red cells from erythropoietin. The paraneoplastic syndrome often appears before the cancer is found, so it should prompt a search for the tumour.
cards.q: Which cancers cause which paraneoplastic syndromes?

cards.a: Hyperviscosity syndrome — the thick blood cannot flow properly, causing blurred vision, headache, nosebleeds and confusion. It is most often due to Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia (IgM) or very high myeloma protein. The urgent treatment is plasmapheresis to remove the excess protein, followed by chemotherapy for the underlying disease.
cards.q: A patient with a paraprotein has blurred vision, headache and nosebleeds. What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?

cards.a: Do a therapeutic thoracentesis to drain the fluid and relieve breathlessness, and send the fluid for cytology. For a recurrent effusion in a patient with limited life expectancy, an indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis prevents it coming back. Treat the underlying cancer as well.
cards.q: A cancer patient has a large malignant pleural effusion causing breathlessness. What is the management?

cards.a: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) — the bowel wall becomes inflamed and necrotic when the white count is very low. It presents with fever, abdominal pain and tenderness, often in the right lower quadrant. Get a CT abdomen, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, keep the patient nil by mouth, and involve surgery — operation is only needed if there is perforation or uncontrolled bleeding.
cards.q: A neutropenic chemotherapy patient develops fever and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: A febrile non-haemolytic reaction — the most common transfusion reaction, caused by antibodies to donor white cells or cytokines in the bag. It causes fever without low blood pressure or breathing difficulty. Stop the transfusion, check the patient, and give paracetamol; future transfusions should use leukoreduced blood.
cards.q: A patient develops a fever during a blood transfusion but is otherwise well. What is the most likely reaction and how is it managed?

cards.a: A mild allergic reaction — itching and hives — is treated by stopping the transfusion and giving an antihistamine. Anaphylaxis — wheeze, low blood pressure, angioedema — is an emergency: stop the transfusion, give intramuscular adrenaline, and support the airway and blood pressure. Patients with IgA deficiency are at particular risk.
cards.q: How do you manage an allergic reaction during a blood transfusion, and what changes if it is anaphylaxis?

cards.a: TACO is volume overload — raised blood pressure, raised JVP, breathlessness that improves with diuretics — and it happens when fluid is given too fast to a patient who cannot handle it. TRALI is immune-mediated lung injury within 6 hours of transfusion, with low blood pressure and no response to diuretics. TACO is treated with diuretics and slow transfusions; TRALI is treated with oxygen and ventilatory support.
cards.q: How do you tell transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) from TRALI?

cards.a: A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction — the patient made antibodies against donor red cell antigens after a previous transfusion, and the transfused cells are destroyed 5 to 10 days later. It causes a falling haemoglobin, jaundice and dark urine. The direct antiglobulin test is positive, and future transfusions need antigen-matched blood.
cards.q: A patient develops a falling haemoglobin and jaundice a week after a blood transfusion. What has happened?

cards.a: Irradiated blood is given to patients with weak immune systems — such as bone marrow transplant recipients and patients on purine analogues — to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, where donor lymphocytes attack the patient. CMV-negative blood is given to pregnant patients, neonates and transplant recipients to prevent CMV infection.
cards.q: Which patients need irradiated blood, and which need CMV-negative blood?

cards.a: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. It causes mucosal bleeding — nosebleeds, heavy periods, bleeding after dental work — with a prolonged bleeding time and low von Willebrand factor. Type 1 is treated with desmopressin, which releases stored von Willebrand factor; more severe types need von Willebrand factor replacement.
cards.q: What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Haemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII, causing deep bleeding into joints and muscles. Treat bleeds early with factor VIII replacement. Avoid intramuscular injections, aspirin and NSAIDs, because they increase bleeding. Mild disease can be treated with desmopressin.
cards.q: What is haemophilia A, and what must you avoid in these patients?

cards.a: Vitamin K deficiency — the liver cannot make clotting factors II, VII, IX and X without vitamin K, so the PT is prolonged but the platelets are normal. It is seen in malnutrition, prolonged antibiotic use, and bile duct obstruction. Give vitamin K, and the PT corrects within a day. Newborns get vitamin K at birth to prevent bleeding.
cards.q: A patient has a prolonged PT with a normal platelet count and no liver disease. What is the likely cause and treatment?

cards.a: Liver disease causes both low platelets and prolonged PT and aPTT, because the liver makes clotting factors. Give a trial of vitamin K, but it often does not correct the PT because the liver itself is failing. Before an invasive procedure, give platelets and plasma to reduce the bleeding risk — but remember these patients can also clot, so do not overcorrect.
cards.q: A patient with liver failure has a prolonged PT and low platelets. How do you manage this before a procedure?

cards.a: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin cause dose-dependent heart damage — a dilated cardiomyopathy with a falling ejection fraction. Check an echocardiogram before starting and during treatment, and do not exceed the lifetime cumulative dose. Dexrazoxane can protect the heart in high-risk patients.
cards.q: What heart toxicity do anthracyclines cause, and how do you monitor for it?

cards.a: Cisplatin causes kidney damage, hearing loss and severe nausea. Give aggressive intravenous hydration before and after each dose to protect the kidneys, and monitor kidney function and hearing. It also causes low magnesium, so replace electrolytes as needed.
cards.q: What are the main toxicities of cisplatin, and how do you prevent the kidney damage?

cards.a: Methotrexate toxicity causes mouth ulcers, low blood counts and kidney failure. Leucovorin rescue bypasses the blocked folate pathway and protects normal cells, so it is given after high-dose methotrexate. Also give aggressive hydration and alkalinise the urine, because methotrexate precipitates in acidic urine.
cards.q: A patient develops mouth ulcers and kidney failure after high-dose methotrexate. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Start screening at age 45 in average-risk adults. Colonoscopy every 10 years is the gold standard because it both finds and removes polyps. Stool FIT testing every year is an alternative — a positive FIT must be followed by colonoscopy. Screening stops when life expectancy is under 10 years.
cards.q: When should colorectal cancer screening start, and what are the options?

cards.a: Mammography every 2 years from age 40 to 74. Screening finds cancers earlier, when they are smaller and more curable. A suspicious mammogram needs a biopsy — imaging alone does not make the diagnosis. Women with BRCA mutations start screening earlier with MRI as well.
cards.q: What is the recommended breast cancer screening?

cards.a: Screening starts at age 21 with a Pap smear, and from age 30 HPV testing is added. If both are negative, screening is every 5 years until age 65. The HPV vaccine prevents most cervical cancers, but it does not replace screening.
cards.q: What is the recommended cervical cancer screening?

cards.a: Low-dose CT scanning once a year for adults aged 50 to 80 who have a heavy smoking history (20 pack-years or more) and currently smoke or quit within the last 15 years. A chest X-ray is not a screening test — it misses early cancers. Screening stops once the patient has not smoked for 15 years.
cards.q: Who should be screened for lung cancer, and with what test?

cards.a: Prostate cancer screening is a shared decision, not an automatic test. Discuss the PSA blood test with men aged 55 to 69, explaining that it can find cancers that would never have caused harm and lead to unnecessary biopsies and treatment. There is no benefit to routine screening after age 70.
cards.q: Should every older man have a PSA test for prostate cancer screening?

cards.a: Offer genetic testing to patients with a strong family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer (BRCA), or early-onset colorectal and endometrial cancer (Lynch syndrome). A positive result means earlier and more frequent screening, and sometimes risk-reducing surgery — for example, risk-reducing mastectomy or oophorectomy in BRCA carriers.
cards.q: When should you offer genetic testing for cancer risk, and what changes if the test is positive?

cards.a: 1-hour bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid fluids if hypotensive or lactate 4 or more, and start vasopressors (norepinephrine) if blood pressure stays low. qSOFA of 2 or more (low BP, fast breathing, altered mental state) predicts a bad outcome.
cards.q: What is the 1-hour sepsis bundle?

cards.a: Bacterial: high white cells and protein in CSF, low glucose, high opening pressure. Viral: white cells raised (mostly lymphocytes), protein mildly raised, glucose normal. Empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis: ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone (given before or with antibiotics), plus ampicillin if age over 50, pregnant, or immunocompromised — to cover Listeria.
cards.q: How does bacterial meningitis differ from viral meningitis on CSF, and what is empiric treatment?

cards.a: CD4 below 200 cells/uL: risk of Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) — give co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. CD4 below 100: toxoplasmosis. CD4 below 50: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) and CMV retinitis. ART (antiretroviral therapy) is started regardless of CD4 count, and it reduces opportunistic infections.
cards.q: What opportunistic infections occur at which CD4 counts in HIV?

cards.a: Cellulitis is a spreading skin infection, usually streptococci or Staph aureus, with redness, warmth and pain — treat with flucloxacillin or cephalexin. Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency: severe pain out of proportion to the skin changes, rapid spread, crepitus (gas in tissue), low blood pressure — needs urgent surgery (debridement) plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.
cards.q: How do you tell cellulitis from necrotising fasciitis?

cards.a: Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, spread by Ixodes ticks. Stage 1: erythema migrans — a bull's-eye rash. Stage 2: heart block, facial nerve palsy, arthritis. Stage 3: chronic arthritis, skin changes. Treatment: doxycycline for early disease, ceftriaxone for severe late disease.
cards.q: What are the stages of Lyme disease?

cards.a: Primary: painless chancre. Secondary: rash on palms and soles, condyloma lata. Latent: no symptoms but tests positive. Tertiary: gummas, neurosyphilis, cardiovascular disease. Screening is with RPR or VDRL (non-treponemal), confirmed with a treponemal test (FTA-ABS / TP-PA). Treatment is penicillin G.
cards.q: What are the stages of syphilis, and how is it diagnosed?

cards.a: A hot, swollen, painful single joint with fever. Aspirate the joint immediately — send for white cell count, Gram stain and culture. Do NOT delay aspiration to wait for blood tests. Treatment is urgent drainage plus IV antibiotics (e.g. flucloxacillin / vancomycin if MRSA risk). Septic arthritis can destroy a joint in days.
cards.q: What is the emergency action in suspected septic arthritis?

cards.a: MRSA: vancomycin or linezolid. Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem. Anaerobes (e.g. abdominal infection): metronidazole. Atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Legionella): macrolide or doxycycline. Always check local resistance patterns and allergies.
cards.q: Which antibiotic covers MRSA, Pseudomonas, anaerobes and atypical pneumonia?

cards.a: Influenza A/B causes fever, cough, myalgia and headache in winter. Complications include secondary bacterial pneumonia (Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae). Treatment: oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptoms in high-risk patients. Vaccination is the main prevention, especially in older people and those with chronic disease.
cards.q: What are the features and treatment of influenza?

cards.a: Fever, rigors, low blood pressure and a new heart murmur after a dental procedure or IV drug use. Blood cultures must be taken BEFORE antibiotics — at least 3 sets. Diagnosis uses the Duke criteria (blood cultures, echocardiogram showing vegetation, fever, risk factors, emboli). Treatment is prolonged IV antibiotics for 4-6 weeks.
cards.q: What are the key steps in diagnosing infective endocarditis?

cards.a: Add vasopressin as a second vasopressor. Norepinephrine is the first-line pressor in septic shock, and vasopressin is the usual add-on when the MAP target is not met, because it raises blood pressure through a different receptor and spares the catecholamine dose. Do not keep escalating norepinephrine alone indefinitely.
cards.q: A patient in septic shock is on high-dose norepinephrine and the MAP is still below 65 mmHg despite fluids. What is the next best step?

cards.a: A raised lactate means tissue hypoperfusion even when blood pressure looks normal, so the patient is still in trouble. Recheck the lactate every 2 to 4 hours and hunt for the source of infection. Falling lactate with treatment is a good sign, but a rising lactate means resuscitation or source control is failing.
cards.q: A septic patient has a lactate of 4.5 mmol/L but normal blood pressure after fluids. What does the lactate tell you, and what do you do next?

cards.a: No. Cultures are negative in about a third of true sepsis cases, often because antibiotics were given first or the source is hard to culture. If the clinical picture fits sepsis and the patient is improving, complete a sensible course and reassess daily. Stopping early risks relapse of an infection you never identified.
cards.q: A patient with suspected sepsis is improving on broad-spectrum antibiotics but all cultures are negative. Should you stop the antibiotics?

cards.a: Take blood cultures and start a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour. Febrile neutropenia is an emergency because these patients have almost no white cells to fight infection. Do not wait for a chest X-ray or other tests before giving antibiotics. Add vancomycin only if there are specific indications such as hypotension, a skin or line infection, or known MRSA.
cards.q: A patient on chemotherapy has a temperature of 38.5 C and an absolute neutrophil count of 400. What is the first action?

cards.a: Treat it as an emergency: blood cultures immediately, then broad-spectrum antibiotics at once, such as ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. Without a spleen, encapsulated organisms like pneumococcus can cause overwhelming post-splenectomy infection that kills within hours. Do not wait for test results. Vaccination against pneumococcus, Haemophilus and meningococcus is prevention for the future, not treatment now.
cards.q: A patient who had a splenectomy 2 years ago arrives with fever, rigors and confusion. What is the first action?

cards.a: Because a blocked, infected kidney cannot drain, so antibiotics cannot reach the infection and pressure builds up. Urgent source control is needed: a urinary catheter, ureteric stent or nephrostomy tube to relieve the obstruction, ideally within 6 to 12 hours. Source control matters as much as antibiotics in any obstructed or walled-off infection.
cards.q: A septic patient has a blocked urinary tract with a stone and is hypotensive. Why are antibiotics alone not enough?

cards.a: Central access is preferred because prolonged vasopressor infusion through a peripheral vein risks extravasation and tissue necrosis, and a central line also allows monitoring. But never delay starting pressors to place the line: start norepinephrine peripherally first, then place the central line. Delaying pressors in shock costs lives.
cards.q: A patient needs vasopressors for several days. Why is central venous access preferred, and should you delay pressors to place the line?

cards.a: Treat the underlying infection; DIC in sepsis is driven by the infection, so antibiotics and source control are the real treatment. Do not give heparin routinely in sepsis-related DIC. Give platelets only if there is active bleeding, or if the count is below 10,000, or below 50,000 before an invasive procedure. Replacing clotting factors without treating the cause does not help.
cards.q: A septic patient develops DIC with low platelets and a raised INR. How do you treat the DIC?

cards.a: Give hydrocortisone only when shock is refractory to fluids and vasopressors, meaning the patient still needs high-dose pressors to hold their blood pressure. Steroids are not routine in all sepsis and do not help patients who respond to fluids and one pressor. The idea is to support a failing stress response, not to treat every septic patient.
cards.q: When should steroids be given in septic shock?

cards.a: No. Procalcitonin is useful for guiding when to STOP antibiotics once a patient is improving, because a falling level supports a shorter course. But a low procalcitonin must never be used to withhold antibiotics from a patient who looks septic. Clinical judgement and the sepsis bundle come first.
cards.q: Can procalcitonin be used to decide whether to withhold antibiotics in suspected sepsis?

cards.a: Do a CT head first, because a focal deficit raises the risk of raised intracranial pressure and brain herniation from a lumbar puncture. But give antibiotics and dexamethasone BEFORE the CT scan. Never delay antibiotics to wait for imaging, because every hour of delay in bacterial meningitis worsens the outcome.
cards.q: A patient with suspected bacterial meningitis has a new focal neurological deficit. Should you do the lumbar puncture first or a CT head first?

cards.a: Add ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes. Listeria is a risk in people over 50, alcoholics, pregnant women and the immunocompromised, and ceftriaxone does not cover it. Missing Listeria coverage in an older patient is a classic Step 3 error.
cards.q: A 65-year-old with suspected bacterial meningitis is started on ceftriaxone and vancomycin. What extra antibiotic should be added, and why?

cards.a: Give dexamethasone before or with the first dose of antibiotics, in suspected pneumococcal meningitis. It dampens the inflammatory response to dying bacteria and reduces hearing loss and death. It does not help if given hours after antibiotics have started, so timing is everything.
cards.q: When should dexamethasone be given in bacterial meningitis, and what does it prevent?

cards.a: Start intravenous acyclovir immediately, before the CSF PCR result comes back. Herpes simplex encephalitis destroys brain tissue hour by hour, and delay is the main cause of death and disability. Send CSF for HSV PCR to confirm, and get an MRI, but do not wait for either before treating.
cards.q: A patient has fever, confusion and seizures, and herpes encephalitis is suspected. What is the first action?

cards.a: Give chemoprophylaxis to close contacts within 24 hours, such as a single dose of ciprofloxacin, rifampin or ceftriaxone. Meningococcal disease spreads by respiratory droplets and close contacts are at real risk. The patient should also be nursed under droplet precautions. Vaccination is for prevention, not for contacts after exposure.
cards.q: A patient is diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. What must be done for close contacts?

cards.a: This is tuberculous meningitis. Start four-drug anti-TB treatment plus dexamethasone straight away. TB cultures take weeks, so waiting for confirmation means the patient deteriorates. The CSF pattern of lymphocytes, very high protein and low glucose is the clue.
cards.q: A patient has subacute meningitis with a lymphocytic CSF, very high protein and low glucose. What is the likely diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Test the CSF for cryptococcal antigen, which is highly sensitive. Treatment starts with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole for maintenance. Measure the opening pressure, because raised intracranial pressure is common and needs repeated lumbar punctures to relieve it. Delay antiretroviral therapy for a few weeks to avoid immune reconstitution syndrome.
cards.q: An HIV patient with a CD4 count of 60 has headache, fever and confusion. What test confirms cryptococcal meningitis, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Do a CT head first. This presentation suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage rather than meningitis, and a lumbar puncture before imaging risks herniation if there is raised pressure or a mass. If the CT is negative but suspicion remains high, do the lumbar puncture afterwards and look for xanthochromia.
cards.q: A patient has the worst headache of their life, neck stiffness and no fever. What is the first investigation, and why not a lumbar puncture straight away?

cards.a: Look for a CSF leak, usually after a skull base fracture or sinus surgery, and for complement deficiency, which predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections. Workup includes imaging of the skull base, CT cisternography for a leak, and complement levels. Recurrent meningitis is never just bad luck.
cards.q: A patient keeps getting bacterial meningitis. What underlying cause should you look for?

cards.a: Group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria are the usual organisms. Empiric treatment is ampicillin plus cefotaxime, because ampicillin covers Listeria and Group B strep while cefotaxime covers Gram-negative organisms. Do not use ceftriaxone in a neonate because it can cause bilirubin problems. Lumbar puncture and blood cultures come first.
cards.q: A 5-day-old baby has fever, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle. Which organisms cause neonatal meningitis, and what is empiric treatment?

cards.a: The tricuspid valve, infected with Staphylococcus aureus. Right-sided endocarditis in IV drug users seeds the lungs, causing septic pulmonary emboli and multiple infiltrates. Left-sided disease instead causes systemic emboli to the brain, spleen and kidneys.
cards.q: An IV drug user has fever, a new murmur and multiple lung infiltrates. Which valve is most likely infected, and with what organism?

cards.a: The commonest cause is antibiotics given before cultures were taken, which sterilises the blood. Other causes are fastidious organisms such as Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella and the HACEK group. Send serology for Coxiella and Bartonella, and if the patient is stable, hold antibiotics and repeat blood cultures before starting treatment.
cards.q: A patient has all the features of endocarditis but blood cultures are repeatedly negative. What are the likely causes?

cards.a: New heart block means the infection has spread into the tissue around the valve, forming a perivalvular abscess that is damaging the conduction system. Get a transoesophageal echocardiogram urgently and call cardiac surgery. This is a surgical indication, not something antibiotics alone will fix.
cards.q: A patient with aortic valve endocarditis develops a new heart block. What does this mean, and what is the next step?

cards.a: Urgent cardiac surgery to remove the vegetation and repair or replace the valve. A large mobile vegetation with embolic events is a surgical indication because the next embolus could be fatal. Do not delay surgery for a completed ischaemic stroke unless there is haemorrhage on imaging.
cards.q: A patient with endocarditis has a large mobile vegetation over 10 mm and has already had an embolic stroke. What is the next step?

cards.a: Coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus. Early prosthetic valve endocarditis is usually acquired at the time of surgery from skin organisms. These infections often need surgery as well as antibiotics because the organisms form biofilm on the prosthetic material.
cards.q: A patient develops endocarditis 3 months after a prosthetic valve replacement. Which organisms are most likely?

cards.a: Order a TEE when there is a prosthetic valve, when the transthoracic echo is poor quality, when an abscess is suspected, or when the transthoracic echo is negative but suspicion remains high. TEE is far more sensitive for vegetations and abscesses, especially on prosthetic valves. A negative TTE never rules out endocarditis in a high-risk patient.
cards.q: When should you order a transoesophageal echo instead of a transthoracic echo for suspected endocarditis?

cards.a: Only the highest-risk patients: those with a prosthetic valve, a previous episode of endocarditis, or unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease. Give amoxicillin before dental work.
