Routine prophylaxis for mitral valve prolapse or a murmur is no longer recommended, because the risk is tiny and the harms of antibiotics outweigh it.
cards.q: Who should now receive antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures to prevent endocarditis?

cards.a: Right-sided endocarditis, usually tricuspid disease in IV drug users, often responds to medical treatment alone because the pressures are lower and emboli go to the lungs rather than the brain. Surgery is needed less often, mainly for very large vegetations, persistent bacteraemia or heart failure. Left-sided disease more often needs surgery for valve destruction, abscess or emboli.
cards.q: How does management differ between right-sided and left-sided infective endocarditis?

cards.a: Use amoxicillin, doxycycline or a macrolide alone. In a healthy outpatient without comorbidities, a single narrow-spectrum agent is enough. Do not reach for a fluoroquinolone or broad-spectrum combination first line, because that drives resistance and adds side effects for no benefit.
cards.q: A healthy 40-year-old has community-acquired pneumonia with no comorbidities and is well enough for outpatient treatment. What is first-line therapy?

cards.a: Give a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin alone. Comorbidities such as COPD, diabetes, heart failure or alcohol use raise the risk of resistant organisms, so single-agent narrow therapy is no longer enough.
cards.q: A patient with COPD and diabetes develops community-acquired pneumonia as an outpatient. How does treatment differ from a healthy patient?

cards.a: Give a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone or cefepime plus a macrolide such as azithromycin. Combination therapy improves outcomes in severe pneumonia. Add MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only if there are specific risk factors, such as prior colonisation, recent hospitalisation or a cavitary infiltrate.
cards.q: A patient with severe community-acquired pneumonia is admitted to the ICU. What is the empiric regimen?

cards.a: Legionella. Clues are hyponatraemia, diarrhoea, confusion and a history of recent travel, hotels or air conditioning exposure. Confirm with a urinary Legionella antigen test. Treat with a macrolide or fluoroquinolone, because Legionella lives inside cells and beta-lactams cannot reach it.
cards.q: A patient has pneumonia with hyponatraemia, diarrhoea and confusion after a hotel stay. What organism is suspected, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Chemical pneumonitis is sterile inflammation from inhaled stomach contents, and it does not need antibiotics at first. Aspiration pneumonia is a true bacterial infection, usually developing 48 hours or more after aspiration with fever and a new infiltrate, and it needs antibiotics with anaerobic cover. The key is timing and clinical picture, not just the history of aspiration.
cards.q: How do you tell aspiration pneumonitis from aspiration pneumonia, and does the difference change treatment?

cards.a: Add MRSA cover with vancomycin or linezolid, plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam. Ventilated patients are at risk of resistant hospital organisms. Take cultures first, then de-escalate once results return. Do not keep broad-spectrum cover going for the whole course if cultures grow a sensitive organism.
cards.q: A ventilated patient develops hospital-acquired pneumonia and has MRSA risk factors. What cover should be added?

cards.a: Reassess rather than just switching antibiotics blindly. Consider a wrong or resistant organism, a complication such as empyema or lung abscess, tuberculosis, or a non-infectious mimic such as pulmonary embolism or heart failure. Get a CT chest, repeat cultures, and consider bronchoscopy. Failure to improve is a diagnostic problem, not just a drug problem.
cards.q: A patient with pneumonia is not improving after 72 hours of antibiotics. What is the next step?

cards.a: Adults aged 65 and over, and younger adults with chronic lung, heart or liver disease, diabetes, asplenia or immunocompromise. Vaccinate before discharge, because the hospital admission is a chance to protect against the next episode. The pneumococcal vaccine prevents invasive disease even though it does not prevent every pneumonia.
cards.q: Which patients with pneumonia should receive pneumococcal vaccination, and when?

cards.a: Nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin for 3 days. These concentrate in the urine and work well for cystitis. Avoid fluoroquinolones as first line because of resistance, tendon injury and C. difficile risk. Always send a urine culture before starting, even when the diagnosis seems obvious.
cards.q: A young woman has uncomplicated cystitis. What is first-line treatment, and what should you avoid?

cards.a: An oral fluoroquinolone or cephalosporin is suitable if the organism is susceptible and the patient can keep fluids down. Admit for intravenous antibiotics if there is vomiting, sepsis, pregnancy, obstruction or a single kidney. Always image if there is no improvement, because an obstructed kidney will not clear with antibiotics alone.
cards.q: A woman has pyelonephritis but is stable and can take oral medication. How do you decide between outpatient and inpatient treatment?

cards.a: Yes. Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy, because it carries a high risk of progressing to pyelonephritis and is linked to preterm birth. Use nitrofurantoin or cephalexin. Avoid fluoroquinolones and trimethoprim in pregnancy. This is the one situation where asymptomatic bacteriuria is always treated.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has bacteria in her urine but no symptoms. Should you treat it?

cards.a: Remove or replace the catheter first, because a colonised catheter is a constant source of bacteria. Treat only if the patient has symptoms such as fever, flank pain or rigors. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in a catheterised patient, because the urine will always be colonised and antibiotics only breed resistance.
cards.q: A catheterised patient has bacteria in the urine but no symptoms. What is the key step, and should you give antibiotics?

cards.a: Yes, a UTI in a man is always considered complicated. Men need a workup for obstruction or prostatitis, a longer course of 7 to 14 days, and urology referral if infections recur. The male urinary tract is long and a UTI usually means something is wrong upstream.
cards.q: A man presents with a urinary tract infection. Is this treated the same as a UTI in a woman?

cards.a: Vaginal oestrogen is the most effective prevention, because it restores the protective vaginal flora and reduces colonisation by uropathogens. Also advise good hydration and voiding after intercourse. Long-term prophylactic antibiotics are a last resort, not the first step.
cards.q: A postmenopausal woman keeps getting recurrent urinary tract infections. What is the best preventive measure?

cards.a: Avoid nitrofurantoin if the eGFR is below 30, because it does not concentrate in the urine enough to work and the risk of toxicity rises. Also never use it for pyelonephritis, because it does not reach the kidney tissue. For upper tract infection you need an agent that penetrates the kidney, such as a fluoroquinolone or cephalosporin.
cards.q: When should nitrofurantoin NOT be used for a urinary infection?

cards.a: Yes, admit for intravenous antibiotics. Fever, flank pain and haematuria mean pyelonephritis, an upper tract infection. Check for obstruction with imaging, because a blocked kidney will not respond to antibiotics alone. Blood cultures and a urine culture should be taken before antibiotics.
cards.q: A patient with cystitis symptoms also has fever, flank pain and haematuria. What does this change?

cards.a: Incision and drainage is the primary treatment, because an abscess will not clear with antibiotics alone. Add antibiotics such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline or clindamycin if the abscess is large, there are systemic signs, or the patient is immunocompromised. Always send the pus for culture.
cards.q: A patient has a fluctuant skin abscess that grows MRSA. What is the main treatment?

cards.a: Think MRSA or a non-infectious mimic. If cellulitis does not respond to flucloxacillin, add MRSA cover such as vancomycin or clindamycin. Also consider deep vein thrombosis, gout, contact dermatitis or a drug reaction, all of which can look like cellulitis but will never respond to antibiotics.
cards.q: Cellulitis is not improving on flucloxacillin. What should you consider?

cards.a: First, do a probe-to-bone test and get an X-ray or MRI to look for osteomyelitis. Then start broad-spectrum antibiotics, offload pressure from the foot, assess the blood supply, and arrange surgical debridement if the infection is deep. Diabetic foot infection is a limb-threatening emergency and needs a multidisciplinary team.
cards.q: A diabetic patient has a deep infected foot ulcer. What is the first assessment, and what else is needed?

cards.a: This is a surgical emergency, likely gas gangrene or a necrotising infection. Start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately and get urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation. Gas in the tissues means bacteria are producing gas as they destroy tissue, and antibiotics alone cannot save the limb or the patient.
cards.q: A diabetic patient has a foot ulcer with gas visible on X-ray. What is the next step?

cards.a: Eikenella corrodens, along with streptococci and staphylococci. Give amoxicillin-clavulanate, which covers Eikenella. Do not close hand bites primarily, because the infection risk is very high, and watch closely for tendon or joint involvement. Human bites are more dangerous than they look.
cards.q: A patient is bitten on the hand by another person. What organism is typical, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Give amoxicillin-clavulanate for cat bites, which carry Pasteurella multocida, and for deep wounds, hand or face bites, or immunocompromised patients. Clean the wound thoroughly and assess rabies risk based on the animal and local prevalence. Cat bites are more likely to infect than dog bites because the teeth are thin and penetrate deeply.
cards.q: A patient is bitten by a cat on the hand. Should they get antibiotic prophylaxis?

cards.a: Erysipelas is a superficial streptococcal infection with a sharp, raised, well-defined edge and fever. Cellulitis is deeper, with a flatter, less defined edge. Erysipelas responds well to penicillin alone. The distinction matters because erysipelas needs narrower therapy and has a more abrupt onset.
cards.q: How does erysipelas differ from cellulitis?

cards.a: Use topical mupirocin if the area is small, or oral cephalexin or flucloxacillin if it is extensive. Impetigo causes honey-coloured crusts and is due to Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci. Keep the child away from school until 24 hours after antibiotics start, because it spreads easily by contact.
cards.q: A child has honey-coloured crusts around the mouth. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Cover Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes, for example piperacillin-tazobactam, or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole. But antibiotics are only half the treatment: source control with surgery or drainage of the perforation or abscess is essential. Without source control, even the best antibiotics fail.
cards.q: A patient has a perforated bowel with peritonitis. What antibiotic cover is needed, and what else is essential?

cards.a: Diagnosis is an ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells per microlitre, even without a positive culture. Treat with cefotaxime plus intravenous albumin. Albumin prevents hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival, so it is as important as the antibiotic. Do not wait for the culture result before treating.
cards.q: A cirrhotic patient with ascites develops fever and abdominal pain. How is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis diagnosed and treated?

cards.a: Stop the offending antibiotic if possible, because continued antibiotics keep driving the infection. Test only if the patient has diarrhoea, and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Metronidazole is no longer first line for severe disease. Isolate the patient and use strict hand hygiene with soap, because alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores.
cards.q: A patient on antibiotics develops watery diarrhoea and tests positive for C. difficile. What is the first step, and what is first-line treatment?

cards.a: Give high-dose oral vancomycin plus intravenous metronidazole, and call surgery urgently for possible colectomy. Fulminant disease with ileus or toxic megacolon can be fatal, and medical therapy alone may not be enough. Never give anti-diarrhoeal drugs, because trapping the toxin in the bowel makes things worse.
cards.q: A patient with C. difficile develops ileus and a massively dilated colon. What is the treatment?

cards.a: After a second recurrence, consider fidaxomicin or a faecal microbiota transplant, which restores normal gut bacteria and has a very high cure rate. Bezlotoxumab, an antibody against the C. difficile toxin, can be added in high-risk patients. Repeated courses of the same antibiotic rarely work.
cards.q: C. difficile keeps coming back after treatment. What is the next step?

cards.a: Uncomplicated diverticulitis can often be managed as an outpatient, and antibiotics are needed for complicated disease, immunocompromise or systemic illness. Confirm the diagnosis with a CT scan, because the symptoms overlap with other causes of abdominal pain. Admit if there is perforation, abscess, obstruction or fistula.
cards.q: A patient has uncomplicated diverticulitis. Do they always need antibiotics and admission?

cards.a: Start antiretroviral therapy immediately, ideally the same day, regardless of the CD4 count. Early ART preserves the immune system and reduces transmission. Also start PCP prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, because the CD4 is below 200, and continue it until the CD4 stays above 200 for at least 3 months.
cards.q: A newly diagnosed HIV patient has a CD4 count of 150. When do you start antiretroviral therapy, and what prophylaxis is needed?

cards.a: Pneumocystis pneumonia. Treat with high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and add corticosteroids if the oxygen level is low, with a PaO2 below 70 mmHg or a wide alveolar-arterial gradient. Steroids reduce the inflammatory damage that worsens as the organisms die. The LDH is often raised and the chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates.
cards.q: An HIV patient with a CD4 count of 120 has dyspnoea, hypoxia and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Toxoplasmosis or primary CNS lymphoma. Start empiric pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis, because it is the commonest cause and is treatable. If there is no improvement in 2 weeks, consider a brain biopsy to look for lymphoma. Multiple ring-enhancing lesions favour toxoplasmosis, while a single lesion favours lymphoma.
cards.q: An HIV patient with a CD4 count of 80 has a ring-enhancing brain lesion and seizures. What is the differential, and what do you do first?

cards.a: Delay antiretroviral therapy for 4 to 6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment. Starting ART too soon triggers immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, which can cause a dangerous rise in intracranial pressure. Treat the cryptococcal infection first, control the pressure, then start ART.
cards.q: An HIV patient is diagnosed with cryptococcal meningitis. When should antiretroviral therapy be started?

cards.a: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome is a paradoxical worsening of a known or hidden infection shortly after starting ART, as the recovering immune system suddenly reacts to the infection. Continue the ART, treat the underlying infection, and give corticosteroids only for severe cases such as CNS involvement or airway compromise.
cards.q: A patient starts antiretroviral therapy and two weeks later develops worsening fever and swollen lymph nodes. What is this, and how is it managed?

cards.a: Think Cryptosporidium or Microsporidia. Diagnosis is by stool antigen or microscopy. There is no reliably effective antiparasitic drug for Cryptosporidium, so the main treatment is antiretroviral therapy to restore immunity. Supportive care with fluids and anti-diarrhoeal drugs helps in the meantime.
cards.q: An HIV patient with a CD4 count of 70 has chronic watery diarrhoea. What organisms are likely, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: CMV retinitis causes painless floaters and vision loss, with a classic pizza-pie appearance on fundoscopy. Treat with systemic valganciclovir, sometimes with intravitreal ganciclovir, and start antiretroviral therapy. Without treatment it progresses to blindness, so any visual symptoms in advanced HIV need urgent ophthalmology review.
cards.q: An HIV patient with a CD4 count of 40 reports painless floaters and blurred vision. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Give azithromycin prophylaxis when the CD4 count falls below 50. Stop it once the CD4 stays above 100 for at least 3 months on antiretroviral therapy. MAC causes fever, weight loss, anaemia and diarrhoea in advanced HIV, and prophylaxis prevents it.
cards.q: When is Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis given in HIV, and when can it be stopped?

cards.a: Start TB treatment first, then add antiretroviral therapy within 2 weeks if the CD4 is below 50, or within 8 weeks if it is higher. Early ART reduces mortality, but watch for immune reconstitution syndrome and drug interactions, especially rifampin lowering antiretroviral levels. A specialist should manage the combination.
cards.q: A patient has both HIV and tuberculosis. In what order do you start treatment, and when is antiretroviral therapy added?

cards.a: Start post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure. The course is 28 days of three antiretroviral drugs. Test the source patient and the exposed person at baseline, and follow up for seroconversion. After 72 hours, PEP is no longer offered.
cards.q: A healthcare worker has a needlestick injury from an HIV-positive patient. When should post-exposure prophylaxis start, and for how long?

cards.a: Sputum AFB smear plus culture; culture is the gold standard. A rapid molecular test such as GeneXpert gives a fast result and detects rifampin resistance. Isolate the patient in a negative-pressure room and use an N95 respirator. Three negative smears on separate days are needed before isolation can be lifted.
cards.q: How is pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed, and what infection control measures are needed?

cards.a: Two months of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by four months of rifampin and isoniazid, for a total of 6 months. Directly observed therapy improves completion rates. Stopping early or taking doses irregularly is the main cause of drug resistance.
cards.q: What is the standard treatment regimen for drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis?

cards.a: Peripheral neuropathy, with numbness and tingling in the hands and feet. Give pyridoxine, vitamin B6, alongside isoniazid, especially in diabetics, alcoholics, pregnant women and malnourished patients. Isoniazid also causes hepatitis, so liver function must be monitored.
cards.q: What is the main side effect of isoniazid, and how is it prevented?

cards.a: Rifampin is a potent liver enzyme inducer, so it lowers the levels of many drugs, including oral contraceptives, warfarin and antiretrovirals. Warn patients that it turns urine, sweat and tears orange, and that it can cause hepatitis. Doses of interacting drugs often need adjusting, and contraception may fail.
cards.q: A patient starting rifampin is on the oral contraceptive pill and warfarin. What must you warn them about?

cards.a: Treat latent TB in people with a positive interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test but no active disease, using isoniazid for 9 months or rifampin for 4 months. Always rule out active TB first with a chest X-ray and sputum tests, because giving a single drug to active TB breeds resistance.
cards.q: Who should receive treatment for latent tuberculosis, and what must you rule out first?

cards.a: Multidrug-resistant TB is resistant to both rifampin and isoniazid. It needs a specialist regimen with second-line drugs, a much longer treatment course, and airborne isolation. It usually results from incomplete or interrupted treatment, which is why directly observed therapy matters.
cards.q: What is multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and how is it managed?

cards.a: Lymph nodes are the commonest extrapulmonary site, causing painless neck swelling known as scrofula. The pleura and spine are also common; spinal TB, or Pott disease, causes back pain and deformity. Diagnosis needs biopsy or culture, because the organisms are few and smears are often negative.
cards.q: What is the commonest site of extrapulmonary tuberculosis?

cards.a: A single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone, plus doxycycline if chlamydia has not been excluded. Always test for other sexually transmitted infections and arrange a test of cure, especially for pharyngeal infection, because resistance is rising. Treat all recent sexual partners.
cards.q: What is the treatment for gonorrhoea, and what follow-up is needed?

cards.a: Doxycycline for 7 days is preferred over single-dose azithromycin, because it is more effective. Treat all sexual partners and retest in 3 months, because reinfection is common. Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so screening of young sexually active people is important to prevent infertility.
cards.q: What is the treatment for chlamydia, and why is retesting needed?

cards.a: Give aciclovir or valaciclovir early in the first episode, because it shortens the illness and reduces severity. For frequent recurrences, offer daily suppressive therapy. If there are active genital lesions at delivery, a caesarean section is needed to protect the baby from neonatal herpes, which is often fatal.
cards.q: How is a first episode of genital herpes treated, and what is the risk at delivery?

cards.a: Pelvic inflammatory disease is diagnosed clinically by cervical motion tenderness plus adnexal tenderness, with fever and discharge. Treat with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline plus metronidazole as an outpatient if mild. Admit if there is a tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, severe illness or failure to improve, because the risk of infertility rises with delay.
cards.q: How is pelvic inflammatory disease diagnosed and treated?

cards.a: Metronidazole, as a single dose, or a 7-day course in HIV-positive patients. Treat the sexual partner too, or reinfection is guaranteed. Advise avoiding alcohol during treatment because of the disulfiram-like reaction. Trichomoniasis causes a frothy yellow-green discharge and is often found with other infections.
cards.q: What is the treatment for trichomoniasis, and what else must be done?

cards.a: Treat with topical podophyllotoxin or imiquimod, or cryotherapy for larger warts. The HPV vaccine prevents most genital warts and cervical cancer, so offer it to eligible patients. Women with HPV also need cervical screening, because high-risk HPV types cause cervical cancer.
cards.q: How are genital warts treated, and what prevention is available?

cards.a: Penicillin G is the only effective treatment in pregnancy, because other antibiotics do not reliably treat the fetus. If the patient is allergic to penicillin, she must be desensitised and then given penicillin anyway. Warn about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, a fever and worsening symptoms in the first 24 hours as the organisms die.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with syphilis. What is the treatment, and what if she is allergic to penicillin?

cards.a: Think chlamydia, which is the commonest cause of non-gonococcal urethritis. Send a nucleic acid amplification test for both gonorrhoea and chlamydia, and treat with doxycycline. Do not use fluoroquinolones for gonorrhoea, because resistance is now widespread.
cards.q: A man has urethritis but the Gram stain shows no gonococci. What is the likely cause, and how do you manage it?

cards.a: Yes, still give it. The 48-hour window applies mainly to mild outpatient illness, but hospitalised and high-risk patients benefit from oseltamivir even when started later. Do not withhold it from a sick patient just because the window has passed.
cards.q: A high-risk patient is admitted with influenza 4 days after symptoms started. Is oseltamivir still worth giving?

cards.a: A biphasic illness: the patient improves, then worsens a few days later with purulent sputum and a new infiltrate. The usual culprits are Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA, or Streptococcus pneumoniae. In severe cases add MRSA cover with vancomycin or linezolid, because post-influenza staphylococcal pneumonia can be rapidly fatal.
cards.q: A patient recovers from influenza, then deteriorates with purulent sputum and a new infiltrate. What is happening, and what organism should you cover?

cards.a: Give dexamethasone if the patient needs oxygen, because it reduces mortality in hypoxic COVID-19. Add remdesivir early in the course, and give prophylactic anticoagulation because of the high clot risk. Avoid antibiotics unless there is clear bacterial superinfection, and avoid steroids in patients who do not need oxygen.
cards.q: A patient is hypoxic with COVID-19 pneumonia. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Older adults, people with COPD, and the immunocompromised. Treatment is mainly supportive, with oxygen and fluids. Ribavirin is rarely used and reserved for severely immunocompromised patients such as transplant recipients, because of toxicity and limited benefit. RSV is now recognised as a significant cause of adult pneumonia.
cards.q: Who is at risk from RSV infection in adults, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots in the mouth, then a spreading red rash. Isolate the patient under airborne precautions, because measles is extremely contagious. Give post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR vaccine within 72 hours, or immunoglobulin within 6 days, to exposed contacts who are not immune.
cards.q: What are the features of measles, and what infection control and post-exposure measures are needed?

cards.a: Varicella in pregnancy carries a risk of severe pneumonia, especially after 20 weeks. Treat with aciclovir if the woman is beyond 20 weeks or has severe disease. If a non-immune pregnant woman is exposed, give varicella immunoglobulin within 10 days. Never give the live varicella vaccine during pregnancy.
cards.q: A pregnant woman develops chickenpox. What are the risks, and how is it managed?

cards.a: Oral thrush in an otherwise healthy person usually follows antibiotics or inhaled steroids. Treat with topical nystatin or oral fluconazole, and advise rinsing the mouth after using a steroid inhaler. If thrush keeps recurring without an obvious cause, check for diabetes or immunocompromise.
cards.q: A patient develops oral thrush after a course of antibiotics. What is the treatment, and what should you advise?

cards.a: Risk factors are a central line, total parenteral nutrition, broad-spectrum antibiotics and abdominal surgery. Treat with fluconazole or an echinocandin such as caspofungin, and remove the central line, because the line is usually the source. Blood cultures confirm the diagnosis, but do not wait for them if the patient is deteriorating.
cards.q: An ICU patient with a central line and total parenteral nutrition develops candidemia. What are the risk factors, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Fever that does not respond to broad-spectrum antibiotics in a neutropenic patient, with a halo sign on CT chest. Treat with voriconazole, which is first line for invasive aspergillosis. Send a serum galactomannan test to support the diagnosis, but start treatment on clinical suspicion, because waiting for confirmation is dangerous.
cards.q: A neutropenic patient has persistent fever despite antibiotics and a halo sign on CT chest. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Diabetic ketoacidosis is the classic setting, with black nasal eschar and orbital involvement. Treat with liposomal amphotericin B plus urgent surgical debridement of dead tissue, and correct the ketoacidosis. Mucormycosis invades blood vessels and kills tissue fast, so surgery is as important as antifungals.
cards.q: A diabetic patient in ketoacidosis develops a black nasal eschar and eye swelling. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Anyone on high-dose steroids, more than 20 mg of prednisolone daily for over 4 weeks, transplant recipients, and patients on intensive chemotherapy. Give trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. PCP prophylaxis is not only for HIV, and forgetting it in a patient on prolonged steroids is a common error.
cards.q: Which patients outside HIV should receive Pneumocystis prophylaxis?

cards.a: Coccidioidomycosis is acquired in the desert southwest of the United States, from inhaling dust containing the fungus. Most infections are mild, but treat symptomatic disease with fluconazole. Disseminated disease is more likely in the immunocompromised and in people of Filipino or African ancestry.
cards.q: A patient returns from Arizona with pneumonia and erythema nodosum. What is the likely diagnosis, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Use topical terbinafine for skin infections such as athlete's foot and ringworm. For nail or scalp infection, oral terbinafine is needed, because topical drugs do not penetrate the nail plate or hair follicles. Check liver function before and during oral therapy.
cards.q: How do you treat dermatophyte skin infections, and when is oral therapy needed instead of topical?

cards.a: Monitor renal function and drug levels, because vancomycin is nephrotoxic, especially when combined with piperacillin-tazobactam or aminoglycosides. Red man syndrome, with flushing and itching during the infusion, is caused by too fast an infusion rate and is not a true allergy, so slow the infusion rather than stopping the drug permanently.
cards.q: What are the main toxicities of vancomycin, and how do you monitor for them?

cards.a: Tendon rupture, especially in older patients and those on steroids, QT prolongation, C. difficile infection, and an increased risk of aortic aneurysm. Avoid fluoroquinolones in pregnancy and children, and reserve them for situations where no safer alternative exists. Patients should be warned to stop the drug and seek help if a tendon becomes painful.
cards.q: What are the key warnings for fluoroquinolone antibiotics?

cards.a: Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins carry the highest risk of C. difficile infection. The single most effective prevention is antibiotic stewardship: stop antibiotics that are not needed, use the narrowest effective agent, and keep courses as short as possible.
cards.q: Which antibiotics carry the highest risk of C. difficile infection, and how is that risk reduced?

cards.a: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, which can be permanent. Use once-daily dosing with drug level monitoring, keep courses short, and avoid combining them with other nephrotoxic drugs such as vancomycin when possible. Check hearing and renal function during treatment.
cards.q: What are the main toxicities of aminoglycosides, and how are they monitored?

cards.a: Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is low, around 2 percent, and depends on similar side chains. A cephalosporin can usually be given if the penicillin reaction was a rash, but avoid it and consider graded challenge or desensitisation if there was anaphylaxis. Always document the exact reaction, not just the word allergy.
cards.q: A patient with a penicillin allergy needs a cephalosporin. Is it safe?

cards.a: Serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs or other serotonergic drugs, thrombocytopenia with courses longer than 2 weeks, and optic or peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use. Reserve linezolid for MRSA or vancomycin-resistant enterococcus, and monitor the platelet count and vision during treatment.
cards.q: What are the important side effects of linezolid?

cards.a: Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, so patients must avoid alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours afterwards. It also causes peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use. It covers anaerobes and protozoa, which is why it is used for intra-abdominal infections, C. difficile and trichomoniasis.
cards.q: What must patients avoid while taking metronidazole, and why?

cards.a: Narrow the antibiotics once cultures and sensitivities return, switch from intravenous to oral when the patient is improving and can swallow, and use the shortest effective course. De-escalation reduces resistance, side effects and cost without worsening outcomes, and it should happen daily on ward rounds.
cards.q: What is antibiotic de-escalation, and why does it matter?

cards.a: For a tetanus-prone wound in someone with an unknown or incomplete vaccine history, give tetanus toxoid plus tetanus immunoglobulin. For a clean minor wound, toxoid alone is enough. Immunoglobulin provides immediate passive protection while the vaccine builds active immunity.
cards.q: A patient with a dirty wound has an unknown tetanus vaccination history. What do you give?

cards.a: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water, then give rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated around the wound plus a course of rabies vaccine on days 0, 3, 7 and 14. Never delay post-exposure prophylaxis, because rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. Wound washing alone is the single most effective first step.
cards.q: A patient is bitten by a stray dog in an area where rabies is common. What is post-exposure prophylaxis?

cards.a: Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus start the hepatitis B vaccine series, ideally within 24 hours. Test the source patient for hepatitis B, and check the exposed person's immunity. Hepatitis B is far more transmissible by needlestick than HIV, so this prophylaxis is urgent.
cards.q: An unvaccinated healthcare worker has a needlestick from a hepatitis B positive patient. What is post-exposure prophylaxis?

cards.a: Pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type B, meningococcal and annual influenza vaccines. Ideally give them at least 2 weeks before an elective splenectomy, or 2 weeks after an emergency splenectomy, so the immune response is adequate. Also give the patient a standby antibiotic supply and education about seeking help immediately for fever.
cards.q: Which vaccines does a patient need after splenectomy, and when should they be given?

cards.a: Live vaccines such as MMR, varicella and live attenuated influenza vaccine are contraindicated in pregnancy and in immunocompromised patients, because the weakened virus can cause disease. Give inactivated vaccines instead. The inactivated influenza vaccine is safe and recommended in pregnancy.
cards.q: In which patients are live vaccines contraindicated?

cards.a: Yes, modern influenza vaccines are safe in egg allergy, including severe egg allergy, because the amount of egg protein is tiny. Observe the patient for 30 minutes afterwards if the allergy was severe. Do not withhold the flu vaccine because of egg allergy, because influenza is far more dangerous than the vaccine.
cards.q: Can a patient with an egg allergy receive the influenza vaccine?

cards.a: Anti-CCP antibody is the most specific test for rheumatoid arthritis. It is often positive years before symptoms. RF (rheumatoid factor) is sensitive but less specific. RA affects MCP and PIP joints symmetrically, spares DIP joints, causes morning stiffness over 1 hour, and can cause erosions and deformity. First-line treatment is methotrexate.
cards.q: What is the most specific antibody test for rheumatoid arthritis?

cards.a: ANA positive in almost all patients, anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and tracks disease activity, anti-Smith is very specific. Signs: malar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, mouth ulcers, arthritis, kidney disease (lupus nephritis), and low complement (C3, C4). Young women are most affected.
cards.q: Which antibodies are used in SLE, and what are the classic signs?

cards.a: Gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals of monosodium urate, under polarised light. Pseudogout: rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals of calcium pyrophosphate. Gout usually affects the big toe (podagra), pseudogout usually affects the knee. Treat acute gout with NSAID, colchicine or steroids — do not start allopurinol during an acute attack.
cards.q: How do gout and pseudogout crystals differ under the microscope?

cards.a: Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) affects people over 50, with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, and vision loss. It is associated with polymyalgia rheumatica. Start high-dose steroids IMMEDIATELY if suspected — do not wait for a biopsy — because vision loss can be permanent. ESR is usually very high.
cards.q: What is giant cell arteritis, and why must steroids be started immediately?

cards.a: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain and stiffness in shoulders and hips in people over 50, high ESR/CRP, no muscle weakness, responds quickly to low-dose steroids. Fibromyalgia: widespread pain and fatigue, tender points, normal labs, no inflammation, sleep disturbance — treat with exercise, sleep hygiene and amitriptyline/duloxetine, not steroids.
cards.q: How do you tell polymyalgia rheumatica from fibromyalgia?

cards.a: HLA-B27 is associated with ankylosing spondylitis. It causes inflammatory back pain in young men, worse in the morning and at night, better with exercise (not rest), sacroiliitis on X-ray, and a stiff spine (bamboo spine) over time. Treatment is NSAIDs first, then TNF inhibitors.
cards.q: What is HLA-B27 associated with, and what is the pattern of back pain?

cards.a: CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Anti-centromere antibody is seen in limited scleroderma (CREST). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is seen in diffuse scleroderma, with lung and kidney involvement. Both cause tight, thickened skin.
cards.q: What is CREST syndrome, and which antibodies are seen in scleroderma?

cards.a: Sjögren's syndrome causes dry eyes and dry mouth, due to autoimmune destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands. Antibodies: anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB). Patients are at increased risk of lymphoma. Use artificial tears and saliva substitutes, and check for other autoimmune diseases.
cards.q: What is Sjögren's syndrome?

cards.a: Osteoarthritis: wear-and-tear, affects weight-bearing joints and DIP joints (Heberden's nodes), pain worse with use, better with rest, no morning stiffness or only briefly, X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes. RA: inflammatory, MCP/PIP, morning stiffness over 1 hour, pain better with use, erosions on X-ray.
cards.q: How do you tell osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis?

cards.a: Aspirate the joint. Septic arthritis: very high white cell count in fluid (usually over 50,000), positive Gram stain/culture, needs urgent drainage and antibiotics. Gout: urate crystals, white cells lower, patient may have fever but joint is less hot and the history is typical. Never assume gout — always aspirate a hot joint if infection is possible.
cards.q: How do you tell septic arthritis from gout in a hot, swollen joint?
A patient is newly diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis with swollen, painful MCP and PIP joints. What disease-modifying drug should you start first, and why start it now?
cards.a: Start methotrexate as soon as the diagnosis is made. It is the first-line DMARD for RA because it slows joint damage and erosions, not just pain. There is a window of opportunity in early RA: starting a DMARD within weeks gives a much better chance of remission than waiting, so do not just give painkillers and watch.

cards.q: A patient starting methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis asks what monitoring and precautions are needed. What do you tell them?
cards.a: Take folic acid with it to reduce mouth ulcers, nausea and liver irritation, avoid alcohol, and have regular blood tests for liver enzymes and full blood count. Methotrexate can cause liver damage and low blood counts, so monitoring catches problems early. It also causes birth defects, so reliable contraception is essential.

cards.q: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate wants to become pregnant. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Stop methotrexate at least 3 months before trying to conceive, because it is teratogenic and can cause miscarriage and birth defects. Switch to pregnancy-safe options such as hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine, and plan the pregnancy when the disease is well controlled, since active RA itself worsens pregnancy outcomes.

cards.q: A patient on methotrexate for RA develops a dry cough, shortness of breath and fever over a few weeks. What should you do first?
cards.a: Hold the methotrexate and evaluate urgently, including a chest X-ray. Methotrexate can cause a hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which looks like an infection but is a drug reaction, and it can progress if the drug is continued. First exclude infection, but do not keep giving methotrexate while you wait.

cards.q: A patient with RA still has active synovitis after 3 months of methotrexate at a good dose. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Escalate treatment by adding a biologic drug, usually a TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab or etanercept, or add other conventional DMARDs. Continuing methotrexate alone when it has clearly failed lets erosions accumulate. The goal is remission or low disease activity, so step up rather than accepting ongoing inflammation.

cards.q: Before starting a TNF inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis, what screening must be done and why?
cards.a: Screen for latent tuberculosis with an interferon-gamma release assay, and check hepatitis B and C. TNF inhibitors suppress the immune system, so latent TB can reactivate and hepatitis B can flare, both of which can be life-threatening. Treat latent TB before starting the biologic, and do not start it during an active infection.

cards.q: A patient on a TNF inhibitor for RA develops a fever and a productive cough. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Hold the TNF inhibitor and work them up for infection urgently, including a chest X-ray and cultures. Biologics blunt the immune response, so infections can progress fast and may present without the usual signs. Do not keep giving immunosuppression through an active infection, and restart it only once the infection has cleared.

cards.q: Why should you avoid TNF inhibitors in a patient with moderate to severe heart failure?
cards.a: TNF inhibitors can worsen heart failure and increase hospitalisation and death in patients with moderate to severe (NYHA class III-IV) heart failure. Choose a different biologic, such as rituximab or abatacept, instead. This is a drug-class contraindication, not a side effect to monitor through.

cards.q: A patient on long-term hydroxychloroquine for RA asks about eye checks. What do you advise and why?
cards.a: Have a baseline eye examination and then annual screening with an ophthalmologist. Hydroxychloroquine can cause retinal toxicity, which is usually irreversible once it affects vision, but it is preventable if caught early on screening. The risk rises with higher doses and longer use, so do not skip the eye checks.

cards.q: A patient with RA is started on sulfasalazine. What side effects should you warn them about?
cards.a: Nausea, stomach upset, rash, headache and orange-coloured urine, which is harmless. It can also lower sperm count reversibly in men and cause haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency. It is one of the few DMARDs that is safe in pregnancy, which is why it is often chosen for women planning a family.

cards.q: A patient with RA is started on leflunomide. What monitoring and cautions apply?
cards.a: Check liver enzymes and blood pressure regularly, because leflunomide can cause liver damage and hypertension. It is teratogenic and stays in the body for a long time, so if pregnancy is planned or toxicity occurs, a cholestyramine washout is needed to clear it. Do not use it in pregnancy.

cards.q: A patient with RA who failed methotrexate and a TNF inhibitor is offered a JAK inhibitor such as tofacitinib. What risks should you discuss?
cards.a: Higher risk of infection, including shingles, and a raised risk of blood clots and cardiovascular events, especially in older patients and smokers. Check lipids, blood counts and liver tests, and make sure they are vaccinated against shingles before starting. It is an oral drug, which patients like, but it is not a low-risk option.

cards.q: A patient on tocilizumab, an IL-6 blocker, for RA needs monitoring. What do you watch for?
cards.a: Liver enzymes, cholesterol and neutrophil counts, because tocilizumab can raise liver enzymes and lipids and lower neutrophils. It also masks fever and CRP, so infections can be harder to spot, and there is a risk of bowel perforation, especially in patients with diverticulitis. Warn them to seek help early for abdominal pain.

cards.q: A patient with severe, refractory RA is offered rituximab. How does it work and what must be checked first?
cards.a: Rituximab depletes B cells by targeting CD20, which reduces the antibodies driving RA. Before starting, screen for hepatitis B, because B-cell depletion can cause a dangerous hepatitis B flare. Watch for infusion reactions during the first dose, and expect the benefit to last months, with repeat courses when symptoms return.

cards.q: A patient with a new RA flare is given prednisone while methotrexate takes effect. What is the plan for the steroid?
cards.a: Use it as a short-term bridge and taper it off over weeks as the DMARD starts working. Steroids relieve pain and swelling quickly, but long-term use causes weight gain, diabetes, high blood pressure, osteoporosis and infections. They are never a substitute for a DMARD in RA.

cards.q: Why are NSAIDs alone not enough treatment for rheumatoid arthritis?
cards.a: NSAIDs only relieve pain and stiffness; they do nothing to stop the immune attack that erodes joints and causes deformity. A patient who feels better on NSAIDs can still be accumulating irreversible joint damage. Always start a DMARD alongside, and do not let a good NSAID response delay it.

cards.q: A patient with RA on a biologic is scheduled for elective hip replacement. What is the perioperative plan?
cards.a: Hold the biologic before surgery, usually for one dosing interval, and restart it only once the wound has healed and there is no infection. Biologics impair wound healing and raise infection risk, including prosthetic joint infection. Methotrexate is usually continued, but coordinate the plan with the surgeon and rheumatologist.

cards.q: A patient with long-standing RA has a large spleen, very low neutrophils and recurrent infections. What syndrome is this, and what is the treatment?
cards.a: This is Felty syndrome, the triad of RA, splenomegaly and neutropenia. Treat the underlying RA more aggressively, and use G-CSF during severe infections or when the neutrophil count is dangerously low. Splenectomy is a last resort. The low neutrophils explain the recurrent infections, not a separate bone marrow disease.

cards.q: A patient with long-standing RA complains of neck pain and tingling in the hands. What complication must you consider before any procedure?
cards.a: Atlantoaxial subluxation, where inflammation weakens the ligaments holding the top neck vertebrae, so the spine can compress the cord. Get cervical spine imaging and a neurology opinion, and warn the anaesthetist before any intubation, because neck extension during intubation can injure the cord. Do not ignore new neck pain in RA.

cards.q: A patient with RA asks why you are so focused on their cholesterol, blood pressure and smoking. What is the link?
cards.a: RA itself is an independent risk factor for heart attacks and strokes, because chronic inflammation damages blood vessels just like high cholesterol does. Patients with RA die more often from cardiovascular disease than from joint damage. Treat risk factors aggressively and keep the RA in remission, since controlling inflammation also lowers cardiovascular risk.

cards.q: A patient with SLE has a facial rash and joint pain but no kidney or brain involvement. What is the first-line treatment?
cards.a: Hydroxychloroquine for every patient with SLE, plus NSAIDs for the joints and low-dose steroids or topical steroids for the rash. Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares, improves skin and joint symptoms and improves long-term survival, so it is the backbone of mild lupus treatment. Sun protection is also important because of photosensitivity.

cards.q: Why should hydroxychloroquine be continued in SLE even when the patient feels well, including during pregnancy?
cards.a: It reduces the number and severity of flares, improves survival and lowers the risk of blood clots and diabetes. Stopping it doubles the risk of a flare. It is also safe in pregnancy and reduces the risk of congenital heart block in babies of mothers with anti-Ro antibodies, so it is continued through pregnancy.

cards.q: A patient with SLE on immunosuppression develops a fever. What is the most important thing to rule out first?
cards.a: Infection, before assuming it is a lupus flare. Fever, joint pain and a raised CRP can look identical in both, and immunosuppressed patients can deteriorate quickly from infection. Take cultures, check a urine sample and chest X-ray, and do not simply increase steroids until infection has been excluded.

cards.q: A patient with SLE has falling C3 and C4 levels and a rising anti-dsDNA titre. What does this mean?
cards.a: Active lupus, often with kidney involvement. Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and tracks disease activity, while low complement levels mean the immune system is actively consuming complement in inflamed tissue, classically the kidney. Check the urine for protein and blood and the creatinine, and consider a renal biopsy.

cards.q: A patient with SLE develops protein in the urine, blood in the urine and a rising creatinine. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Arrange a kidney biopsy. Lupus nephritis has several classes that look the same on blood tests but need different treatment, and the biopsy tells you how active and how scarred the kidney is. Do not guess the treatment from the urine alone, and do not delay the biopsy while the kidney is actively being damaged.

cards.q: A patient with lupus nephritis is found to have diffuse proliferative disease on biopsy. What is the induction treatment?
cards.a: High-dose steroids plus mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide to switch off the inflammation quickly. This is the most severe form of lupus nephritis and can cause permanent kidney failure if treated weakly. After 3 to 6 months of induction, switch to maintenance therapy with mycophenolate or azathioprine.

cards.q: After induction treatment for lupus nephritis, what is the maintenance plan?
cards.a: Continue mycophenolate or azathioprine for years, keep taking hydroxychloroquine, and control blood pressure, usually with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker. Maintenance prevents relapse, which is common if immunosuppression is stopped too early. Monitor urine protein, creatinine and blood counts regularly.

cards.q: A patient with lupus nephritis is offered cyclophosphamide. What serious side effects must you warn them about?
cards.a: Infertility and early menopause, haemorrhagic cystitis (blood in the urine from bladder damage), infections and a higher long-term risk of bladder cancer and other malignancies. Give it with plenty of fluids and mesna to protect the bladder, and discuss fertility preservation before starting, especially in young patients.

cards.q: A woman with SLE wants to become pregnant. When is it safe, and which drugs must be changed?
cards.a: Plan the pregnancy when the lupus has been quiet for at least 6 months. Continue hydroxychloroquine, which is safe and protective, but stop mycophenolate and cyclophosphamide before conception because they cause birth defects, switching to azathioprine if needed. A pregnancy during active lupus risks a flare, pre-eclampsia and pregnancy loss.

cards.q: A pregnant woman with SLE has anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies. What complication must you monitor for in the baby?
cards.a: Congenital heart block, where the mother's antibodies cross the placenta and damage the baby's conduction system. Monitor the fetal heart rate with serial fetal echocardiograms from around 16 weeks. Continuing hydroxychloroquine lowers this risk, and a complete heart block, once established, is usually permanent and needs a pacemaker.

cards.q: A woman with SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome has had two miscarriages and a deep vein thrombosis. What is the treatment plan, including in pregnancy?
cards.a: Long-term anticoagulation with warfarin when not pregnant, because antiphospholipid syndrome causes clots and pregnancy loss. During pregnancy, switch to heparin (low molecular weight heparin), which does not cross the placenta, plus low-dose aspirin. Warfarin causes birth defects, so it must be stopped before or very early in pregnancy.

cards.q: A patient with SLE develops seizures and confusion. What is the approach?
cards.a: First exclude infection, metabolic causes and drugs, because immunosuppressed lupus patients can have meningitis or a metabolic problem that mimics brain lupus. If it is neuropsychiatric lupus, treat with high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or another immunosuppressant, and add anti-seizure medication. Brain involvement is a severe, organ-threatening manifestation, not a mild flare.

cards.q: A patient with SLE has a platelet count of 30,000 with bruising but no bleeding. What is the first-line treatment?
cards.a: High-dose steroids, which usually raise the platelet count within days. If steroids fail or the count is dangerously low, add immunosuppression such as rituximab or azathioprine, and consider intravenous immunoglobulin for a rapid rise. Splenectomy is a last resort. Treat the immune destruction of platelets, not just the bruising.

cards.q: A patient with SLE on immunosuppression asks about vaccines. What do you advise?
cards.a: Give inactivated vaccines such as influenza, pneumococcal and COVID vaccines, because infection is a leading cause of death in lupus. Avoid live vaccines, such as MMR and live shingles vaccine, while on strong immunosuppression, because the weakened virus can cause disease. Vaccinate before starting a biologic whenever possible.

cards.q: A patient develops a sudden, severely painful, red, swollen big toe joint overnight. What is the acute treatment?
cards.a: Start an NSAID, colchicine or a steroid as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, because early treatment shortens the attack. All three work for an acute gout flare, so choose based on the patient's other problems: avoid NSAIDs in kidney disease or heart failure, and avoid colchicine in severe kidney or liver disease.

cards.q: Why is colchicine most effective when given early in a gout attack?
cards.a: It works best within the first 36 hours, before the inflammation has fully built up. After that it still helps, but less. The dose-limiting side effect is diarrhoea and stomach cramps, so warn the patient and stop it if severe diarrhoea develops. It is a good choice when NSAIDs cannot be used.

cards.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease has an acute gout flare. Which treatment do you choose and which do you avoid?
cards.a: Use colchicine at a reduced dose or a short course of steroids, and avoid NSAIDs. NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys and can push chronic kidney disease into acute kidney injury, as well as raising blood pressure and causing fluid retention. Steroids are often the safest option in kidney disease, with blood sugar monitoring.

cards.q: A patient in the middle of an acute gout attack asks to start allopurinol today. What do you do?
cards.a: Do not start it during the flare. Starting urate-lowering therapy during an acute attack can prolong it or trigger another one, because shifting uric acid levels destabilises the crystals. Treat the flare first, then start allopurinol a few weeks later. If they are already taking allopurinol, keep it going through the flare.

cards.q: A patient with recurrent gout attacks is started on long-term urate-lowering therapy. What drug is first-line and what is the target?
cards.a: Allopurinol is first-line, titrated up until the serum uric acid is below 6 mg/dL. Getting below this target dissolves the crystals over months and prevents further attacks and tophi. Give flare prophylaxis with low-dose colchicine or an NSAID for the first few months, because starting allopurinol can itself trigger flares.

cards.q: A patient started on allopurinol develops a widespread rash and fever. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Stop allopurinol immediately and do not restart it. This can be a severe hypersensitivity reaction, including DRESS syndrome or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which can be fatal. The risk is higher in people with kidney disease and in those carrying the HLA-B*5801 gene, which is more common in some Asian populations. Seek urgent dermatology help.

cards.q: When starting allopurinol for gout, why do you start low and increase slowly, and what do you give alongside it?
cards.a: Start low and titrate up to the uric acid target to avoid triggering flares and to reduce the risk of hypersensitivity. Give low-dose colchicine or an NSAID for the first 3 to 6 months as flare prophylaxis, because the sudden drop in uric acid mobilises crystals and can provoke attacks. Warn the patient that early flares do not mean the drug has failed.

cards.q: A patient with gout and chronic kidney disease needs urate-lowering therapy. How do you manage this?
cards.a: Use allopurinol at a lower starting dose with slow titration and close monitoring, or use febuxostat as an alternative. Dose-adjust colchicine too, because it accumulates in kidney disease. Kidney disease is itself a reason to treat gout properly, since high uric acid and gout are linked to worse kidney outcomes, but the drugs need careful dosing.

cards.q: A patient cannot tolerate allopurinol because of a rash. What is the alternative urate-lowering drug, and what caution applies?
cards.a: Febuxostat, which works the same way by blocking uric acid production but is a different molecule. It is used when allopurinol is not tolerated or not effective. Use it cautiously in patients with cardiovascular disease, because there has been concern about a higher rate of cardiovascular events with febuxostat compared with allopurinol.

cards.q: A patient with gout has large tophi on their fingers and elbows. What is the treatment, and when is surgery needed?
cards.a: Long-term urate-lowering therapy to a uric acid below 6 mg/dL, which slowly dissolves the tophi over months to years. Surgery is reserved for tophi that are infected, ulcerated, compressing nerves or severely limiting function. Do not cut out tophi as a first step, because they shrink with good medical control of uric acid.

cards.q: A patient has an acutely swollen, painful knee with rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals in the joint fluid. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Pseudogout, caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Treat the acute attack like gout, with an NSAID, colchicine or an intra-articular steroid injection. Also look for an underlying cause, such as haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism or low magnesium, because treating that reduces recurrence.

cards.q: What finding on X-ray supports a diagnosis of pseudogout rather than gout?
cards.a: Chondrocalcinosis, which is calcification of the cartilage, seen as a white line within the joint cartilage, typically in the knee or wrist. Gout does not cause this. Pseudogout also tends to affect larger joints such as the knee, while gout classically affects the big toe, though either can occur in any joint.

cards.q: A patient with gout is on a diuretic for blood pressure and keeps having flares. What should you consider?
cards.a: Diuretics raise uric acid and trigger gout, so consider switching to a different blood pressure drug, such as losartan, which actually lowers uric acid, or a calcium channel blocker. Also counsel on alcohol, especially beer, and purine-rich foods. Do not stop the diuretic abruptly without a replacement, since blood pressure control still matters.

cards.q: A 72-year-old with a new headache, scalp tenderness and pain when chewing is suspected of having giant cell arteritis. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Start high-dose steroids immediately, before any test result. Do not wait for the temporal artery biopsy, because the next event can be sudden, permanent blindness. The biopsy can still be done within 2 weeks of starting steroids and usually remains positive, so starting treatment first does not lose the diagnosis.

cards.q: A patient with giant cell arteritis develops sudden vision loss in one eye. What is the immediate management?
cards.a: Give intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone urgently and get an immediate ophthalmology review. Vision loss in giant cell arteritis is an emergency, because the other eye can go blind within days if the inflammation is not switched off. This is one of the few rheumatology situations where intravenous steroids are given straight away.

cards.q: A patient with giant cell arteritis keeps relapsing when steroids are tapered. What steroid-sparing treatment can be added?
cards.a: Tocilizumab, an IL-6 blocker, which allows the steroid dose to be reduced and keeps more patients in remission. It is used for relapsing or large-vessel giant cell arteritis. Monitor for infection, liver enzymes and lipids, and remember that it suppresses CRP, so a normal CRP does not always mean the disease is quiet.

cards.q: A 68-year-old has aching and stiffness in the shoulders and hips for 6 weeks, worse in the morning, with a very high ESR. The muscle strength is normal and the CK is normal. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Polymyalgia rheumatica. Treat with low-dose prednisone, and expect a dramatic improvement within days, which itself supports the diagnosis. It affects people over 50, causes girdle pain and stiffness without true weakness, and has a high ESR. Always check for giant cell arteritis at the same time, since the two often occur together.

cards.q: A patient with polymyalgia rheumatica does not improve on low-dose prednisone. What should you reconsider?
cards.a: The diagnosis. Polymyalgia rheumatica normally responds dramatically to low-dose steroids within a week. If it does not, consider giant cell arteritis, inflammatory myopathy, malignancy, infection or hypothyroidism instead. Do not just keep raising the steroid dose without rethinking the diagnosis.

cards.q: A patient with polymyalgia rheumatica develops a new headache, jaw pain and blurred vision. What must you do urgently?
cards.a: Evaluate for giant cell arteritis and start high-dose steroids immediately if suspected. Up to a fifth of patients with polymyalgia rheumatica also have giant cell arteritis, and the headache and visual symptoms are warning signs of impending blindness. The steroid dose for giant cell arteritis is much higher than for polymyalgia rheumatica alone.

cards.q: A patient has sinusitis, nosebleeds, a cough with blood, and a rising creatinine with blood in the urine. ANCA testing shows c-ANCA (anti-PR3). What is the diagnosis and the induction treatment?
cards.a: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's). It affects the upper airway, lungs and kidneys. Induction is high-dose steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide to switch off the inflammation quickly. This is organ-threatening disease, so do not treat it with steroids alone, and involve nephrology and respiratory teams.

cards.q: How do you distinguish microscopic polyangiitis from granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
cards.a: Microscopic polyangiitis is usually p-ANCA (anti-MPO) positive, causes kidney and lung disease, but does not cause the granulomatous upper airway disease, such as sinusitis, nosebleeds and saddle-nose deformity, that is typical of GPA. Both are small-vessel ANCA vasculitis and both are treated with steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide, but the clinical pattern differs.

cards.q: A patient with long-standing asthma, a high eosinophil count, numbness in the feet and a rash is found to be p-ANCA positive. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, formerly Churg-Strauss). The clue is asthma that comes years before the vasculitis, with eosinophilia and nerve involvement. Treat with high-dose steroids, adding immunosuppression for severe disease, and consider mepolizumab, an anti-IL-5 drug, for relapsing disease.

cards.q: A patient with ANCA vasculitis develops coughing up blood, a falling haemoglobin and diffuse infiltrates on chest X-ray. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Admit to intensive care and give high-dose steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide urgently. This is diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, a life-threatening complication where the lung capillaries bleed. Plasmapheresis is considered in the most severe cases. Do not wait for more tests while the patient is bleeding into their lungs.

cards.q: After induction treatment for ANCA vasculitis, what is the maintenance plan, and should you follow the ANCA level alone?
cards.a: Maintain remission with rituximab or azathioprine for at least 18 to 24 months, and taper steroids. Do not treat the ANCA titre alone: a rising ANCA can precede a relapse, but many patients relapse without a rise and some stay positive in remission. Treat the patient's symptoms, urine and kidney function, using the ANCA level only as supporting information.

cards.q: A patient with known ANCA vasculitis develops a fever, a rising CRP and worsening kidney function. How do you tell a flare from an infection?
cards.a: You cannot tell from blood tests alone, since both raise the CRP. Take blood and urine cultures, check a chest X-ray and look for a source of infection before increasing immunosuppression. Giving more steroids and cyclophosphamide to a patient who actually has an infection can be fatal, so exclude infection first, urgently.

cards.q: A patient has painful nodules along the arteries, livedo reticularis on the legs, high blood pressure and a positive hepatitis B test, with negative ANCA. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Polyarteritis nodosa, a medium-vessel vasculitis that is classically associated with hepatitis B and is ANCA-negative. Treat with steroids plus cyclophosphamide for severe disease, and add antiviral treatment for the hepatitis B, since the virus is driving the vasculitis. Without antivirals, immunosuppression alone lets the hepatitis flare.

cards.q: A young woman has arm claudication, a weak pulse in one arm, a blood pressure difference between the arms and a bruit over the subclavian artery. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
cards.a: Takayasu arteritis, a large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches that typically affects young women. Start high-dose steroids to control the inflammation, then add a steroid-sparing drug such as methotrexate or tocilizumab. Surgery or stenting is only done when the disease is quiet, because operating on inflamed arteries fails.

cards.q: A patient with diffuse scleroderma develops a sudden rise in blood pressure and a rising creatinine over a few days. What is the diagnosis and the immediate treatment?
cards.a: Scleroderma renal crisis, a life-threatening emergency. Start an ACE inhibitor immediately, even if the creatinine is rising, because ACE inhibitors are the only treatment proven to save the kidney and the patient in this situation. Do not stop the ACE inhibitor because the creatinine goes up at first; that rise is expected.

cards.q: Why should high-dose steroids be avoided in a patient with diffuse scleroderma?
cards.a: High-dose steroids are a risk factor for scleroderma renal crisis, the sudden kidney failure with severe hypertension that can kill. Use the lowest steroid dose possible, and if steroids are unavoidable, monitor the blood pressure and creatinine very closely. This is the opposite of most rheumatic diseases, where high-dose steroids are the rescue treatment.

cards.q: A patient with limited scleroderma (CREST) develops progressive breathlessness. What complication must you screen for?
cards.a: Pulmonary arterial hypertension, which is common in limited scleroderma and causes breathlessness, fatigue and eventually right heart failure. Screen with an echocardiogram and lung function tests, looking for a low DLCO with preserved lung volumes. Early detection matters because treatment with pulmonary vasodilators works best before the right heart fails.

cards.q: A patient with scleroderma has a dry cough, breathlessness and crackles, with ground-glass change on CT. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Interstitial lung disease, the leading cause of death in scleroderma. Confirm with lung function tests and high-resolution CT, then treat with mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide to slow the scarring. Steroids alone are not enough and carry the risk of renal crisis, so the immunosuppressant is the key treatment.

cards.q: A patient with scleroderma has painful, white-then-blue fingers in the cold. What is the first-line treatment for Raynaud's phenomenon?
cards.a: Keep the hands warm and use a calcium channel blocker such as nifedipine or amlodipine, which relaxes the blood vessels and reduces the attacks. Avoid beta-blockers and other vasoconstrictors, which make it worse, and stop smoking. For severe digital ulcers, add a PDE5 inhibitor such as sildenafil.

cards.q: A patient with scleroderma has severe heartburn and difficulty swallowing solids and liquids. What is the cause and the management?
cards.a: Oesophageal dysmotility from fibrosis of the oesophagus, which is part of scleroderma. Treat the reflux with a proton pump inhibitor, advise small meals and not lying flat after eating, and screen for Barrett's oesophagus with endoscopy. The dysmotility itself does not reverse, so the aim is to prevent reflux damage and aspiration.

cards.q: A patient with scleroderma develops a painful ulcer on a fingertip that will not heal. What is the management?
cards.a: Optimise blood flow with a calcium channel blocker and, if needed, a PDE5 inhibitor such as sildenafil, plus meticulous wound care and treatment of any infection. Keep the hand warm and avoid trauma and vasoconstrictors. Digital ulcers in scleroderma are ischaemic, so they heal only if the blood supply improves; antibiotics alone will not fix them.

cards.q: A patient has a purple rash around the eyes, raised red knuckles, weak shoulders and hips, and difficulty swallowing. What is the diagnosis and what screening is essential?
cards.a: Dermatomyositis, suggested by the heliotrope rash around the eyes and Gottron papules over the knuckles, with proximal muscle weakness and a high CK. Screen for an underlying cancer, because dermatomyositis in adults is strongly associated with malignancy, especially in older patients. Treat with high-dose steroids and arrange age-appropriate cancer screening.

cards.q: An older man has slowly progressive weakness in the fingers and the quadriceps over years, with only a mildly raised CK, and steroids have not helped. What is the likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Inclusion body myositis. Unlike polymyositis, it affects distal muscles such as finger flexors and quadriceps, progresses slowly, and responds poorly to steroids. The clue is the pattern of weakness and the lack of response to immunosuppression. Do not keep escalating steroids; focus on physiotherapy, falls prevention and supportive care.

cards.q: A patient with polymyositis is started on high-dose steroids. What is the long-term treatment plan?
cards.a: Taper the steroids slowly and add a steroid-sparing drug such as methotrexate or azathioprine, so the steroid dose can be reduced without a flare. Monitor muscle strength and CK levels, and watch for steroid complications including diabetes, weight gain and bone loss. The goal is remission on the lowest possible steroid dose.

cards.q: A patient with dermatomyositis develops severe difficulty swallowing and chokes on liquids. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Admit them, arrange a swallow assessment, keep them nil by mouth if aspiration is a risk, and give intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) for severe, refractory disease with dysphagia. Dysphagia in myositis risks aspiration pneumonia, which is a leading cause of death. IVIG works faster than oral immunosuppressants in this situation.

cards.q: A patient on a statin develops muscle pain and a very high CK. The symptoms do not improve weeks after stopping the statin. What should you consider?
cards.a: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, an autoimmune muscle disease triggered by statins, often with anti-HMGCR antibodies. Unlike ordinary statin myopathy, it does not settle when the statin is stopped, because the immune system keeps attacking the muscle. It needs steroids and immunosuppression, not just stopping the statin.

cards.q: A patient has muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease, cracked skin on the fingers (mechanic's hands) and Raynaud's phenomenon. What antibody and syndrome is this?
cards.a: Anti-synthetase syndrome, most often with anti-Jo-1 antibodies. It links inflammatory myositis with lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud's and mechanic's hands. The lung disease often determines the prognosis, so check lung function and CT early, and treat with steroids plus a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as mycophenolate or azathioprine.

cards.q: A patient with Sjogren's syndrome has severe dry eyes and dry mouth despite artificial tears. What is the next step?
cards.a: Try a saliva stimulant such as pilocarpine or cevimeline, which stimulate the remaining gland function to produce more saliva and tears. These only work if some gland function remains, so they help early disease more than late disease. Continue artificial tears and saliva substitutes, and arrange regular dental care, since dry mouth causes rapid tooth decay.

cards.q: A patient with Sjogren's syndrome has a persistently enlarged parotid gland and a low-grade fever. What complication must you rule out?
cards.a: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, usually a MALT lymphoma of the parotid gland. Patients with Sjogren's have a much higher risk of lymphoma, and a persistently swollen parotid, fever, weight loss or a falling complement level are warning signs. Arrange urgent imaging and a biopsy, and involve haematology.

cards.q: A patient with Sjogren's syndrome develops numbness and tingling in the feet and a purpuric rash on the legs. What does this mean and how is it treated?
cards.a: Systemic Sjogren's with vasculitis and peripheral neuropathy, which means the disease has spread beyond the glands. Treat with steroids and, for severe disease, rituximab or another immunosuppressant. Dry eyes and mouth alone need only symptom relief, but nerve and blood vessel involvement needs immunosuppression.

cards.q: A patient with Sjogren's syndrome keeps getting dental cavities despite brushing. Why, and what should you advise?
cards.a: Saliva protects teeth, and Sjogren's destroys the salivary glands, so the mouth is dry and cavities develop rapidly. Advise fluoride toothpaste and fluoride treatments, saliva substitutes, sugar-free gum to stimulate saliva, frequent dental checks and avoiding sugary drinks. Dental care is part of Sjogren's treatment, not an afterthought.

cards.q: A patient with Sjogren's syndrome has dry eyes and mouth but negative anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies. How can the diagnosis still be confirmed?
cards.a: With a minor salivary gland (lip) biopsy showing lymphocytic inflammation, or with objective tests such as a Schirmer test for tear production and measurement of saliva flow. Up to a third of patients with Sjogren's are antibody-negative, so a negative blood test does not exclude it. The biopsy is the most specific test when the antibodies are negative.

cards.q: A young man with ankylosing spondylitis has ongoing back pain despite regular NSAIDs and physiotherapy. What is the first-line drug treatment, and what is next if it fails?
cards.a: NSAIDs plus regular exercise and physiotherapy are first-line, because they reduce pain and stiffness and keep the spine mobile. If pain and inflammation persist despite NSAIDs, the next step is a TNF inhibitor (or an IL-17 inhibitor), which controls the inflammation and slows the fusion of the spine. Do not add a conventional DMARD such as methotrexate for the spine, because it does not work for axial disease.

cards.q: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has recurrent painful red eyes. Which biologic is preferred, and which should be avoided?
cards.a: A monoclonal TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab or infliximab is preferred, because it treats both the spine and the uveitis. Avoid etanercept, a soluble TNF receptor, because it does not prevent uveitis flares and is less effective for eye inflammation. The choice of biologic depends on which other organs are involved, not just the back pain.

cards.q: A patient has ankylosing spondylitis with inflammatory bowel disease. Which biologic do you choose, and which do you avoid?
cards.a: Choose a monoclonal TNF inhibitor such as infliximab or adalimumab, which treats both the joints and the bowel. Avoid etanercept, which does not treat bowel inflammation, and avoid IL-17 inhibitors, which can worsen inflammatory bowel disease. The drug must cover every organ involved, so the bowel disease decides the choice.

cards.q: A patient with psoriatic arthritis has swollen joints and severe skin psoriasis. What is the treatment approach?
cards.a: Start with NSAIDs, then methotrexate if the joints remain active, but for severe skin disease or joints that do not respond, use a biologic such as a TNF, IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor, which treats both the skin and the joints. Methotrexate helps the joints and skin modestly, but biologics are much more effective when both are severe.

cards.q: A patient with psoriatic arthritis has failed methotrexate and has severe psoriasis covering most of the body. Which drug class is preferred?
cards.a: An IL-17 inhibitor or IL-23 inhibitor, or a TNF inhibitor, all of which treat both the skin and the joints. IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors are particularly effective for the skin. Choose based on other features: avoid IL-17 inhibitors if there is inflammatory bowel disease, and consider a TNF inhibitor if there is uveitis.

cards.q: A young man develops a painful swollen knee, red eyes and painful urination a few weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. What is the diagnosis and management?
cards.a: Reactive arthritis, an inflammatory arthritis triggered by an infection elsewhere, usually the gut or the urinary tract, often in HLA-B27 positive people. Treat with NSAIDs and physiotherapy, and treat any ongoing infection, but do not give antibiotics for the arthritis itself once the infection has cleared. It usually resolves over months, though some patients develop chronic disease.
