cards.q: A patient has urethritis, conjunctivitis and arthritis together. What is this triad called, and what infection should you screen for?
cards.a: Reiter's syndrome, the classic triad of reactive arthritis. Screen for sexually transmitted infections, especially chlamydia, and for gut infections such as Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter. Treat the infection if it is still present, and manage the arthritis with NSAIDs.

cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops painful, swollen knees. What is the diagnosis, and what treatment caution applies?
cards.a: Enteropathic arthritis, the joint inflammation that accompanies inflammatory bowel disease. Treating the bowel disease often improves the joints. Use NSAIDs cautiously, because they can flare the bowel disease, and prefer a monoclonal TNF inhibitor, which treats both. Steroids for the joints alone are not the answer.

cards.q: A patient with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has a minor fall and now has severe, localised back pain. What must you do?
cards.a: Get a CT scan of the spine urgently. A fused, rigid spine fractures easily even with minor trauma, and the fracture is often missed on plain X-ray. A missed spinal fracture can cause cord injury and paralysis. Do not dismiss new back pain after trauma in ankylosing spondylitis as just a flare.

cards.q: A 30-year-old has back pain that is worse in the morning and at night, improves with exercise, and gets better with NSAIDs. What type of back pain is this, and what does it suggest?
cards.a: Inflammatory back pain, which suggests a spondyloarthritis such as ankylosing spondylitis. Mechanical back pain is worse with movement and better with rest, while inflammatory back pain is worse with rest and better with movement, with morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes. This pattern in a young person should prompt testing for HLA-B27 and imaging of the sacroiliac joints.

cards.q: A patient with knee osteoarthritis asks what treatment works best before considering surgery. What do you recommend first?
cards.a: Weight loss if overweight, regular low-impact exercise such as walking or swimming, and physiotherapy to strengthen the quadriceps. These reduce pain and improve function as well as any drug, and they slow progression. Add topical NSAIDs for pain relief. Drugs alone without exercise and weight loss give a much poorer result.

cards.q: A patient with knee osteoarthritis needs pain relief but has a history of stomach ulcer and kidney disease. What is the safest drug option?
cards.a: A topical NSAID, such as diclofenac gel, applied to the knee. It relieves pain with very little absorption into the bloodstream, so it avoids the stomach, kidney and heart risks of oral NSAIDs. Acetaminophen is another option, though it is less effective. Avoid oral NSAIDs in this patient unless there is no alternative, and then only with a proton pump inhibitor.

cards.q: A patient with knee osteoarthritis has a hot, swollen knee during a flare. What injection can help, and what should you avoid injecting?
cards.a: An intra-articular corticosteroid injection, which reduces the inflammation and pain for weeks. It is useful for flares, but should not be given repeatedly in the same joint many times a year, and must not be given if infection is suspected. Hyaluronic acid injections are not routinely recommended, as the evidence for benefit is weak.

cards.q: A patient with severe hip osteoarthritis has pain that limits walking and sleep despite weight loss, exercise, physiotherapy and painkillers. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Refer for total hip replacement. Joint replacement is the definitive treatment for end-stage osteoarthritis when pain and loss of function persist despite conservative treatment, and it reliably relieves pain and restores mobility. Do not keep adding painkillers indefinitely when the joint is worn out; the operation is the treatment.

cards.q: An elderly patient with osteoarthritis and chronic kidney disease needs pain relief. What should you avoid and what can you use instead?
cards.a: Avoid oral NSAIDs, because they reduce kidney blood flow, raise blood pressure, cause fluid retention and worsen kidney disease. Use topical NSAIDs, acetaminophen within safe daily limits, physiotherapy and weight loss instead. If pain remains severe, consider a referral for joint replacement rather than accepting the risks of long-term oral NSAIDs.

cards.q: A patient with osteoarthritis of the hands has bony lumps on the finger joints and pain when gripping. What are the lumps, and what is the treatment?
cards.a: Heberden's nodes at the DIP joints and Bouchard's nodes at the PIP joints, which are bony swellings from osteoarthritis. Treat with topical NSAIDs, hand exercises, splinting and avoiding heavy gripping. Do not give DMARDs or biologics, which are for inflammatory arthritis and do not help osteoarthritis.

cards.q: A patient with widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep and normal blood tests is diagnosed with fibromyalgia. What is the most effective treatment?
cards.a: Graded exercise, good sleep habits and cognitive behavioural therapy, with a drug such as duloxetine, pregabalin or low-dose amitriptyline if needed. Exercise is the single most effective treatment, even though it feels counterintuitive when in pain. Explain that fibromyalgia is a problem of pain processing, not joint damage, so the joints are not being destroyed.

cards.q: A patient with fibromyalgia asks for opioids or steroids for their pain. What do you advise?
cards.a: Do not use opioids or steroids for fibromyalgia. Opioids make pain worse over time through opioid-induced hyperalgesia and cause dependence, and steroids do not help because there is no inflammation to suppress. The effective treatments are exercise, sleep, psychological support and drugs such as duloxetine or pregabalin. Prescribing opioids for fibromyalgia is a common error.

cards.q: A patient with widespread pain and fatigue is found to have a very high TSH and low free T4. What is the relevance to their pain?
cards.a: Hypothyroidism can mimic fibromyalgia, causing widespread muscle pain, fatigue, stiffness and poor sleep. Always check thyroid function before diagnosing fibromyalgia, because treating the thyroid can resolve the symptoms. Other mimics to exclude are inflammatory arthritis, vitamin D deficiency and depression.

cards.q: A patient with fibromyalgia also has depression. How does treating the mood affect the pain?
cards.a: Treating the depression often improves the pain, because fibromyalgia, depression and poor sleep amplify each other through shared pathways in the brain. Drugs such as duloxetine and amitriptyline help both mood and pain. Do not treat the pain and the mood as separate problems; addressing both together gives a much better result.

cards.q: A patient has a hot, swollen knee with fever. What is the first investigation, and should you wait for the result before giving antibiotics?
cards.a: Aspirate the joint immediately and send the fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals. If the patient is unwell or the fluid looks infected, start antibiotics after the aspiration without waiting for the culture result, and get an orthopaedic opinion urgently. Delaying treatment for septic arthritis destroys the cartilage within days.

cards.q: A patient with septic arthritis of the knee is started on intravenous antibiotics. What else is essential for treatment?
cards.a: Drainage of the joint, usually by surgical washout, repeated aspiration, or arthroscopy. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus from a closed joint space, and the infected fluid destroys cartilage quickly. Continue intravenous antibiotics for weeks, guided by the culture result and an infectious diseases opinion.

cards.q: A young sexually active patient has migratory joint pains, tenosynovitis of the wrist, and small pustules on the skin. What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Disseminated gonococcal infection causing gonococcal arthritis. Treat with ceftriaxone, and screen for other sexually transmitted infections including chlamydia and HIV, and treat sexual partners. The joint fluid culture is often negative, so the diagnosis is clinical. Do not dismiss it as a viral arthritis.

cards.q: A patient with a knee replacement develops pain, swelling and fever 6 months after surgery. What is the concern and the management?
cards.a: Prosthetic joint infection, which is a serious complication of joint replacement. Refer urgently to orthopaedics and infectious diseases. Treatment usually requires surgery, often removal of the prosthesis and a staged revision, plus prolonged antibiotics. Do not just give oral antibiotics and hope, because bacteria form a biofilm on the metal that antibiotics cannot clear.

cards.q: A patient has a hot, swollen joint with a very high white cell count in the fluid, but the Gram stain and culture are negative. What should you do?
cards.a: Still treat as septic arthritis if the clinical suspicion is high. Cultures can be negative, especially if antibiotics were given before the aspiration, and gonococcal and some other infections are hard to grow. Also consider that gout and infection can coexist in the same joint, so finding crystals does not exclude infection. When in doubt, treat for infection.

cards.q: A patient about to start a biologic drug has never had the shingles vaccine. What should you do, and why does the timing matter?
cards.a: Give the recombinant shingles vaccine before starting the biologic if possible, and avoid live vaccines once immunosuppression has started. Biologics and JAK inhibitors raise the risk of shingles, and live vaccines are unsafe on immunosuppression because the weakened virus can cause disease. Inactivated vaccines should be given before or during treatment, but live vaccines must be given at least 4 weeks before starting.

cards.q: A patient on methotrexate is prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary infection. What is the problem with this combination?
cards.a: Both drugs suppress the bone marrow, and together they can cause severe pancytopenia, a dangerous drop in all blood cells. Avoid the combination: choose a different antibiotic for the infection, or hold the methotrexate. This is a classic drug interaction that is easy to miss because both drugs are common.

cards.q: A patient on azathioprine for lupus is started on allopurinol for gout. What is the danger, and what must you do?
cards.a: Allopurinol blocks the breakdown of azathioprine, so azathioprine levels rise sharply and cause severe bone marrow suppression. Either avoid the combination or reduce the azathioprine dose to about a quarter and monitor blood counts very closely. This interaction is a common cause of life-threatening pancytopenia.

cards.q: A patient on hydroxychloroquine is started on another drug that prolongs the QT interval. What should you check?
cards.a: Check an ECG for QT prolongation, because hydroxychloroquine can prolong the QT interval and the combination increases the risk of a dangerous arrhythmia. Check potassium and magnesium too, since low levels worsen the risk. Review the drug list for other QT-prolonging drugs and stop or replace them where possible.

cards.q: A patient with RA takes daily prednisone and an NSAID together. What extra drug should you prescribe, and why?
cards.a: A proton pump inhibitor, because steroids plus NSAIDs together greatly increase the risk of stomach ulcer and gastrointestinal bleeding. Either drug alone raises the risk, but the combination is much worse. Do not wait for stomach pain to appear; the first sign of a bleed can be a life-threatening haemorrhage.

cards.q: A patient will be on prednisone 10 mg daily for many months for a rheumatic disease. What bone and infection precautions are needed?
cards.a: Give calcium and vitamin D, and a bisphosphonate to prevent steroid-induced osteoporosis, since bone loss is fastest in the first months of steroids. Monitor blood pressure and blood sugar, and consider Pneumocystis prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if the dose is high or combined with another immunosuppressant. Long-term steroids need a prevention plan, not just a prescription.

cards.q: A 28-week preterm infant has grunting, nasal flaring, retractions and hypoxaemia minutes after birth, with a ground-glass chest X-ray and air bronchograms. What is the diagnosis and the single most important missing substance?
cards.a: Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency. Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and keeps alveoli open at end-expiration; without it alveoli collapse, causing atelectasis, hypoxaemia and increased work of breathing. Management is CPAP plus surfactant replacement, not just oxygen alone.

cards.q: A preterm infant with RDS is on CPAP but still needs more than 40 percent oxygen and has worsening work of breathing. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Give surfactant, ideally early and rescue rather than waiting for failure. Surfactant directly replaces what is missing and improves oxygenation and compliance. CPAP alone cannot fix surfactant deficiency, and delaying surfactant increases the risk of air leak and prolonged ventilation.

cards.q: A mother at 30 weeks is in preterm labour. What single antenatal drug most reduces neonatal RDS, and when should it be given?
cards.a: Antenatal corticosteroids, betamethasone or dexamethasone, given to the mother before delivery. Steroids accelerate fetal lung maturity and surfactant production. They work best when delivery occurs 48 hours after the first dose but benefit is seen even with a shorter interval, so give them even if delivery seems imminent.

cards.q: A preterm infant with RDS is intubated. Why is CPAP preferred over prolonged mechanical ventilation when the baby can breathe on its own?
cards.a: CPAP keeps alveoli open with continuous positive pressure without an endotracheal tube, reducing ventilator-induced lung injury and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Mechanical ventilation saves lives when needed, but volutrauma and barotrauma from the ventilator damage the immature lung, so the least invasive support that works is best.

cards.q: A 26-week infant on a ventilator develops a sudden fall in oxygen saturation, absent breath sounds on the right and a hyperresonant chest. What happened and what do you do first?
cards.a: Tension pneumothorax, an air leak complication of RDS and positive pressure ventilation. The trapped air compresses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, collapsing venous return. This is an emergency: needle decompression followed by a chest tube, before waiting for a chest X-ray.

cards.q: A preterm infant with RDS is improving on CPAP. What is the most common long-term lung complication of prematurity and ventilation, and what causes it?
cards.a: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia, chronic lung disease of prematurity. It results from oxygen toxicity, ventilator injury, inflammation and arrested lung development in the very preterm lung. Prevention is minimising ventilation time and oxygen exposure, using CPAP early and surfactant, rather than treating it after it is established.

cards.q: Why is a patent ductus arteriosus more common and more problematic in preterm infants with RDS?
cards.a: The preterm ductus is less responsive to oxygen and more sensitive to prostaglandins, so it stays open, and the low pulmonary resistance of RDS lets blood shunt left to right, flooding the lungs and stealing blood from the systemic circulation. It worsens respiratory failure and raises the risk of necrotising enterocolitis and intraventricular haemorrhage.

cards.q: A preterm infant with a haemodynamically significant PDA and worsening ventilation is being considered for treatment. What is the first-line medical option and what must be checked first?
cards.a: A cyclo-oxygenase inhibitor such as indomethacin or ibuprofen, which blocks prostaglandin synthesis and closes the ductus. Check renal function, platelet count and bleeding risk first, because these drugs can impair kidney perfusion and platelet function, and do not give them if there is active bleeding or severe renal failure.

cards.q: An infant with RDS is on high ventilator pressures and develops abdominal distension and a falling blood pressure. Besides pneumothorax, what ventilator-related complication should you consider?
cards.a: Air leak with pulmonary interstitial emphysema, where air dissects into the lung interstitium from overdistension. It worsens gas exchange and can progress to pneumothorax. Management is reducing ventilator pressures and tidal volumes, allowing permissive hypercapnia rather than forcing normal carbon dioxide levels.

cards.q: A mother is offered antenatal steroids at 34 weeks for threatened preterm birth. Why is this still worthwhile at this gestation?
cards.a: Steroids still reduce RDS, intraventricular haemorrhage and neonatal death even in late preterm infants, because lung maturity is incomplete until term. The benefit is smaller than at 28 weeks but real, and a single course is low risk, so it is given whenever preterm birth is expected before 37 weeks.

cards.q: A 3-day-old term infant has fever, lethargy, poor feeding and a temperature of 38.5 C. What is the most likely diagnosis and why must you act before cultures return?
cards.a: Early-onset neonatal sepsis, usually from Group B Streptococcus or E. coli acquired around delivery. Neonates decompensate fast and show few localising signs, so you start empiric antibiotics immediately after cultures are drawn. Waiting for culture results can be fatal, because bacteraemia progresses to shock within hours.

cards.q: A newborn with suspected sepsis has blood cultures drawn. Which two antibiotics are started empirically for early-onset sepsis, and why this combination?
cards.a: Ampicillin plus gentamicin. Ampicillin covers Group B Streptococcus and Listeria, which gentamicin misses, while gentamicin covers Gram-negative organisms such as E. coli. Together they cover the organisms most likely to kill a newborn in the first week of life.

cards.q: A 10-day-old infant presents with fever, irritability and poor feeding. How does the empiric antibiotic choice differ from early-onset sepsis?
cards.a: Late-onset sepsis needs broader cover, typically vancomycin plus gentamicin or a third-generation cephalosporin, because coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negatives predominate after the first week. Early-onset cover with ampicillin plus gentamicin is too narrow for these hospital-acquired organisms.

cards.q: A term infant born to a mother with prolonged rupture of membranes for 20 hours is well-appearing with normal vital signs. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Observe closely and obtain a sepsis screen with blood culture, but do not automatically start antibiotics in a well-appearing term infant. Prolonged rupture raises risk, yet most such infants are not infected; close monitoring with prompt antibiotics if signs appear avoids unnecessary antibiotic exposure and NICU admission.

cards.q: A neonate with suspected sepsis has a full septic workup. When is a lumbar puncture mandatory, and when can it be deferred?
cards.a: Do a lumbar puncture when the infant has signs of meningitis such as lethargy, irritability, seizures, a bulging fontanelle, or when sepsis is clinically likely and the baby is stable enough. Defer it only if the infant is too unstable or has a coagulopathy, and do it as soon as the baby stabilises, because meningitis changes the antibiotic choice and duration.

cards.q: A neonatal blood culture grows Group B Streptococcus. The infant is improving on ampicillin and gentamicin. What is the next best step in management?
cards.a: Stop the gentamicin and continue ampicillin alone once the organism and its sensitivities are known. Narrowing antibiotics reduces nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity from gentamicin while still treating the infection, and it is a core principle of antimicrobial stewardship.

cards.q: A 5-day-old infant with sepsis develops a falling platelet count, prolonged clotting times and bleeding from venepuncture sites. What complication has developed and why?
cards.a: Disseminated intravascular coagulation. Severe sepsis triggers widespread clotting that consumes platelets and clotting factors, so the baby paradoxically bleeds. Treat the underlying sepsis urgently, support with blood products as needed, and do not give heparin routinely in neonatal DIC.

cards.q: A mother was Group B Streptococcus positive but received no intrapartum antibiotics. Her term baby is well. What is the most important thing to do in the first 24 hours?
cards.a: Close observation for at least 24 to 48 hours with vital signs and feeding assessment, and a low threshold for a sepsis workup. Most exposed infants do not develop disease, so routine antibiotics for every well baby are not indicated, but early-onset GBS sepsis can present within hours and must be caught early.

cards.q: A preterm infant with sepsis is hypotensive despite fluids and antibiotics. What is the next step, and why do neonates respond differently to shock than adults?
cards.a: Start a vasopressor such as dopamine or adrenaline, and consider hydrocortisone if refractory. Neonatal shock is often cardiogenic as well as distributive, with poor myocardial reserve, so fluids alone frequently fail and early inotropic support is needed to maintain perfusion to the brain and gut.

cards.q: A neonate has suspected sepsis and a lumbar puncture shows a high white cell count with low glucose in the cerebrospinal fluid. How long must antibiotics be continued?
cards.a: At least 14 to 21 days for bacterial meningitis, much longer than for bacteraemia alone. The blood-brain barrier limits antibiotic penetration, so a short course risks relapse and brain injury. A repeat lumbar puncture is often done to confirm the fluid has sterilised.

cards.q: A term infant born by caesarean section develops respiratory distress and fever on day 2, with a maternal history of chorioamnionitis. What organism should you cover beyond Group B Streptococcus?
cards.a: E. coli and other Gram-negatives, plus Listeria. Chorioamnionitis exposes the fetus to a broad range of organisms, and E. coli is the leading cause of early-onset sepsis in preterm infants and in mothers with chorioamnionitis. Ampicillin plus gentamicin covers this spectrum.

cards.q: A 2-day-old term infant has yellow skin starting on the face and spreading downward, is feeding well and is otherwise normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Physiologic jaundice. It appears after 24 hours of life, peaks at 3 to 5 days and resolves by 1 to 2 weeks, caused by increased red cell breakdown plus an immature liver that conjugates bilirubin slowly. It needs monitoring, not automatic treatment, because it is a normal transition.

cards.q: A newborn is jaundiced within the first 24 hours of life. Why is this always pathologic, and what is the first step?
cards.a: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is never physiologic and suggests haemolysis, most often ABO or Rh incompatibility. The first step is urgent total and direct bilirubin, blood group, Coombs test and haemoglobin, because bilirubin can rise fast enough to cause kernicterus within hours.

cards.q: A 3-day-old breastfed infant has jaundice with a bilirubin of 14 mg per dL and is otherwise well. What is the most likely cause and what is the management?
cards.a: Breastfeeding jaundice from inadequate milk intake and reduced stooling, which increases enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. Management is supporting breastfeeding with frequent feeds and monitoring bilirubin, not stopping breastfeeding. Stopping feeds worsens the problem by reducing gut motility.

cards.q: A 2-week-old breastfed infant remains jaundiced with a bilirubin of 12 mg per dL, is gaining weight well and has normal stools. What is the diagnosis and what should you NOT do?
cards.a: Breast milk jaundice, caused by substances in breast milk that inhibit bilirubin conjugation. It is benign and resolves over weeks. Do not stop breastfeeding and do not order extensive testing in a thriving infant, because the history and the well appearance make other causes unlikely.

cards.q: A newborn has a total bilirubin of 18 mg per dL at 48 hours, is lethargic and has a high-pitched cry. What is the feared complication and where does bilirubin damage the brain?
cards.a: Kernicterus, bilirubin-induced brain injury, which deposits unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei. The lethargy and high-pitched cry are early signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. This is a neurologic emergency requiring immediate lowering of bilirubin.

cards.q: A term infant has a bilirubin level above the phototherapy threshold but below the exchange transfusion threshold. What is the treatment and how does it work?
cards.a: Phototherapy. Blue light converts unconjugated bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble isomers that can be excreted in urine and stool without liver conjugation. Maximise skin exposure, protect the eyes, maintain hydration, and recheck bilirubin regularly.

cards.q: During phototherapy, what are the two most important practical steps that are often forgotten?
cards.a: Eye protection and maintaining hydration and temperature. The intense light can damage the retina, so eye shields must stay on, and phototherapy increases insensible water loss and can cause overheating or dehydration, so fluids and temperature need close monitoring.

cards.q: A newborn with haemolytic disease has a bilirubin rising despite intensive phototherapy and shows signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. What is the definitive treatment?
cards.a: Exchange transfusion. It removes bilirubin, antibody-coated red cells and circulating antibodies, replacing them with donor blood. It is reserved for bilirubin at or above the exchange threshold or clinical encephalopathy, because it carries risks of infection, electrolyte shifts and cardiac instability.

cards.q: A newborn is jaundiced with a predominantly direct, conjugated bilirubin. Why does this change the workup completely?
cards.a: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiologic and indicates cholestasis, most urgently biliary atresia. Phototherapy does not treat it, and delaying the diagnosis risks irreversible liver damage. Urgent workup includes liver function tests, ultrasound and referral to paediatric hepatology.

cards.q: An infant with biliary atresia is diagnosed at 8 weeks. Why is the timing of surgery critical?
cards.a: The Kasai portoenterostomy works best when done before 60 days of life, because ongoing bile duct destruction leads to irreversible cirrhosis. Every week of delay worsens the outcome, so conjugated jaundice in a young infant must be investigated urgently and never watched.

cards.q: A newborn has ABO incompatibility, mother blood group O and baby group A, with a positive direct Coombs test. What is the mechanism of jaundice here?
cards.a: Maternal anti-A IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red cells, causing haemolysis and a rapid rise in unconjugated bilirubin. This is why jaundice appears early, anaemia develops, and the baby needs close bilirubin monitoring and often phototherapy.

cards.q: A mother is Rh negative and her baby is Rh positive. What preventive treatment should she have received, and what happens if she did not?
cards.a: Anti-D immunoglobulin during pregnancy and after delivery. It prevents the mother from forming anti-D antibodies that would attack the red cells of this and future Rh-positive babies, causing severe haemolytic disease. Without it, sensitisation can cause hydrops fetalis in a later pregnancy.

cards.q: A 1-hour-old infant of a diabetic mother is jittery, sweaty and lethargic with a blood glucose of 30 mg per dL. What is the mechanism and the immediate treatment?
cards.a: Neonatal hypoglycaemia from hyperinsulinism. High maternal glucose drove high fetal insulin, and after the cord is cut the glucose supply stops but insulin remains high. Give intravenous dextrose immediately, because the brain depends on glucose and prolonged hypoglycaemia causes seizures and permanent brain injury.

cards.q: A term infant has a blood glucose of 45 mg per dL at 1 hour of life, is feeding well and is asymptomatic. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Feed the baby and recheck the glucose. Asymptomatic borderline hypoglycaemia in a well term infant is often transient and responds to early feeding. Intravenous dextrose is reserved for symptomatic babies or persistently low glucose despite feeding.

cards.q: A newborn has recurrent hypoglycaemia despite frequent feeds and intravenous dextrose, requiring a very high glucose infusion rate. What is the most likely underlying cause?
cards.a: Congenital hyperinsulinism, persistent excess insulin secretion. The clue is the high glucose infusion rate needed to maintain normal glucose, because insulin keeps driving glucose into cells. This needs urgent endocrine referral, as diazoxide or surgery may be required.

cards.q: A small-for-gestational-age infant is at high risk of hypoglycaemia. Why, and how often should glucose be checked in the first day?
cards.a: Small infants have low glycogen stores and limited fat to mobilise, so they cannot maintain glucose between feeds. Check glucose before feeds in the first 24 hours, feed early and frequently, and start intravenous dextrose if feeds alone cannot keep glucose up.

cards.q: A newborn has hypoglycaemia with a blood glucose of 35 mg per dL and a seizure. After giving dextrose, what is the most important next step?
cards.a: Recheck the glucose and monitor continuously, and investigate the cause rather than assuming a single low reading is fixed. A seizure means the brain was starved of glucose, so the baby needs ongoing monitoring, a secure dextrose infusion and a workup for hyperinsulinism or other causes.

cards.q: A mother with poorly controlled diabetes delivers a large baby who is jittery. Besides hypoglycaemia, what other complications should you screen for in this infant?
cards.a: Respiratory distress syndrome, polycythaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia and congenital heart defects, especially transposition of the great arteries and ventricular septal defects. Maternal hyperglycaemia affects lung maturity, red cell mass and cardiac development, so the infant of a diabetic mother needs a full systems check.

cards.q: A newborn is cyanotic from birth with a single loud second heart sound and a chest X-ray showing an egg-on-a-string heart. What is the diagnosis and the immediate drug?
cards.a: Transposition of the great arteries. The aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood circulate in two separate loops. Start prostaglandin E1 to keep the ductus arteriosus open, which allows mixing, and arrange urgent balloon atrial septostomy.

cards.q: A newborn has severe cyanosis that does not improve with 100 percent oxygen. Why does oxygen fail, and what does this tell you?
cards.a: This is a right-to-left shunt, not a lung problem. Deoxygenated blood bypasses the lungs entirely, so extra oxygen in the alveoli never reaches the systemic circulation. Failure to improve with oxygen points to cyanotic congenital heart disease, and the baby needs prostaglandin E1 and urgent cardiology input.

cards.q: A 2-day-old infant becomes profoundly cyanotic and shocked when the ductus arteriosus closes. Which lesions are ductal-dependent for pulmonary blood flow?
cards.a: Pulmonary atresia, severe tetralogy of Fallot and tricuspid atresia. In these, blood can only reach the lungs through the ductus, so closure cuts off pulmonary flow and the baby turns blue and collapses. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the ductus and is life-saving.

cards.q: A newborn presents with shock, poor perfusion and weak femoral pulses after the ductus closes. Which lesions are ductal-dependent for systemic blood flow?
cards.a: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome, critical aortic stenosis and severe coarctation of the aorta. Here the body depends on the ductus to supply the systemic circulation, so closure causes circulatory collapse. Start prostaglandin E1 immediately and avoid high inspired oxygen, which can close the ductus further.

cards.q: A newborn is started on prostaglandin E1 for ductal-dependent heart disease. What side effect must you watch for that may require intubation?
cards.a: Apnoea. Prostaglandin E1 commonly causes apnoea, fever, flushing and hypotension in neonates, so the baby must be monitored in an intensive care setting and often needs elective intubation before transfer. Do not stop the drug for apnoea, support the airway instead.

cards.q: A 2-week-old infant has poor feeding, sweating during feeds, tachypnoea and a pansystolic murmur. What is the diagnosis and why do symptoms appear at this age?
cards.a: A large ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunt and heart failure. Symptoms appear at 2 to 6 weeks as pulmonary vascular resistance falls, letting more blood shunt left to right and flood the lungs. The baby is in heart failure, not just noisy, and needs diuretics and cardiology referral.

cards.q: A newborn has cyanosis, a harsh systolic murmur and a boot-shaped heart on chest X-ray. What is the diagnosis and what are its four components?
cards.a: Tetralogy of Fallot: ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. The pulmonary stenosis limits blood to the lungs, so deoxygenated blood shunts right to left across the defect, causing cyanosis that worsens with crying or agitation.

cards.q: An infant with tetralogy of Fallot suddenly becomes deeply cyanotic, limp and inconsolable during crying. What is this and what is the first manoeuvre?
cards.a: A tet spell, a hypercyanotic spell caused by a sudden increase in right-to-left shunting as pulmonary stenosis worsens with infundibular spasm. First, bring the knees to the chest to increase systemic vascular resistance and reduce the shunt, give oxygen, and calm the baby. Morphine and fluids follow if it does not settle.

cards.q: A newborn has a continuous machine-like murmur at the left upper sternal border, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Patent ductus arteriosus. Blood flows continuously from the aorta to the pulmonary artery, through systole and diastole, producing the continuous murmur. The run-off into the lungs causes bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure, and a large PDA can cause heart failure.

cards.q: A newborn has absent femoral pulses and a blood pressure gradient between the arms and legs. What is the diagnosis and why is it an emergency when the ductus closes?
cards.a: Coarctation of the aorta, a narrowing of the aorta that reduces blood flow to the lower body. While the ductus is open it can bypass the narrowing, but closure causes acute lower-body hypoperfusion, shock and renal failure. Start prostaglandin E1 and arrange urgent cardiology and surgical review.

cards.q: A newborn is pink at birth but becomes cyanotic on day 3 with a chest X-ray showing increased pulmonary blood flow. What lesion should you suspect?
cards.a: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return with obstruction, or a large left-to-right shunt becoming apparent as pulmonary resistance falls. Early cyanosis that appears after the first days, rather than at birth, still points to congenital heart disease and needs an urgent echocardiogram, not just oxygen.

cards.q: A newborn with suspected congenital heart disease has a pulse oximetry difference between the right hand and a foot. What does this tell you?
cards.a: It suggests a ductal-dependent lesion or coarctation. The right hand reflects pre-ductal blood from the aorta before the ductus, while the foot reflects post-ductal blood that may be mixed with deoxygenated blood through the ductus. A significant difference is a red flag for urgent echocardiography.

cards.q: A newborn is born flat, apnoeic and bradycardic with a heart rate of 60 beats per minute. What is the single most important first step in resuscitation?
cards.a: Effective positive pressure ventilation. Most newborn bradycardia is caused by inadequate ventilation, not primary cardiac disease, so the heart rate recovers when the lungs are inflated and oxygenated. Chest compressions are not started until ventilation has been given and the heart rate remains below 60.

cards.q: A newborn has a heart rate of 55 beats per minute despite 30 seconds of adequate positive pressure ventilation. What is the next step?
cards.a: Start chest compressions coordinated with ventilation at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath. The heart rate has not responded to ventilation alone, so the baby now needs circulatory support. Continue ventilation as the priority, because compressions without ventilation cannot correct hypoxia.

cards.q: A newborn needs chest compressions and the heart rate remains below 60 despite compressions and ventilation. What drug is given next, and by which route?
cards.a: Adrenaline, given intravenously through an umbilical venous catheter, or endotracheally while access is obtained. Adrenaline increases coronary perfusion pressure and heart rate, but it cannot work without effective ventilation and compressions, so it is never a substitute for them.

cards.q: A newborn is vigorous at birth with meconium-stained fluid. Should you suction the trachea routinely?
cards.a: No. A vigorous infant with good tone, breathing and a heart rate above 100 does not need routine tracheal suctioning, which can cause trauma and delay ventilation. Suction only if the baby is non-vigorous, and prioritise ventilation over suctioning in that case.

cards.q: A newborn is non-vigorous with meconium-stained fluid, is not breathing and has a heart rate of 80. What is the priority?
cards.a: Positive pressure ventilation, not prolonged suctioning. Brief suctioning of the mouth and nose is reasonable, but the baby is hypoxic and the fastest way to raise the heart rate is to inflate the lungs. Delaying ventilation to suction repeatedly worsens hypoxia and bradycardia.

cards.q: A 1-minute Apgar score is 4. What does this mean, and should you wait for the 5-minute score before intervening?
cards.a: An Apgar of 4 means the baby needs active resuscitation now. The Apgar score describes the baby's condition, it does not decide whether to resuscitate, and you never wait for the next score before acting. Resuscitation is guided by heart rate, breathing and tone in real time.

cards.q: A newborn is apnoeic at birth but has a heart rate of 120 and good tone. What is the first intervention?
cards.a: Stimulation and then positive pressure ventilation if the baby does not start breathing. Drying and rubbing the back often triggers breathing, but persistent apnoea needs ventilation, because the baby cannot oxygenate without spontaneous breaths. Oxygen alone without ventilation does not help an apnoeic baby.

cards.q: A preterm infant at 26 weeks is born and needs resuscitation. Why should you avoid 100 percent oxygen from the start?
cards.a: Excess oxygen in the preterm infant causes oxidative injury, retinopathy of prematurity and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Start with a lower oxygen concentration and titrate to target saturations, because the preterm baby needs enough oxygen to survive, not as much as possible.

cards.q: A newborn has a heart rate below 60 after birth and you are giving chest compressions. Why is the compression to ventilation ratio 3 to 1 in newborns, unlike adults?
cards.a: Because newborn arrest is almost always respiratory, not cardiac. The 3 to 1 ratio delivers 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute, prioritising ventilation and oxygenation over circulation alone. Adult ratios assume a primary cardiac cause, which is rare in a newborn.

cards.q: A term infant is born through thick meconium, is vigorous and crying. What is the most important monitoring after delivery?
cards.a: Watch for respiratory distress from meconium aspiration syndrome in the first hours. A vigorous baby still may have aspirated meconium, which causes airway obstruction, chemical pneumonitis and air leak. Observe breathing, oxygen saturation and work of breathing closely, even if the baby looks well initially.

cards.q: A newborn is delivered after a prolonged difficult birth, is limp and apnoeic, and the cord blood gas shows severe metabolic acidosis. What is the most likely cause of the depression?
cards.a: Perinatal asphyxia with hypoxic-ischaemic injury. The acidosis proves prolonged oxygen deprivation, not just a brief delay in breathing. The baby needs resuscitation and then evaluation for therapeutic hypothermia, because the injury continues after delivery.

cards.q: A newborn requires prolonged resuscitation and is now breathing but remains hypotensive and acidotic. What is the next best step after stabilising the airway and breathing?
cards.a: Establish vascular access, correct hypoglycaemia and acidosis, and assess for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy. The post-resuscitation phase is when secondary brain injury evolves, so monitoring, temperature control and early neurology involvement matter as much as the resuscitation itself.

cards.q: A 2-week-old preterm infant who has started enteral feeds develops abdominal distension, bloody stools and feeding intolerance with a falling platelet count. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Necrotising enterocolitis. Ischaemia and bacterial invasion damage the immature gut wall, causing distension, blood in the stool and systemic illness. It is the most serious gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants and can progress to perforation within hours.

cards.q: An abdominal X-ray in a preterm infant with suspected NEC shows pneumatosis intestinalis. What does this finding mean?
cards.a: Gas within the bowel wall, a hallmark of NEC. Bacteria produce gas that dissects into the damaged intestinal wall, and its presence confirms NEC rather than simple feeding intolerance. It is a sign to stop feeds, start antibiotics and involve surgery.

cards.q: An infant with NEC has an abdominal X-ray showing free air under the diaphragm. What is the diagnosis and the immediate management?
cards.a: Bowel perforation, a surgical emergency. Free air means the intestine has ruptured and contents are leaking into the abdomen, causing peritonitis and shock. Make the baby nil by mouth, give intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and get an urgent surgical review.

cards.q: A preterm infant has suspected NEC but no perforation. What are the three immediate management steps?
cards.a: Stop all enteral feeds, start intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and place a nasogastric tube on free drainage. Resting the bowel removes the substrate for bacterial overgrowth, while antibiotics and fluids treat the systemic infection. Serial abdominal examinations and X-rays guide whether surgery becomes needed.

cards.q: A preterm infant is being advanced on feeds quickly and develops NEC. What feeding practice increases the risk, and what is the safer approach?
cards.a: Rapid advancement of enteral feeds, especially with formula rather than breast milk. The immature gut cannot handle large volumes, and ischaemia plus bacterial colonisation triggers NEC. Advance feeds slowly, prefer breast milk, and hold feeds at the first sign of intolerance.

cards.q: A preterm infant had NEC and recovered medically. What late complication should you watch for weeks later?
cards.a: Intestinal stricture, a narrowing of the healed bowel that causes obstruction, distension and feeding intolerance. Scar tissue forms where the bowel was damaged, so any infant recovering from NEC who later develops obstructive symptoms needs imaging and surgical review.

cards.q: An infant with NEC is deteriorating despite medical management, with a fixed dilated bowel loop on X-ray and worsening acidosis. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Urgent surgical consultation for possible laparotomy or peritoneal drain. A fixed loop suggests necrotic bowel that will not recover with antibiotics alone, and worsening acidosis means the dead bowel is causing systemic toxicity. Delaying surgery in this situation is fatal.

cards.q: A preterm infant is at risk of NEC. Why is breast milk protective compared with formula?
cards.a: Breast milk contains antibodies, lactoferrin and growth factors that promote a healthy gut microbiome and strengthen the intestinal barrier. Formula lacks these defences and alters gut colonisation, so breast milk, including donor milk, is the single most effective preventive measure against NEC.

cards.q: A 28-week infant is now 32 weeks corrected age and is on prolonged oxygen. What eye complication must be screened for, and when does screening start?
cards.a: Retinopathy of prematurity. Screening starts at 31 weeks postmenstrual age or 4 weeks after birth, whichever is later, with serial dilated eye examinations. Abnormal retinal blood vessels grow in response to oxygen and prematurity, and late detection leads to retinal detachment and blindness.

cards.q: An infant with retinopathy of prematurity has plus disease with dilated tortuous vessels. What does this mean and what is the treatment?
cards.a: Plus disease means the retinopathy is severe and progressing, with abnormal vessel dilation and tortuosity. It needs urgent treatment with laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF injection to stop abnormal vessel growth, because without treatment the retina can detach and cause permanent blindness.

cards.q: A preterm infant is on high oxygen saturations of 98 to 100 percent. Why is this harmful for the eyes and the lungs?
cards.a: Excess oxygen suppresses normal retinal vessel growth, then triggers abnormal vessel proliferation when oxygen is reduced, and it also damages the immature lung. Target saturations of 90 to 95 percent in preterm infants balance the need for oxygen against the risks of retinopathy and lung injury.

cards.q: A preterm infant has stage 3 retinopathy of prematurity in zone 1. Why is the zone important?
cards.a: Zone 1 is the most posterior and central part of the retina, closest to the optic disc, so disease here threatens central vision and progresses fastest. Zone 1 disease is treated more urgently than peripheral zone 3 disease, because the risk of detachment and blindness is much higher.

cards.q: A preterm infant has completed laser treatment for retinopathy of prematurity. What follow-up is still essential?
cards.a: Continued ophthalmology follow-up through childhood. Treated infants remain at risk of myopia, strabismus, amblyopia and late retinal detachment, so screening does not stop at discharge. Parents need to know that eye follow-up is lifelong, not a one-off check.

cards.q: A term infant is born after a prolonged labour with a low Apgar, is lethargic, hypotonic and has seizures at 12 hours of life. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy from perinatal asphyxia. The brain was deprived of oxygen and blood flow during delivery, causing evolving injury that presents as depressed consciousness, poor tone and seizures in the first day. The severity is graded as mild, moderate or severe.

cards.q: A term infant meets criteria for moderate hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy at 3 hours of life. What is the single treatment that improves outcome, and when must it start?
cards.a: Therapeutic hypothermia, cooling the baby to 33.5 C for 72 hours. It must start within 6 hours of birth, because it slows the secondary energy failure and brain injury that evolves after the initial insult. Cooling started after 6 hours has little benefit.

cards.q: A baby is being cooled for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy. Why is the baby kept cool for 72 hours and then rewarmed slowly?
cards.a: The secondary phase of brain injury evolves over 72 hours, so cooling must cover the whole window. Rapid rewarming can cause rebound injury, seizures and haemodynamic instability, so rewarming is done slowly over 6 to 12 hours with close monitoring.

cards.q: A term infant has mild hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, is alert and feeding. Should therapeutic hypothermia be started?
cards.a: No. Cooling is indicated for moderate to severe encephalopathy, not mild disease, which usually recovers fully with supportive care. Cooling carries risks of coagulopathy, bradycardia and hypotension, so it is reserved for babies who meet strict criteria for moderate or severe injury.

cards.q: An infant with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is being cooled. What monitoring is essential during cooling?
cards.a: Continuous heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood gases, electrolytes, coagulation and seizure monitoring with amplitude-integrated EEG. Cooling affects every organ system, so the baby needs intensive care monitoring, not just a cooling blanket, and seizures may be silent without EEG.

cards.q: A baby with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy develops seizures on day 2 despite cooling. What is the first-line anticonvulsant, and why is seizure control important?
cards.a: Phenobarbital. Seizures increase brain metabolic demand and worsen injury in an already damaged brain, so they must be treated promptly. Phenobarbital is first-line in neonates, and the baby needs EEG monitoring because many neonatal seizures are subclinical.

cards.q: A baby who had severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is being discharged. What is the most important counselling for the parents?
cards.a: The baby needs long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up, because cerebral palsy, learning difficulties and epilepsy may only become apparent over months to years. Early intervention and physiotherapy improve outcomes, so discharge is not the end of care, and parents should be given a clear follow-up plan.

cards.q: A 5-day-old term infant has focal clonic jerking of the right arm. What is the most likely cause of neonatal seizures at this age?
cards.a: Hypoxic-ischaemic injury, intracranial haemorrhage, infection or a metabolic cause such as hypoglycaemia or hypocalcaemia. Neonatal seizures are rarely idiopathic epilepsy, so the priority is finding the underlying cause with glucose, electrolytes, cultures, imaging and EEG, not just stopping the movements.

cards.q: A newborn has jitteriness that stops when the limb is held still. How do you distinguish this from a seizure?
cards.a: Jitteriness is stimulus-sensitive, symmetric and stops with gentle restraint, while a seizure is not suppressed by holding the limb and is often accompanied by abnormal eye movements or apnoea. Mistaking jitteriness for seizures leads to unnecessary anticonvulsants, so observe carefully before treating.

cards.q: A 3-day-old infant has seizures and a blood calcium of 6.5 mg per dL. What is the cause and the treatment?
cards.a: Early neonatal hypocalcaemia, common in preterm infants, infants of diabetic mothers and those with perinatal asphyxia. Treat with intravenous calcium gluconate under cardiac monitoring, because hypocalcaemia lowers the seizure threshold. Also check magnesium and phosphate, as hypomagnesaemia can make hypocalcaemia refractory.

cards.q: A newborn has seizures that do not respond to phenobarbital and levetiracetam, and the baby has a distinctive smell and poor feeding. What rare cause should you consider?
cards.a: A pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy or another inborn error of metabolism. Seizures resistant to standard anticonvulsants in a neonate should prompt a metabolic workup, including ammonia, lactate and amino acids, and a trial of pyridoxine, because the treatment is a vitamin, not another anticonvulsant.

cards.q: A newborn has seizures, a bulging fontanelle and a fever. What is the priority investigation and treatment?
cards.a: Lumbar puncture for meningitis, with blood cultures, after stabilising the baby, and empiric antibiotics plus acyclovir until herpes is excluded. Neonatal meningitis presents with seizures and a bulging fontanelle, and delaying antibiotics or missing herpes encephalitis causes devastating brain injury.

cards.q: A newborn has subtle seizures with only lip smacking, eye deviation and apnoea. Why are these easy to miss, and how are they confirmed?
cards.a: Neonatal seizures are often subtle, not generalised tonic-clonic, because the newborn brain cannot sustain organised seizure activity. They are easily mistaken for normal movements, so confirmation needs EEG monitoring, which shows electrographic seizures even when the baby looks still.

cards.q: A newborn has a seizure and the blood glucose is 28 mg per dL. What is the management, and why must you not just give an anticonvulsant?
cards.a: Give intravenous dextrose first. Hypoglycaemia is a reversible cause of seizures, and an anticonvulsant will not stop seizures driven by a starving brain. Correct the glucose, recheck it, and then investigate why it was low, because the seizure will recur if the metabolic cause is not fixed.

cards.q: A newborn has microcephaly, intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis. The mother had a flu-like illness in pregnancy. What is the most likely infection?
cards.a: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection. It is the commonest congenital infection and causes microcephaly, calcifications, chorioretinitis, hearing loss and hepatosplenomegaly. Diagnosis is by CMV PCR in urine or saliva within the first 3 weeks of life.

cards.q: A newborn with congenital CMV has hearing loss detected on screening. What is the management and why is timing important?
cards.a: Urgent audiology referral and consideration of valganciclovir if the baby is symptomatic, ideally started in the first month of life. Antiviral treatment can improve hearing outcomes in symptomatic congenital CMV, but it is less effective when started late, so early diagnosis and referral matter.

cards.q: A newborn has a vesicular rash, microcephaly and chorioretinitis, and the mother had genital lesions in pregnancy. What is the diagnosis and the treatment?
cards.a: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection. It can present as skin, eye and mouth disease, central nervous system disease or disseminated disease with liver failure and shock. Treat immediately with intravenous acyclovir and do not wait for PCR results, because delay increases mortality and brain injury.

cards.q: A mother has a primary herpes simplex infection at the time of delivery. What is the delivery management to protect the baby?
cards.a: Caesarean section if there are active genital lesions at the onset of labour. Primary infection carries the highest transmission risk because the mother has no protective antibodies. The baby still needs close observation and often empiric acyclovir, because caesarean section reduces but does not eliminate the risk.

cards.q: A newborn has a maculopapular rash, hepatosplenomegaly, snuffles and periostitis on X-ray. The mother had no prenatal care. What is the diagnosis and the treatment?
cards.a: Congenital syphilis. The rash, enlarged liver and spleen, persistent nasal discharge and bone changes are classic. Treat with intravenous penicillin G for 10 days, and screen the mother and baby for HIV, because co-infection is common and the baby needs long-term follow-up.

cards.q: A newborn has cataracts, a patent ductus arteriosus and sensorineural deafness. The mother had a rash in the first trimester. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Congenital rubella syndrome. The classic triad is cataracts, cardiac defects, especially PDA and pulmonary stenosis, and deafness. It occurs when the mother contracts rubella in early pregnancy, and prevention is maternal vaccination before pregnancy, not treatment after birth.

cards.q: A pregnant woman is exposed to toxoplasmosis. Her newborn has hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis. What is the treatment for the baby?
cards.a: Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid for 12 months. Congenital toxoplasmosis causes the classic triad of hydrocephalus, calcifications and chorioretinitis, and prolonged treatment reduces the risk of later eye and brain damage, even if the baby looks well at birth.

cards.q: A newborn has a petechial rash, thrombocytopenia and hepatosplenomegaly, and the mother had a viral illness in pregnancy. How do you distinguish congenital CMV from congenital rubella?
cards.a: By timing, serology and PCR testing, because both can cause a blueberry muffin rash and hepatosplenomegaly. CMV is more likely to cause microcephaly and periventricular calcifications, while rubella classically causes cataracts and cardiac defects. Send CMV PCR, rubella IgM and a full TORCH screen rather than guessing from the rash alone.

cards.q: A newborn has a blueberry muffin rash with purpuric spots. What does this rash represent, and what is the most urgent step?
cards.a: Extramedullary haematopoiesis, blood formation outside the bone marrow in the skin, caused by a congenital infection such as CMV, rubella or toxoplasmosis, or a haematologic disorder. The urgent step is a full TORCH workup, blood count and liver function tests, because the underlying cause determines treatment and prognosis.

cards.q: A mother is HIV positive and delivers a baby. What is the immediate management for the newborn?
cards.a: Start antiretroviral prophylaxis within hours of birth, usually zidovudine, and avoid breastfeeding where safe formula feeding is available. The baby needs HIV PCR testing at intervals, not just antibody testing, because maternal antibodies cross the placenta and make antibody tests unreliable in the newborn.

cards.q: A 2-day-old infant born to a mother on methadone is irritable, tremulous, sneezing and feeding poorly with loose stools. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Neonatal abstinence syndrome from in-utero opioid exposure. The baby is in withdrawal after the placental opioid supply is cut off, with central nervous system irritability, autonomic overactivity and gastrointestinal upset. Score the baby with a standard withdrawal scale and manage in a quiet, low-stimulation environment.

cards.q: A baby with neonatal abstinence syndrome has a high withdrawal score despite supportive care. What is the first-line drug treatment?
cards.a: Morphine, titrated to the withdrawal score. Opioid replacement controls withdrawal safely and allows gradual weaning, whereas sedatives alone do not treat the underlying opioid withdrawal. Supportive care with swaddling, frequent small feeds and a quiet room continues alongside the drug.

cards.q: A mother used heroin during pregnancy. Her baby is jittery and irritable on day 1. Why should you not discharge this baby early?
cards.a: Opioid withdrawal can be delayed, peaking at 2 to 3 days for heroin and later for methadone, so a baby who looks well on day 1 can deteriorate after discharge. The baby needs at least 4 to 5 days of observation with serial withdrawal scoring before discharge is safe.

cards.q: A baby with neonatal abstinence syndrome is being treated with morphine. What is the weaning principle, and what must be checked before discharge?
cards.a: Wean slowly, by about 10 percent per day once the baby is stable, and only discharge when the baby is feeding well, gaining weight and has low withdrawal scores off or on a stable low dose. Rapid weaning causes rebound withdrawal, and the family needs a safe follow-up plan and social support.

cards.q: A pregnant woman on methadone maintenance asks if she should stop it to protect her baby. What do you advise?
cards.a: Do not stop methadone abruptly. Continued maintenance is safer than withdrawal, which risks miscarriage, preterm birth and relapse to illicit use. The baby may develop neonatal abstinence syndrome, but it is treatable, whereas uncontrolled opioid use in pregnancy carries far greater risks.

cards.q: An infant of a diabetic mother is large for gestational age with a rounded face and a thick body. What cardiac lesion is most associated with this, and how is it screened?
cards.a: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy, a thickened heart muscle that can obstruct blood flow out of the left ventricle. It is screened with an echocardiogram, especially if there is a murmur or respiratory distress. It usually resolves over weeks as maternal glucose control improves, but severe obstruction needs cardiology care.

cards.q: An infant of a diabetic mother has a haematocrit of 70 percent. What is the diagnosis and what is the main risk?
cards.a: Polycythaemia, an excess of red blood cells caused by chronic fetal hypoxia from maternal hyperglycaemia driving extra erythropoietin. The main risk is hyperviscosity, which slows blood flow and can cause stroke, renal failure and necrotising enterocolitis. Symptomatic polycythaemia may need a partial exchange transfusion.

cards.q: An infant of a diabetic mother is polycythaemic and has a bilirubin of 16 mg per dL. Why are these two problems linked?
cards.a: More red cells means more haemoglobin to break down, so bilirubin production is higher and jaundice is worse. Polycythaemia also increases blood viscosity, which can impair liver perfusion and bilirubin clearance. Treat the jaundice with phototherapy and monitor the haematocrit closely.

cards.q: A mother has gestational diabetes controlled by diet alone. Does her baby still need glucose monitoring after birth?
cards.a: Yes. Even diet-controlled gestational diabetes can cause fetal hyperinsulinism and neonatal hypoglycaemia, though the risk is lower than with insulin-treated diabetes. Check glucose before feeds in the first 24 hours, feed early, and watch for jitteriness or lethargy.

cards.q: A term infant born by caesarean section develops tachypnoea and mild retractions within hours of birth, with a chest X-ray showing fluid in the fissures and prominent vascular markings. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn. Fluid that is normally squeezed out during vaginal delivery remains in the lungs after caesarean section, delaying clearance. It usually resolves within 24 to 72 hours with supportive oxygen, unlike RDS which worsens.

cards.q: A term infant has respiratory distress and a chest X-ray shows a ground-glass appearance. The baby was born by elective caesarean at 37 weeks. How do you distinguish transient tachypnoea from RDS?
cards.a: By course and X-ray. Transient tachypnoea has fluid in the fissures, perihilar streaking and rapid improvement within 24 to 72 hours, while RDS has ground-glass opacification with air bronchograms, needs more oxygen and worsens without surfactant. A term baby with ground-glass lungs and rising oxygen needs should be treated as RDS until proven otherwise.

cards.q: A baby with transient tachypnoea of the newborn is on 40 percent oxygen and improving. What treatment should you NOT give?
cards.a: Surfactant and prolonged mechanical ventilation. Transient tachypnoea is a fluid clearance problem, not surfactant deficiency, so surfactant does not help and intubation is rarely needed. Support with oxygen and CPAP if needed, keep the baby nil by mouth if tachypnoeic, and wait for the fluid to clear.

cards.q: A 38-week infant born after a rapid vaginal delivery has tachypnoea and a chest X-ray with a small pneumothorax. Why did this happen, and what is the management?
cards.a: Transient tachypnoea with air leak from overdistension as the baby tries to clear retained fluid. Most small pneumothoraces in this setting resolve without a chest tube if the baby is stable. Monitor closely, give oxygen, and intervene with needle decompression only if the baby deteriorates.

cards.q: A term infant with meconium aspiration develops severe hypoxaemia, a loud second heart sound and a chest X-ray with a normal-sized heart but clear lung fields. What complication has developed?
cards.a: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. The pulmonary vessels remain constricted as they were in fetal life, so blood shunts right to left and bypasses the lungs. The clear lung fields with severe hypoxaemia are the clue that the problem is vascular, not alveolar.

cards.q: A newborn with persistent pulmonary hypertension is hypoxic despite 100 percent oxygen and ventilation. What is the targeted treatment?
cards.a: Inhaled nitric oxide, which selectively dilates the pulmonary vessels without dropping systemic blood pressure. It improves oxygenation by increasing blood flow to ventilated lung areas. If nitric oxide fails, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is considered in a specialist centre.

cards.q: A newborn with persistent pulmonary hypertension is being ventilated. Why should you avoid hyperventilation to a very low carbon dioxide level?
cards.a: Profound hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and brain injury, and the benefit of hyperventilation is short-lived as the vessels adapt. Aim for gentle ventilation with normal carbon dioxide, use inhaled nitric oxide for the pulmonary hypertension, and support the systemic blood pressure so blood flows to the lungs.

cards.q: A newborn with persistent pulmonary hypertension is hypotensive. Why does treating the low blood pressure help the hypoxaemia?
cards.a: Because a higher systemic pressure reverses the right-to-left shunt, pushing blood through the lungs instead of bypassing them. Inotropes and volume support raise systemic vascular resistance above pulmonary resistance, so oxygenated blood reaches the body. Treating hypotension is therefore part of treating the hypoxaemia.

cards.q: A newborn has persistent pulmonary hypertension after perinatal asphyxia. What is the underlying mechanism, and why is this different from meconium aspiration?
cards.a: Asphyxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling without airway obstruction. In meconium aspiration the vessels constrict because of hypoxia and chemical inflammation, while in asphyxia the insult is global hypoxia and acidosis. Both lead to the same right-to-left shunt, but the asphyxiated baby also needs evaluation for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy.

cards.q: A 4-day-old infant has a total bilirubin of 15 mg per dL. What are the four essential investigations before deciding on treatment?
cards.a: Total and direct bilirubin, blood group and direct Coombs test, full blood count with reticulocyte count, and a clinical assessment for haemolysis and dehydration. These distinguish haemolytic from non-haemolytic jaundice, identify the cause, and tell you how fast bilirubin is rising, which decides phototherapy versus observation.

cards.q: A newborn has a rising bilirubin and a falling haemoglobin with a positive Coombs test. What additional test helps you judge the severity of haemolysis, and what management does it change?
cards.a: A reticulocyte count and peripheral blood film, plus serial haemoglobin and bilirubin. A high reticulocyte count confirms active haemolysis, and a rapidly falling haemoglobin with a fast-rising bilirubin pushes you toward intensive phototherapy and early preparation for exchange transfusion, rather than observation alone.

cards.q: A 2-month-old infant does not smile socially and does not coo. What is the next best step in management?
cards.a: Do not reassure and wait — document the missed milestones and re-screen development at the next visit while checking hearing and vision. Social smile and cooing are expected by 2 months; missing them is an early red flag for developmental delay or hearing loss, and early identification matters because early intervention improves outcomes.

cards.q: What gross motor milestones are expected by 4 months, and what delay at this age should prompt action?
cards.a: By 4 months an infant should hold the head steady, push up on elbows when prone, and bring hands to midline. If head control is absent at 4 months, evaluate for hypotonia, cerebral palsy risk factors, or neuromuscular disease, and refer for early intervention rather than waiting several more months.

cards.q: A 6-month-old cannot sit without support and does not babble. What is the most appropriate next step?
cards.a: Refer for developmental evaluation and early intervention services, and check hearing. Sitting unsupported is expected around 6 months and babbling begins around 6 months; delay in two domains suggests global developmental delay, and waiting until 12 months loses the window when therapy helps most.

cards.q: What milestones should a 9-month-old have, and which missing milestone is most concerning?
cards.a: By 9 months a baby should sit without support, crawl or scoot, pull to stand, say 'mama/dada' nonspecifically, and play peek-a-boo. Not sitting by 9 months is the most concerning single miss because sitting is a foundation for later motor skills; it warrants prompt developmental referral and a search for causes such as cerebral palsy or hypotonia.

cards.q: A 12-month-old is not walking, says no words, and does not point. What should you do first?
cards.a: Do a structured developmental screening, check hearing and vision, and refer to early intervention plus developmental pediatrics. Walking is expected by 12 to 15 months, first words by 12 months, and pointing by 12 months; missing language and social milestones together raises concern for autism or global delay, so do not simply advise waiting until 18 months.

cards.q: What are the expected milestones at 15 months, and what delay here triggers referral?
cards.a: By 15 months a child should walk independently, say 3 to 5 words, point to desired objects, and follow one-step commands. Absence of any words at 15 months is a clear trigger for hearing testing and speech-language referral, because expressive language delay at this age rarely resolves on its own without help.

cards.q: An 18-month-old walks well but says only 2 words and does not imitate. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Screen with the M-CHAT-R/F for autism and refer for speech-language evaluation and hearing testing. At 18 months a child should say about 10 to 20 words and imitate simple actions; isolated language delay still needs evaluation, and an autism screen is routine at the 18-month visit.

cards.q: What milestones define normal development at 2 years, and which miss is most urgent?
cards.a: By 2 years a child should run, kick a ball, use 2-word phrases, point to body parts, and engage in parallel play. The most urgent miss is no 2-word phrases by 24 months, because it predicts persistent language disorder and may signal autism or hearing loss; refer immediately for hearing testing, speech therapy, and developmental evaluation.

cards.q: A 3-year-old cannot pedal a tricycle, speaks in 2-word phrases only, and avoids eye contact. What is the priority?
cards.a: Screen for autism spectrum disorder and refer for comprehensive developmental and speech-language evaluation. By 3 years a child should speak in 3-word sentences, pedal a tricycle, and play interactively; combined language delay with poor eye contact and social avoidance points toward autism, which needs early intensive behavioural intervention.

cards.q: What should a 4-year-old be able to do, and what does failure to do it suggest?
cards.a: By 4 years a child should hop on one foot, draw a person with 2 to 4 body parts, tell a simple story, play cooperatively, and answer simple questions. Inability to speak in sentences or to play with other children at 4 years suggests intellectual disability, autism, or severe language disorder, and warrants formal developmental testing and preschool special-education referral.

cards.q: A 5-year-old cannot skip, draw a 6-part person, or count to 10. What is the next step?
cards.a: Perform formal developmental and cognitive testing and refer to developmental pediatrics, because these are expected 5-year milestones and delay across motor, drawing, and counting suggests global developmental delay or intellectual disability. Also check vision and hearing first, since uncorrected sensory loss can mimic cognitive delay.

cards.q: A child met all milestones on time but at 18 months stops talking and loses eye contact. What is the most important action?
cards.a: Treat this as developmental regression, which is never normal, and urgently evaluate for autism spectrum disorder and other causes such as Rett syndrome or neurodegenerative disease. Regression requires prompt referral to developmental pediatrics and neurology, plus hearing testing, rather than reassurance that the child will catch up.

cards.q: What is the difference between developmental delay and developmental regression, and why does it change management?
cards.a: Delay means milestones are reached late but skills are not lost; regression means previously acquired skills disappear. Delay is managed with early intervention and screening for causes, while regression is a red flag that demands urgent workup for autism, metabolic or neurodegenerative disorders, seizures, and Rett syndrome, because some causes are treatable and all need rapid diagnosis.

cards.q: A 9-month-old has head lag, poor trunk control, and brisk reflexes. What is the most likely category of diagnosis and the next step?
cards.a: This suggests cerebral palsy from an early brain injury, with spasticity causing brisk reflexes and delayed motor milestones. The next step is referral to neurology and early intervention physical therapy, plus brain MRI if indicated, because early therapy improves motor outcomes even though the brain injury itself is not reversible.

cards.q: When should formal developmental screening be done in primary care, and with what tools?
cards.a: Developmental surveillance happens at every well-child visit, with formal screening at 9, 18, and 30 months using a validated tool such as the Ages and Stages Questionnaire, plus autism-specific screening with the M-CHAT-R/F at 18 and 24 months. Screening at set ages catches delays that surveillance alone misses, and a positive screen must lead to referral, not just watchful waiting.

cards.q: A parent says their 12-month-old 'will talk when ready' because an older sibling was a late talker. What is the correct response?
cards.a: Acknowledge the family history but still screen formally and check hearing, because late talking in a sibling does not rule out hearing loss, autism, or language disorder in this child. Explain that early intervention is free, low-risk, and most effective when started early, and that waiting can turn a small gap into a large one.

cards.q: What does a positive M-CHAT-R/F screen mean, and what is the next step?
cards.a: A positive M-CHAT-R/F means the child is at increased risk for autism spectrum disorder, not that the diagnosis is certain. The next step is the structured follow-up interview for intermediate scores, and for high scores, immediate referral for a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and early intervention services — do not wait for a repeat screen months later.

cards.q: At what ages is autism screening recommended, and why those ages?
cards.a: The M-CHAT-R/F is recommended at the 18-month and 24-month well-child visits, because social communication deficits become visible in the second year of life and early intensive behavioural intervention before age 3 has the strongest evidence for improving language and social outcomes.

cards.q: A 2-year-old screens positive on the M-CHAT-R/F but the parents decline referral, saying the child is just shy. What should you do?
cards.a: Explore their concerns respectfully, explain that screening is not a diagnosis and that evaluation is the only way to know, and document the discussion and re-offer referral at the next visit. Also offer early intervention referral, which does not require a diagnosis. Do not simply accept the refusal and drop the issue, because delay in autism intervention worsens long-term outcomes.

cards.q: What is the first-line management for a child newly diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder?
cards.a: Refer for early intensive behavioural intervention, such as applied behaviour analysis, plus speech-language therapy and occupational therapy, and connect the family with support services and the school system. There is no drug that treats the core features of autism; medications are reserved for specific problems such as irritability, hyperactivity, or anxiety when behavioural approaches are not enough.

cards.q: Which medication is used for severe irritability and aggression in autism, and what monitoring does it require?
cards.a: Risperidone or aripiprazole can be used for severe irritability in autism when behavioural therapy alone is insufficient. Both require monitoring for weight gain, metabolic syndrome, and extrapyramidal side effects, so check weight, glucose, and lipids regularly, and use the lowest effective dose with ongoing behavioural therapy.

cards.q: A 3-year-old with autism has chronic constipation and sleep problems. How should these be managed?
cards.a: Treat constipation first with dietary fibre, fluids, and a stool softener such as polyethylene glycol if needed, because untreated constipation worsens irritability and behaviour. For sleep, start with sleep hygiene and behavioural strategies, and consider melatonin only after those fail. Medical problems in autism are common and often drive behaviour, so look for them before increasing behavioural or psychiatric drugs.

cards.q: A toddler fails the M-CHAT-R/F and also has macrocephaly and delayed walking. What workup is indicated?
cards.a: In addition to autism evaluation, check for an underlying genetic or metabolic cause: consider chromosomal microarray, fragile X testing, and brain MRI given the macrocephaly and motor delay. A genetic diagnosis changes recurrence counselling for the family and may identify associated medical problems that need surveillance.

cards.q: What is the role of genetic testing in a child with global developmental delay or intellectual disability?
cards.a: Chromosomal microarray is first-line testing for unexplained global developmental delay or intellectual disability, because it detects microdeletions and duplications missed by a standard karyotype. Add fragile X testing, especially in boys, and consider metabolic testing if there is regression, seizures, or dysmorphic features. A diagnosis guides prognosis, surveillance, and family counselling.

cards.q: A 4-year-old with developmental delay has normal microarray and fragile X testing. What is the next step?
cards.a: Refer to genetics for consideration of whole exome sequencing, and continue early intervention and therapies while the workup proceeds. A negative first-tier workup does not end the search when delay is unexplained, and many children remain without a specific genetic diagnosis, in which case management focuses on maximising function and supporting the family.

cards.q: A child with Down syndrome is not sitting at 10 months. Is this expected, and what should you do?
cards.a: Mild motor delay is expected in Down syndrome because of hypotonia, so sitting may come a few months late, but the child should still be referred to early intervention physical therapy. Use Down syndrome-specific growth charts for tracking, and do not use a single delayed milestone to predict intellectual outcome.

cards.q: What red flags in a developmental history should prompt same-visit referral rather than watchful waiting?
cards.a: Loss of any previously acquired skill, no social smile by 3 months, no babbling by 9 months, no words by 15 months, no 2-word phrases by 24 months, no pointing by 12 months, and persistent primitive reflexes.
