cards.a: Put the child knee-to-chest, give 100 percent oxygen, calm the child, give intravenous fluids and morphine to reduce infundibular spasm and systemic venous return changes, and correct acidosis. Knee-to-chest increases systemic vascular resistance, which reduces right-to-left shunting and improves pulmonary blood flow; beta-blockers or phenylephrine may be used if the spell does not settle, and urgent cardiology referral for surgical repair is needed.

cards.q: What should you NOT do during a tet spell in a child with tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: Do not give a drug that lowers systemic vascular resistance or increases right-to-left shunting, and do not leave the child flat and agitated while waiting. Anything that drops systemic resistance worsens cyanosis because more blood bypasses the lungs; keep the child knee-to-chest, give oxygen and fluids, and treat the infundibular spasm rather than giving vasodilators.

cards.q: When is surgery done for tetralogy of Fallot, and what does it involve?
cards.a: Complete repair is usually done in infancy, often before 12 months, with closure of the VSD and relief of the right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Early repair prevents prolonged cyanosis, hypercyanotic spells and right ventricular hypertrophy; a shunt (Blalock-Taussig) is only a temporary palliation in a very small or unstable infant who cannot yet have a full repair.

cards.q: A 2-day-old is deeply cyanotic, does not improve with 100 percent oxygen, and has a chest X-ray showing an egg-on-a-string heart. What is the diagnosis and the immediate life-saving drug?
cards.a: This is transposition of the great arteries (TGA). Start a prostaglandin E1 infusion immediately to keep the ductus arteriosus open, because survival depends on mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood through the ductus and foramen ovale. Arrange urgent balloon atrial septostomy if mixing is inadequate, and definitive arterial switch surgery in the first weeks of life.

cards.q: Why does a baby with transposition of the great arteries fail the hyperoxia test, and what must you not do while waiting for cardiology?
cards.a: The hyperoxia test fails because oxygenated blood from the lungs returns to the left ventricle and is pumped back to the lungs, while deoxygenated blood goes to the body — giving more oxygen cannot fix the parallel circulation. Do not stop prostaglandin or delay transfer; keep the ductus open, support ventilation, and get the baby to a cardiac centre urgently for septostomy and arterial switch.

cards.q: What is the definitive surgery for transposition of the great arteries and when is it done?
cards.a: The arterial switch operation, usually within the first 2 to 3 weeks of life, before the left ventricle loses its ability to pump against systemic pressure. The great arteries are switched back to their correct ventricles and the coronary arteries are reimplanted; delaying risks left ventricular deconditioning and a worse outcome.

cards.q: A 10-year-old has high blood pressure in the arms, weak femoral pulses, and a systolic murmur with radiofemoral delay. What is the diagnosis and the next step?
cards.a: Coarctation of the aorta. Confirm with echocardiography and check blood pressure in all four limbs, then refer to paediatric cardiology for repair — balloon angioplasty with or without stenting, or surgery, depending on age and anatomy. The narrowing causes upper-body hypertension and lower-body hypoperfusion, so untreated coarctation leads to heart failure, stroke and early cardiovascular disease.

cards.q: A child with coarctation of the aorta is found to have a bicuspid aortic valve. What else must be screened for and why does it change management?
cards.a: Screen for associated congenital heart disease, especially bicuspid aortic valve and intracranial aneurysm risk, and monitor the aortic valve and ascending aorta long term. Bicuspid valves are common with coarctation and can develop stenosis or regurgitation and aortic dilatation, so even after coarctation repair the child needs lifelong cardiology follow-up, not discharge.

cards.q: A newborn with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is stable on prostaglandin but deteriorating. What is the staged surgical plan, and what is the alternative if surgery is not possible?
cards.a: The Norwood procedure in the first week of life, then the Glenn procedure at around 4 to 6 months, then the Fontan procedure at around 2 to 4 years, creating a single-ventricle circulation. Prostaglandin keeps the ductus open so systemic blood flow is maintained until the Norwood; heart transplantation is the alternative for children who are not candidates for staged palliation, and the choice needs urgent specialist counselling with the family.

cards.q: Why is prostaglandin E1 the first drug in a newborn with suspected ductal-dependent congenital heart disease, and what side effect must you watch for?
cards.a: Prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus arteriosus open, which is the only route for blood to reach the lungs or the body in ductal-dependent lesions such as HLHS, critical pulmonary stenosis or TGA. Watch for apnoea, which is common and may require intubation, plus fever, hypotension and flushing; do not stop the infusion while the baby is being transferred to a cardiac centre.

cards.q: A 3-month-old with a large VSD develops increasing tachypnoea and poor feeding despite diuretics. What finding on echo would push you toward earlier surgery?
cards.a: Evidence of pulmonary hypertension, a large left-to-right shunt with left heart dilatation, or failure to thrive despite maximal medical therapy. These mean the shunt is causing irreversible pulmonary vascular disease if left, so surgical closure should be brought forward rather than continuing medical therapy alone.

cards.q: A child with a small ASD is going for dental surgery. Does he need infective endocarditis prophylaxis, and why?
cards.a: No — a small isolated ASD that has been repaired without residual defect, or an unrepaired small ASD without other risk factors, does not need antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures under current guidance. Prophylaxis is reserved for the highest-risk lesions such as prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic disease or repaired disease with residual defects, because the risk of endocarditis in a simple ASD is very low and routine antibiotics cause more harm than benefit.

cards.q: A newborn has a continuous murmur, bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure. The mother took no prostaglandin inhibitors. What lesion is this and what is the risk if it is left untreated in a term infant?
cards.a: A patent ductus arteriosus. If left untreated, a large PDA causes left-to-right shunting, pulmonary overcirculation, heart failure, failure to thrive and eventually pulmonary hypertension with shunt reversal (Eisenmenger syndrome), so a haemodynamically significant PDA in a term infant needs closure.

cards.q: A 5-year-old with tetralogy of Fallot has had a complete repair. What long-term complication must be watched for, and what follow-up is needed?
cards.a: Pulmonary regurgitation with progressive right ventricular dilatation, plus arrhythmias, especially ventricular tachycardia. The child needs lifelong cardiology follow-up with regular echocardiograms, ECGs and exercise testing, and may need pulmonary valve replacement in adolescence or adulthood if right ventricular dilatation progresses.

cards.q: A 2-week-old presents with poor feeding, tachypnoea and a gallop rhythm. Echo shows a large VSD and poor left ventricular function. What is the first-line drug to improve contractility in this child with heart failure?
cards.a: Start diuretics and afterload reduction first, and add digoxin if needed for symptomatic heart failure, with cardiology guidance. Digoxin improves contractility and helps control heart rate, but it has a narrow therapeutic window and is not the first step — relieving pulmonary congestion with diuretics and reducing afterload are the priority, and the underlying shunt still needs surgical planning.

cards.q: A newborn with critical aortic stenosis is in shock with poor perfusion. What is the immediate management before definitive intervention?
cards.a: Start prostaglandin E1 to keep the ductus open so systemic perfusion is maintained, support ventilation and perfusion, and arrange urgent balloon valvuloplasty or surgery. The ductus provides an alternative route for blood to the body while the stenotic aortic valve limits forward flow, so closing the ductus would worsen shock.

cards.q: What is Eisenmenger syndrome, and why is closing the defect then dangerous?
cards.a: Eisenmenger syndrome is irreversible pulmonary hypertension with reversal of a left-to-right shunt to right-to-left, causing cyanosis, after years of a large unrepaired shunt. Closing the defect at this stage is dangerous because the right ventricle depends on the shunt as a pressure-relief valve — closing it would cause acute right heart failure. Management is supportive, avoidance of pregnancy and dehydration, and referral to a pulmonary hypertension centre.

cards.q: A 7-year-old with Down syndrome and a complete atrioventricular septal defect is being worked up for surgery. What preoperative assessment is especially important in this child?
cards.a: Assess pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension carefully, because children with Down syndrome develop pulmonary vascular disease earlier and may become inoperable sooner. Cardiac catheterisation may be needed to check if the pulmonary pressures are still reversible; if pulmonary vascular resistance is fixed and high, surgery is contraindicated.

cards.q: A 4-month-old with a moderate VSD has a respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and is deteriorating faster than expected. Why are children with congenital heart disease at higher risk, and what is the next step?
cards.a: Children with haemodynamically significant heart disease have less cardiopulmonary reserve, so RSV bronchiolitis causes more severe hypoxia, heart failure and prolonged admission. Admit for monitoring, oxygen and supportive care, consider palivizumab prophylaxis in future seasons if eligible, and involve cardiology early rather than managing as routine bronchiolitis.

cards.q: A child with coarctation of the aorta has surgery at age 8. Why does he still need blood pressure monitoring for life?
cards.a: Because hypertension often persists or recurs after repair, even when the coarctation is successfully relieved, due to abnormal aortic compliance and vascular remodelling. Lifelong blood pressure checks, exercise testing and cardiology follow-up are needed to detect and treat persistent hypertension and recoarctation early.

cards.q: An infant with a large left-to-right shunt is started on furosemide and develops a low potassium. Why does this matter, and what is the next step?
cards.a: Hypokalaemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity and arrhythmias, and worsens muscle weakness. Check electrolytes regularly, replace potassium, and consider adding a potassium-sparing diuretic such as spironolactone, which also helps in heart failure; do not continue escalating furosemide without monitoring electrolytes and renal function.

cards.q: A 6-month-old with heart failure is on furosemide and captopril and is not gaining weight. What nutritional step improves outcome in infant heart failure?
cards.a: Give high-calorie feeds, often with fortified formula or concentrated feeds, and consider nasogastric feeding if oral intake is inadequate. Infants with heart failure burn extra calories through increased work of breathing and tire during feeds, so they need more calories per millilitre and smaller, more frequent feeds; without this they fail to thrive even when the heart failure drugs are optimised.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of heart failure in an infant, and how does it differ from the most common cause in an older child?
cards.a: In infants the most common cause is congenital heart disease with a large left-to-right shunt; in older children it is more often cardiomyopathy or myocarditis. That is why an infant with heart failure needs an echocardiogram to look for a structural lesion, while an older child needs work-up for myocarditis, cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia as well as structural disease.

cards.q: A 9-year-old with dilated cardiomyopathy is in heart failure with a low ejection fraction. What is the mainstay of long-term medical therapy?
cards.a: An ACE inhibitor plus a beta-blocker (once stable) and diuretics for congestion, with close monitoring of blood pressure, renal function and electrolytes. ACE inhibitors reduce afterload and remodelling, beta-blockers improve long-term survival once the child is euvolaemic, and diuretics relieve symptoms — but beta-blockers should not be started during acute decompensated heart failure.

cards.q: A child with heart failure is started on digoxin. What signs suggest digoxin toxicity, and what electrolyte abnormality makes it more likely?
cards.a: Nausea, vomiting, visual changes, bradycardia and arrhythmias suggest toxicity; hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and renal impairment all increase the risk. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window, so check electrolytes and renal function, hold the drug and seek cardiology advice if toxicity is suspected, and do not give extra doses to catch up.

cards.q: A 12-year-old with heart failure needs an ACE inhibitor but has a cough and a rising creatinine. What is the next step?
cards.a: Check for other causes of cough, review the dose, check renal function and potassium, and consider switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker if the cough is truly ACE-inhibitor related. A small rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected because renal perfusion pressure falls, but a large rise, hyperkalaemia or symptomatic hypotension means the drug should be held and cardiology involved.

cards.q: A child with congenital heart disease is undergoing dental extraction. Which children need antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis, and what is the usual regimen?
cards.a: Prophylaxis is needed only for the highest-risk group: prosthetic heart valves, prior infective endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, or repaired disease with residual defects or prosthetic material in the first 6 months. Give a single dose of amoxicillin before the procedure if not allergic; children with simple repaired defects without residual shunt do not need it.

cards.q: A child with a prosthetic heart valve develops fever and a new murmur 3 weeks after dental work. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Admit urgently, take multiple blood cultures before antibiotics, and do an echocardiogram to look for vegetations. Fever plus a new murmur in a high-risk child is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise; blood cultures must be taken before antibiotics so the organism can be identified, and treatment is prolonged intravenous antibiotics with cardiology and infectious diseases input.

cards.q: Why is good dental hygiene more important than antibiotic prophylaxis for most children with congenital heart disease?
cards.a: Because most cases of endocarditis come from everyday bacteraemia during brushing and chewing, not from a single dental procedure. Daily brushing, flossing and regular dental care reduce the overall bacterial load, while a single dose of antibiotics only covers one procedure; prophylaxis is therefore reserved for the highest-risk lesions.

cards.q: A 3-year-old with unrepaired cyanotic heart disease needs a non-cardiac operation. What preoperative step reduces the risk of endocarditis and other complications?
cards.a: Involve paediatric cardiology and anaesthesia early, optimise oxygenation and hydration, and give endocarditis prophylaxis if indicated for the procedure. Cyanotic children are at high risk of endocarditis, paradoxical embolism and perioperative desaturation, so they need a specialist plan, not routine anaesthesia.

cards.q: A 7-year-old suddenly develops a narrow-complex tachycardia at 220 beats per minute, is alert and has a normal blood pressure. What is the first-line drug, and what must you do before giving it?
cards.a: Give adenosine by rapid intravenous push followed immediately by a saline flush, after first trying vagal manoeuvres if the child is stable. Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node and terminates supraventricular tachycardia that depends on AV nodal re-entry; it must be given rapidly into a large vein because its half-life is only seconds, and the child should be on a cardiac monitor with resuscitation equipment nearby.

cards.q: A child with SVT is hypotensive, poorly perfused and altered. What is the next best step, and why is adenosine not the first choice here?
cards.a: Give synchronised electrical cardioversion immediately. In an unstable child with hypotension or shock, cardioversion restores sinus rhythm at once, whereas adenosine and vagal manoeuvres take time and may fail; do not delay definitive treatment in an unstable child.

cards.q: A 6-month-old has recurrent SVT despite adenosine. What is the next step for long-term prevention?
cards.a: Start a prophylactic antiarrhythmic such as a beta-blocker, with cardiology guidance, and look for a cause such as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome or congenital heart disease. Recurrent SVT in infancy often needs maintenance therapy until the child outgrows it, and an ECG in sinus rhythm should be checked for a delta wave suggesting an accessory pathway.

cards.q: A teenager faints during exercise and has a prolonged QT interval on ECG. What is the diagnosis, what drug must be avoided, and what is the first-line treatment?
cards.a: Congenital long QT syndrome. Avoid QT-prolonging drugs such as certain antihistamines, antibiotics and antiarrhythmics, because they can trigger torsades de pointes. First-line treatment is a beta-blocker, with avoidance of strenuous exercise and swimming, correction of electrolytes, and consideration of an implantable defibrillator if there is recurrent syncope or cardiac arrest despite beta-blockers.

cards.q: A child with long QT syndrome is prescribed a new antibiotic. What must you check before prescribing?
cards.a: Check whether the drug prolongs the QT interval, and check potassium, magnesium and calcium, because hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia increase the risk of torsades. If a QT-prolonging drug is unavoidable, use the lowest dose, monitor the ECG and correct electrolytes; otherwise choose an alternative that does not prolong the QT.

cards.q: An infant with SVT has a heart rate of 260 and is feeding poorly. Why is this more dangerous in an infant than in an older child, and what is the urgency?
cards.a: Infants tolerate sustained tachycardia poorly and can develop heart failure and cardiogenic shock quickly because their cardiac output is rate-dependent and they have little reserve. Treat promptly, monitor closely, and admit — do not discharge an infant with SVT after a single episode without a cardiology plan.

cards.q: A 10-year-old has palpitations and an ECG shows Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with a delta wave. He is asymptomatic. What is the management?
cards.a: Refer to paediatric cardiology for risk stratification, including exercise testing and possibly an electrophysiology study, and advise avoidance of drugs that block the AV node if he develops atrial fibrillation. Asymptomatic WPW still carries a small risk of sudden death if atrial fibrillation conducts rapidly down the accessory pathway, so risk assessment is needed even without symptoms.

cards.q: A child in SVT is given adenosine and briefly becomes asystolic on the monitor. What do you do?
cards.a: Stay calm and continue monitoring — a brief pause of a few seconds is expected after adenosine and sinus rhythm usually resumes. Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node, so a short asystole is a known effect; only intervene with resuscitation if the pause is prolonged or the child becomes unstable.

cards.q: A newborn has a heart rate of 55 and the mother has systemic lupus erythematosus. What is the cause and the management?
cards.a: Congenital complete heart block from maternal anti-Ro antibodies crossing the placenta and damaging the fetal conduction system. Many babies need a pacemaker, especially if they are symptomatic, have a very slow rate or have heart failure; monitor the heart rate, perfusion and growth, and involve cardiology urgently.

cards.q: A 5-year-old with asthma has daytime symptoms twice a week and wakes once a week at night. What step of therapy is he on, and what is the next step?
cards.a: He has persistent asthma that is not well controlled on a short-acting beta-agonist alone. Start a daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid as controller therapy, with a short-acting beta-agonist as needed for relief. Inhaled steroids reduce airway inflammation and prevent exacerbations, whereas reliever-only treatment leaves the underlying inflammation untreated.

cards.q: A child with asthma is using a salbutamol inhaler 4 times a day and still has symptoms. What is the most important thing to check before stepping up therapy?
cards.a: Check inhaler technique and adherence, and ask about triggers. Poor technique is the most common reason for poor control in children — if the drug is not reaching the airways, stepping up the dose will not help. Watch the child use the inhaler with a spacer, correct the technique, and only then step up if symptoms persist.

cards.q: Why should a spacer be used with a pressurised metered-dose inhaler in a child with asthma?
cards.a: A spacer slows the aerosol, reduces deposition in the mouth and throat, and increases the amount reaching the lungs, especially in a child who cannot coordinate actuation with inhalation. It improves drug delivery, reduces oral thrush and hoarseness from inhaled steroids, and makes the inhaler easier to use correctly.

cards.q: A 9-year-old with moderate persistent asthma is on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid but still has weekly symptoms. What is the next step in stepwise therapy?
cards.a: Step up to a medium-dose inhaled corticosteroid, or add a long-acting beta-agonist as combination therapy, depending on age and local guidance. Adding a long-acting beta-agonist improves control without increasing the steroid dose as much, but it must never be used alone without an inhaled corticosteroid, because that increases the risk of severe exacerbations.

cards.q: A child with asthma presents with a severe exacerbation: oxygen saturation 90 percent, unable to speak in full sentences, and a peak flow less than 50 percent of best. What is the immediate management?
cards.a: Give high-flow oxygen to keep saturation above 92 to 94 percent, nebulised or spacer-delivered salbutamol with ipratropium, and oral or intravenous corticosteroids early. Admit for monitoring, check blood gases and chest X-ray if needed, and do not discharge until the child is stable on inhalers; early steroids reduce the severity and duration of the exacerbation.

cards.q: Why are oral corticosteroids given early in a moderate to severe asthma exacerbation in a child, even though they take hours to work?
cards.a: Because they reduce airway inflammation and prevent relapse, and their benefit is greatest when given early in the exacerbation. Bronchodilators relieve bronchospasm quickly, but steroids address the underlying inflammation that keeps the airways narrowed; delaying steroids prolongs the exacerbation and increases the chance of admission.

cards.q: A child with asthma is prescribed a daily inhaled corticosteroid. The parent worries about growth suppression. What do you advise?
cards.a: Reassure them that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids have a very small effect on growth, usually about 1 cm in the first year, and that uncontrolled asthma itself harms growth more. Monitor height regularly, use the lowest effective dose with a spacer, rinse the mouth after use, and do not stop the controller because of this concern — the benefit of preventing severe exacerbations outweighs the small growth effect.

cards.q: A 12-year-old with severe asthma is on high-dose inhaled steroids plus a long-acting beta-agonist and still has frequent exacerbations. What is the next step before considering a biologic?
cards.a: Confirm the diagnosis, check adherence and inhaler technique, look for triggers and comorbidities such as allergic rhinitis, reflux and obesity, and check for other diagnoses. Many children labelled as severe asthma have poor technique, missed doses or an alternative diagnosis; a biologic should only be considered after these have been addressed and specialist assessment confirms severe asthma.

cards.q: Which children with asthma are candidates for a biologic such as omalizumab or dupilumab, and what must be checked first?
cards.a: Children with severe allergic or eosinophilic asthma who remain uncontrolled despite high-dose inhaled therapy and correct technique. Check IgE levels, eosinophil count, allergy testing and exacerbation history with a specialist, because the choice of biologic depends on the phenotype — omalizumab for allergic IgE-mediated asthma, and anti-IL-5 or dupilumab for eosinophilic disease.

cards.q: A child with asthma has a written asthma action plan. What should it include, and why does it reduce admissions?
cards.a: It should list daily controller medicines, how to recognise worsening symptoms, when and how to increase reliever use, when to start oral steroids, and when to seek urgent care. A clear plan helps families act early before an exacerbation becomes severe, which reduces emergency visits and admissions.

cards.q: A 4-year-old with viral-induced wheeze has no symptoms between colds. Does he need a daily inhaled corticosteroid?
cards.a: No — if wheeze only occurs with viral infections and the child is completely well between episodes, intermittent treatment during colds is usually enough. Daily inhaled steroids are for persistent asthma with symptoms between episodes; giving a daily controller to a child with only episodic viral wheeze adds side effects without benefit.

cards.q: A child with asthma is admitted with a severe exacerbation and is not improving on nebulised salbutamol. What intravenous treatment is used next, and what monitoring is needed?
cards.a: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate, and consider intravenous salbutamol or aminophylline in intensive care if there is no response. Magnesium relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and is safe and effective in severe exacerbations; monitor blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation and electrolytes, and involve intensive care early if the child is tiring.

cards.q: Why should a long-acting beta-agonist never be used alone in a child with asthma?
cards.a: Because it relieves bronchospasm without treating the underlying airway inflammation, which masks worsening asthma and increases the risk of a severe or fatal exacerbation. Long-acting beta-agonists must always be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, which treats the inflammation.

cards.q: A teenager with asthma says she only uses her inhaler when she feels wheezy and skips her preventer. What is the most effective counselling point?
cards.a: Explain that the preventer inhaler works by reducing inflammation over weeks, so it only helps if taken every day even when she feels well, while the reliever only opens the airways temporarily. Skipping the preventer leaves the airways inflamed and prone to sudden severe attacks; link daily use to a routine such as brushing teeth to improve adherence.

cards.q: A 7-year-old with asthma is going on a school trip. What practical advice should be given about his inhalers?
cards.a: Make sure he carries his reliever inhaler and spacer at all times, has a copy of his asthma action plan, and that a teacher knows how to help him use it. Children should not have their reliever locked away or left at home, because an exacerbation can develop quickly and early reliever use prevents it becoming severe.

cards.q: A 3-month-old with bronchiolitis is tachypnoeic, feeding poorly and has an oxygen saturation of 89 percent on air. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Admit for monitoring, give supplemental oxygen to keep saturation above 90 to 92 percent, and support feeding with small frequent feeds or nasogastric feeds if needed. Bronchiolitis is a viral infection of the small airways causing oedema and mucus plugging; management is supportive, with oxygen and hydration as the mainstays.

cards.q: A 6-month-old with RSV bronchiolitis is wheezy. Should you give nebulised salbutamol, and why or why not?
cards.a: No, routine bronchodilators are not recommended in bronchiolitis. The wheeze is from oedema and mucus in the small airways, not from bronchospasm, so salbutamol does not improve outcomes and can cause tachycardia; supportive care with oxygen and fluids is the treatment.

cards.q: What treatments should NOT be given routinely in bronchiolitis, and why?
cards.a: Do not give antibiotics, corticosteroids, nebulised adrenaline or bronchodilators routinely. Bronchiolitis is viral, so antibiotics do not help unless there is a bacterial superinfection; steroids and bronchodilators have not been shown to improve outcomes and add side effects; supportive care is the evidence-based treatment.

cards.q: A 2-month-old with bronchiolitis has apnoea, poor feeding and an oxygen saturation of 88 percent. Where should he be managed?
cards.a: Admit to a high-dependency or intensive care setting with continuous monitoring, because apnoea is a red flag in young infants with RSV. Young infants can deteriorate quickly with apnoea and respiratory failure, so they need close observation, oxygen, and readiness for respiratory support such as high-flow nasal cannula or CPAP.

cards.q: A parent asks if their child with bronchiolitis needs a chest X-ray. When is imaging indicated?
cards.a: A chest X-ray is not routinely needed in typical bronchiolitis. Order one only if the diagnosis is uncertain, the child is severely ill, not improving, or there is concern for pneumonia, pneumothorax or another complication. Unnecessary X-rays add radiation and do not change management in straightforward bronchiolitis.

cards.q: How can RSV bronchiolitis be prevented in a high-risk premature infant, and who is eligible?
cards.a: Give palivizumab, a monoclonal antibody against RSV, monthly during RSV season to eligible high-risk infants such as those born very prematurely or with chronic lung disease or haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease. It reduces the severity and admission rate but does not prevent all infection, so families should still practise hand hygiene and avoid smoke exposure.

cards.q: A 9-month-old with bronchiolitis is improving but still needs oxygen. What criteria suggest he is ready for discharge?
cards.a: He is feeding adequately, maintaining oxygen saturation above 90 to 92 percent on air, has no apnoea, and the family can manage follow-up and return if he worsens. Discharge is based on stable oxygenation and feeding, not on complete resolution of wheeze or cough, which can persist for weeks.

cards.q: A child with bronchiolitis is dehydrated and refusing feeds. What is the best way to give fluids?
cards.a: Give small frequent oral feeds if tolerated, or nasogastric feeds if oral intake is inadequate; use intravenous fluids only if nasogastric feeding is not possible or the child is severely dehydrated. Nasogastric feeding is safer and better tolerated than intravenous fluids in most cases, and avoids the risks of overhydration.

cards.q: Why is suctioning used cautiously in bronchiolitis, and when is it helpful?
cards.a: Gentle nasal suctioning can help clear mucus and improve feeding and oxygenation, but aggressive or frequent suctioning irritates the airways and causes distress without benefit. Use it before feeds and when secretions are clearly obstructing breathing, and avoid routine deep suctioning.

cards.q: A 5-year-old with cystic fibrosis has a positive newborn screen. What test confirms the diagnosis, and what value is diagnostic?
cards.a: A sweat chloride test — a sweat chloride above 60 millimoles per litre is diagnostic of cystic fibrosis. The sweat test measures chloride in sweat, which is raised because the faulty CFTR channel cannot reabsorb chloride; genetic testing for CFTR mutations supports the diagnosis but the sweat test remains the gold standard.

cards.q: A child with cystic fibrosis has greasy, bulky stools and poor weight gain. What is the cause and the treatment?
cards.a: Pancreatic insufficiency from blocked pancreatic ducts, causing malabsorption of fat and protein. Give pancreatic enzyme replacement with every meal and snack, plus fat-soluble vitamin supplements (A, D, E and K) and a high-calorie, high-fat diet; without enzymes the child will remain malnourished despite eating well.

cards.q: Why must pancreatic enzymes be taken with food in cystic fibrosis, and what happens if the dose is too low?
cards.a: Enzymes must mix with food in the gut to digest fat and protein, so they are taken at the start of and during meals. If the dose is too low, the child will have steatorrhoea, abdominal pain and poor weight gain; if the dose is too high, there is a risk of fibrosing colonopathy, so the dose is titrated to symptoms and growth.

cards.q: A 10-year-old with cystic fibrosis has a pulmonary exacerbation with increased cough, sputum and a fall in FEV1. What is the first-line treatment?
cards.a: Admit for intensive airway clearance, nebulised bronchodilators and mucolytics, and intravenous antibiotics targeted at the organisms in the sputum, usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Exacerbations are treated aggressively to restore lung function, because each exacerbation causes permanent loss of lung function if not fully treated.

cards.q: A child with cystic fibrosis grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa in sputum for the first time. What is the management and why is it urgent?
cards.a: Start eradication therapy promptly, usually with inhaled tobramycin plus oral ciprofloxacin, to clear the organism before it becomes chronic. Once Pseudomonas becomes chronic it is almost impossible to eradicate and causes progressive lung damage, so early aggressive treatment at first isolation is the priority.

cards.q: What is the role of dornase alfa in cystic fibrosis, and how does it work?
cards.a: Dornase alfa is a nebulised mucolytic that breaks down DNA from dead neutrophils in the thick sputum, making it less viscous and easier to clear. It improves lung function and reduces exacerbations when used daily with airway clearance, because the DNA in CF sputum is a major cause of its thickness.

cards.q: A teenager with cystic fibrosis and the F508del mutation asks about CFTR modulators. What do they do, and who benefits?
cards.a: CFTR modulators such as ivacaftor and the triple combination elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor improve the function of the faulty CFTR protein, increasing chloride transport and thinning secretions. They benefit patients with specific responsive mutations, most notably F508del, and can improve lung function, weight and exacerbation rate, but they do not cure the disease and need specialist initiation and monitoring.

cards.q: A child with cystic fibrosis has a low body mass index despite enzyme replacement. What else should be checked?
cards.a: Check adherence to enzymes, dietary intake, diabetes (CF-related diabetes), liver disease, and chronic infection. Poor weight in CF is multifactorial — inadequate calories, malabsorption, increased energy needs from lung disease, and diabetes all contribute — so a dietitian, diabetes screen and sputum review are all needed.

cards.q: Why do children with cystic fibrosis need regular sputum cultures, even when they feel well?
cards.a: To detect new organisms early, especially Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, so eradication therapy can start before chronic infection is established. Regular cultures also guide antibiotic choice during exacerbations and monitor for resistant organisms such as Burkholderia.

cards.q: A 12-year-old with cystic fibrosis has haemoptysis. What is the most likely cause and the next step?
cards.a: Bleeding from hypertrophied bronchial arteries due to chronic airway inflammation and bronchiectasis. Admit, keep the child calm, monitor oxygenation, stop airway clearance temporarily if bleeding is heavy, and involve a specialist — massive haemoptysis may need bronchial artery embolisation.

cards.q: A child with cystic fibrosis is found to have CF-related diabetes. How is it treated, and why is insulin preferred over oral agents?
cards.a: Treat with insulin, because CF-related diabetes is mainly from loss of insulin production due to pancreatic damage, not insulin resistance. Insulin improves weight, lung function and survival in CF, whereas oral agents are less effective and metformin is poorly tolerated; screening with an oral glucose tolerance test is done annually from age 10.

cards.q: A newborn with cystic fibrosis develops meconium ileus. What is the management?
cards.a: Give hyperosmolar contrast enemas to relieve the obstruction if there is no perforation, with surgical intervention if the enema fails or there is perforation or volvulus. Meconium ileus is caused by thick, sticky meconium blocking the bowel in CF, and early recognition and treatment prevent bowel necrosis.

cards.q: A child with cystic fibrosis has clubbing, chronic cough and recurrent chest infections. What does clubbing indicate, and what should you do?
cards.a: Clubbing indicates chronic hypoxia and suppurative lung disease with bronchiectasis. Optimise airway clearance, treat infection aggressively, check lung function and oxygen saturation, and involve a CF specialist — clubbing is a sign of established chronic lung disease, not an acute finding.

cards.q: A 4-year-old with pneumonia has a large pleural effusion on chest X-ray and is in respiratory distress. What is the next step?
cards.a: Admit, give oxygen and intravenous antibiotics, and involve paediatrics and respiratory specialists to assess whether the effusion needs drainage. A large effusion compresses the lung and causes hypoxia; a diagnostic tap can distinguish a simple parapneumonic effusion from empyema, and drainage is needed if the fluid is infected, loculated or causing significant respiratory compromise.

cards.q: A child with pneumonia develops an empyema with thick, loculated fluid. What is the definitive management?
cards.a: Drain the empyema, usually with a chest drain plus intrapleural fibrinolytics, or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery if drainage fails. Empyema is infected pus in the pleural space that antibiotics alone cannot clear because the fluid is loculated and poorly penetrated; drainage removes the pus, allows the lung to re-expand and shortens the illness.

cards.q: A 6-year-old with pneumonia has a small pleural effusion, is comfortable on oxygen and improving on antibiotics. Does he need a chest drain?
cards.a: No — a small, uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion usually resolves with antibiotics alone and does not need drainage. Drainage is reserved for large effusions, empyema, or effusions causing respiratory distress or not improving; an unnecessary drain adds pain and risk without benefit.

cards.q: A child with pneumonia has persistent fever after 5 days of antibiotics and a repeat X-ray shows a round opacity. What complication should you consider?
cards.a: Consider a lung abscess or a complicated effusion, and arrange further imaging such as ultrasound or CT with specialist input. Persistent fever despite antibiotics suggests a collection that is not being cleared, and a lung abscess needs prolonged antibiotics and sometimes drainage.

cards.q: A 3-year-old with pneumonia develops a pneumothorax. What is the management, and when is a chest drain needed?
cards.a: Give oxygen, monitor closely, and insert a chest drain if the pneumothorax is large, causing respiratory distress, or under tension. A small pneumothorax in a stable child may resolve with observation and oxygen, but a large or tension pneumothorax compresses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, so drainage is urgent.

cards.q: A child with pneumonia is not improving and the sputum grows Staphylococcus aureus. What complication is this organism associated with, and what should you look for?
cards.a: Staphylococcal pneumonia is associated with pneumatoceles, empyema, lung abscess and rapid deterioration. Look for cavitary lesions and pleural collections on imaging, involve a specialist, and ensure antibiotic cover is appropriate for Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA cover if locally indicated.

cards.q: A 2-year-old with pneumonia has a pleural effusion that is sampled. The fluid has a low pH, low glucose and many neutrophils. What does this mean for management?
cards.a: This is a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema, and drainage is needed. A low pH and low glucose mean bacteria are actively metabolising in the fluid and it will not resolve with antibiotics alone; a chest drain should be placed promptly.

cards.q: A 2-month-old has noisy breathing since birth that is worse when lying on the back and improves when prone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Laryngomalacia, the most common cause of stridor in infants, caused by floppy supraglottic tissue collapsing on inspiration. It typically presents in the first weeks of life, worsens with crying and feeding, and usually resolves by 12 to 18 months as the cartilage stiffens; most cases need only reassurance and monitoring.

cards.q: An infant with laryngomalacia is failing to thrive and has apnoea and chest retractions. What is the next step?
cards.a: Refer urgently to ENT and paediatrics for airway assessment, as this is severe laryngomalacia. Most cases are mild, but failure to thrive, apnoea, cyanosis or severe retractions mean the airway obstruction is significant and the child may need supraglottoplasty or other intervention; do not simply reassure in a child with these red flags.

cards.q: A 3-year-old has sudden onset inspiratory stridor, drooling and a high fever, and is sitting forward. What is the diagnosis and what must you NOT do?
cards.a: Acute epiglottitis. Do not examine the throat with a tongue depressor, do not lay the child flat, and do not leave the child unattended — keep the child upright and comfortable, give oxygen, and call anaesthesia and ENT immediately for a controlled airway in theatre. The swollen epiglottis can obstruct completely if disturbed, so airway management must be done by the most experienced team in a controlled setting.

cards.q: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, inspiratory stridor and a low-grade fever at night. What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
cards.a: Viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone, which reduces airway oedema and improves symptoms within hours, and give nebulised adrenaline if there is severe stridor at rest. Most children can be managed at home if they are not in respiratory distress, but severe croup needs admission and monitoring.

cards.q: A child with croup is given dexamethasone but still has stridor at rest and chest retractions. What is the next step?
cards.a: Give nebulised adrenaline and admit for observation. Adrenaline constricts the mucosal blood vessels and reduces oedema quickly, but its effect lasts only 1 to 2 hours, so the child needs monitoring for rebound stridor after it wears off; do not discharge a child who needed adrenaline until they have been observed for several hours.

cards.q: How do you distinguish laryngomalacia from croup in a child with stridor?
cards.a: Laryngomalacia is chronic from birth, worse when supine and with feeding, and the child is usually afebrile and well between episodes; croup is acute, with a barking cough, fever and a recent viral illness, and it resolves over a few days. The history — age of onset, duration and associated features — separates them, and the management is very different.

cards.q: A 6-year-old snores loudly, has witnessed apnoeas and is sleepy at school. What is the most likely cause and the first-line treatment?
cards.a: Obstructive sleep apnoea, most commonly from adenotonsillar hypertrophy in children. Refer for sleep assessment and consider adenotonsillectomy, which is the first-line treatment when enlarged tonsils and adenoids are the cause; it improves sleep, behaviour, growth and daytime functioning.

cards.q: A child with obstructive sleep apnoea is obese and has no tonsillar hypertrophy. What is the management?
cards.a: Address weight, sleep hygiene and nasal obstruction, and consider continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) if apnoea persists. Adenotonsillectomy will not help if the tonsils are not enlarged, so weight management, positional therapy and CPAP are the mainstays, with specialist sleep input.

cards.q: Why is obstructive sleep apnoea in a child not just a snoring problem, and what complications should you look for?
cards.a: Because repeated hypoxia and fragmented sleep cause poor growth, behavioural problems, poor school performance, and in severe cases pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain. Look for failure to thrive, daytime sleepiness, hyperactivity, morning headaches and raised pulmonary pressures, and treat the apnoea rather than dismissing it as simple snoring.

cards.q: A 4-year-old with Down syndrome snores and has pauses in breathing at night. Why is he at higher risk, and what should you do?
cards.a: Children with Down syndrome have a higher risk of sleep apnoea from midface hypoplasia, macroglossia, hypotonia and adenotonsillar hypertrophy. Arrange a sleep study and ENT review, because sleep apnoea is common and under-recognised in this group and treatment improves cognition, behaviour and cardiac health.

cards.q: A 9-year-old with congenital heart disease develops progressive breathlessness, fatigue and a loud P2. Echo shows raised pulmonary artery pressures. What is the diagnosis and the next step?
cards.a: Pulmonary hypertension, likely secondary to the heart disease or to chronic lung disease. Refer urgently to a pulmonary hypertension specialist centre for confirmation by cardiac catheterisation and assessment for targeted therapy; do not start a pulmonary vasodilator without specialist guidance, as the wrong drug can worsen the underlying shunt.

cards.q: A child with pulmonary hypertension is started on sildenafil. How does it work, and what must be monitored?
cards.a: Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor that dilates the pulmonary arteries and reduces pulmonary vascular resistance. Monitor blood pressure, oxygen saturation, exercise tolerance and for side effects such as headache and flushing, and review regularly with a specialist, because the dose is titrated to response and the disease can progress despite treatment.

cards.q: A child with pulmonary hypertension becomes acutely breathless and hypoxic during a respiratory infection. What is the immediate management?
cards.a: Give oxygen, treat the infection, avoid hypoxia, acidosis and pain, which all raise pulmonary vascular resistance, and involve intensive care and the pulmonary hypertension team early. A pulmonary hypertensive crisis can cause acute right heart failure, so keep the child calm, well oxygenated and avoid anything that increases pulmonary pressures.

cards.q: Why should a child with pulmonary hypertension avoid dehydration and prolonged fasting before a procedure?
cards.a: Because dehydration reduces right ventricular preload and can precipitate acute right heart failure in a child whose right ventricle is already struggling against high pulmonary pressures. Keep the child well hydrated, minimise fasting time, and ensure anaesthesia is given by a team experienced in pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: A child with pulmonary hypertension has a syncopal episode. What does this indicate, and what is the urgency?
cards.a: Syncope in pulmonary hypertension indicates severe disease with inability to increase cardiac output on exertion, and it is a poor prognostic sign. This is an urgent specialist review — the child needs reassessment of pulmonary pressures, optimisation of therapy, and counselling about activity restriction and the risk of sudden death.

cards.q: A 2-year-old suddenly starts coughing and choking while eating peanuts, then becomes quieter but still wheezy. What is the diagnosis and the next step?
cards.a: Foreign body aspiration, most likely a peanut in the airway. Arrange urgent bronchoscopy to remove it, even if the child looks better, because the foreign body can move, cause complete obstruction, or lead to pneumonia and atelectasis. Do not wait for imaging to be definitive — a normal chest X-ray does not exclude a radiolucent foreign body.

cards.q: A 3-year-old has recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe and a persistent wheeze that does not respond to bronchodilators. What should you suspect?
cards.a: A retained foreign body in the airway causing recurrent infection and localised wheeze in one lobe. Ask about a choking episode, arrange imaging and bronchoscopy, and do not keep escalating asthma therapy for a wheeze that is unilateral and unresponsive to bronchodilators.

cards.q: A toddler is choking on a foreign body and cannot cough, cry or breathe. What is the immediate first aid?
cards.a: Give back blows and chest thrusts for an infant, or abdominal thrusts for an older child, to dislodge the obstruction, and call for help. Do not do a blind finger sweep, which can push the object further down; if the child becomes unresponsive, start CPR and look in the mouth only if the object is visible.

cards.q: Why are peanuts and small round foods particularly dangerous for toddlers, and what advice should parents be given?
cards.a: Because toddlers have narrow airways, poor chewing and a tendency to inhale while eating or laughing, and peanuts can swell and fragment, making them hard to remove. Advise parents to avoid whole nuts, grapes, popcorn and hard sweets in children under 5, to supervise eating, and to cut grapes lengthways.

cards.q: A 12-year-old has sharp chest pain after exercise that is reproducible on palpation of the chest wall. What is the most likely cause, and what red flags would change your management?
cards.a: Musculoskeletal chest pain or costochondritis, the most common cause of chest pain in children. Red flags that need urgent cardiac work-up are pain with exertion plus syncope, palpitations, a family history of sudden death, a murmur, or pain that is not reproducible and is associated with breathlessness or sweating.

cards.q: A teenager has chest pain during exercise, faints, and has a harsh systolic murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis and the next step?
cards.a: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or severe aortic stenosis causing outflow obstruction. Stop exercise immediately, admit, do an ECG and echocardiogram urgently, and refer to cardiology — this child is at risk of sudden death and must not exercise until cleared by a specialist.

cards.q: A child has chest pain and a pericardial friction rub after a viral illness. What is the diagnosis and the treatment?
cards.a: Acute pericarditis. Treat with anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, with colchicine in older children if advised by a specialist, and rest from strenuous exercise. Check for a pericardial effusion on echo, because a large effusion can cause tamponade and needs drainage.

cards.q: A 10-year-old has chest pain that is worse when lying flat and better when sitting forward, with diffuse ST elevation on ECG. What is the diagnosis and what should you avoid?
cards.a: Acute pericarditis. Avoid giving anticoagulants or thrombolytics, which are used for a heart attack in adults but would worsen pericardial bleeding here. Treat the inflammation, monitor for tamponade, and do not mistake this for an acute coronary syndrome, which is very rare in children.

cards.q: A 14-year-old faints while standing in a hot room after standing for a long time. He recovers quickly and has a normal ECG and examination. What is the most likely cause and the management?
cards.a: Vasovagal syncope, the most common cause of syncope in adolescents, triggered by prolonged standing, heat and dehydration causing venous pooling and a vagal response. Reassure, advise adequate fluids, salt, avoiding prolonged standing, and to lie down at the first warning symptoms; no further cardiac testing is needed if the history and ECG are normal.

cards.q: A child faints during exercise, has no warning symptoms, and has a family history of sudden death. What is the next step?
cards.a: This is high-risk syncope and needs urgent cardiology referral with an ECG, echocardiogram and rhythm monitoring. Exercise-induced syncope without warning, especially with a family history of sudden death, suggests an arrhythmia or structural heart disease such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or long QT syndrome, and the child must not exercise until assessed.

cards.q: A teenager with recurrent syncope is found to have postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS). What is the first-line management?
cards.a: Increase fluid and salt intake, use compression stockings, avoid triggers such as heat and prolonged standing, and start a graded exercise programme. These measures increase blood volume and venous return and reduce symptoms; drugs such as beta-blockers or fludrocortisone are only added if conservative measures fail, with specialist guidance.

cards.q: A 12-year-old has blood pressure consistently above the 95th percentile on three separate visits. What is the next step in diagnosis?
cards.a: Confirm with correctly sized cuffs and repeated measurements, check for secondary causes, and do baseline bloods, urine testing, renal ultrasound and an echocardiogram to look for end-organ damage. Hypertension in children is often secondary to renal disease, so a secondary work-up is needed rather than assuming essential hypertension as in adults.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of hypertension in a young child, and what should you look for on examination?
cards.a: Renal disease, including renal parenchymal disease and renal artery stenosis. Look for oedema, a renal bruit, poor growth, and signs of the underlying renal disease, and check urine, renal function and renal imaging; a young child with hypertension should not be labelled as essential hypertension without excluding a renal cause.

cards.q: A 15-year-old obese teenager has hypertension and a family history of hypertension. What is the first-line management?
cards.a: Lifestyle modification — weight loss, a low-salt diet, regular exercise and reduced screen time — with regular blood pressure monitoring. In adolescents, essential hypertension is more common and lifestyle change is the first step; drugs are added if blood pressure remains high despite lifestyle measures or if there is end-organ damage.

cards.q: A child with hypertension is started on an ACE inhibitor. What must be monitored, and what counselling is needed for a teenage girl?
cards.a: Monitor blood pressure, renal function and potassium, and counsel teenage girls that ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and must be stopped before pregnancy. Check renal function and electrolytes a few weeks after starting, and ensure effective contraception is discussed if the drug is continued in an adolescent girl.

cards.q: A child with severe hypertension has headache, vomiting and blurred vision. What is this, and what is the management?
cards.a: Hypertensive emergency with possible hypertensive encephalopathy. Admit to intensive care, lower blood pressure gradually with intravenous antihypertensives, and look for the cause. Blood pressure must not be dropped too quickly, because rapid lowering can cause cerebral ischaemia — aim for a controlled, gradual reduction under specialist supervision.

cards.q: A 2-year-old has 6 watery stools in 24 hours, is alert, has moist mucous membranes and normal skin turgor, and is still drinking. What is the next best step in management?
cards.a: Give oral rehydration solution (ORS) at home and continue normal feeding, including breastfeeds. Mild dehydration is best treated with ORS rather than IV fluids or stopping feeds, because ORS replaces water and salts in the right balance and early feeding shortens the illness. Teach the parents red flags: no urine for 8 hours, very sleepy, sunken eyes, blood in stool, or persistent vomiting.

cards.q: A 9-month-old with acute diarrhoea has sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced urine, and a capillary refill of 3 seconds. He is vomiting but alert. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Start oral rehydration with small frequent sips of ORS, about 50 to 100 mL per kg over 4 hours for moderate dehydration, and reassess often. ORS works even with some vomiting if given slowly, and it avoids an IV line. Admit if he cannot keep ORS down, becomes lethargic, or worsens. Do not use plain water, juice, or sports drinks, which have the wrong salt and sugar balance.

cards.q: A 3-year-old with severe dehydration from diarrhoea is lethargic, has cold hands, a weak pulse, and almost no urine. What is the first management step?
cards.a: Give an IV bolus of isotonic crystalloid, such as normal saline or Ringer lactate, 20 mL per kg over 20 to 30 minutes, and repeat as needed while checking pulse, blood pressure, and mental status. Severe dehydration with shock needs rapid IV volume first, because ORS cannot be absorbed fast enough and the child is at risk of circulatory collapse. Once stable, switch to ORS and find the cause.

cards.q: A 14-month-old has acute watery diarrhoea for 2 days. Which anti-diarrhoeal drug should be avoided, and why?
cards.a: Avoid loperamide and other anti-motility drugs in young children with acute diarrhoea. Slowing the gut traps infection and toxins, can cause ileus and toxic megacolon, and does not treat dehydration, which is the real danger. Focus on ORS, zinc, and feeding. Antibiotics are not routine for watery diarrhoea, which is usually viral.

cards.q: A 2-year-old in a low-resource setting has acute diarrhoea. Why is zinc given, and for how long?
cards.a: Give zinc for 10 to 14 days alongside ORS. Zinc shortens the diarrhoea, reduces its severity, and lowers the chance of another episode in the next few months, because diarrhoea depletes zinc and zinc helps the gut lining recover and fight infection. It is an adjunct, not a replacement for rehydration.

cards.q: A 4-year-old has diarrhoea with blood and mucus, fever, and severe abdominal pain. What is the next best step, and what should NOT be given?
cards.a: Admit, rehydrate, send stool culture, and start antibiotics for suspected bacterial dysentery, such as Shigella, while monitoring for complications. Do NOT give loperamide, because slowing the bowel in bloody dysentery increases the risk of toxic megacolon and perforation. Bloody diarrhoea, high fever, and severe pain are red flags that need hospital care, not home ORS alone.

cards.q: A 5-year-old with diarrhoea has not passed urine for 10 hours, is very drowsy, and has a sunken fontanelle check that is not applicable at this age, plus dry mucous membranes. Which features mandate admission?
cards.a: Admit for severe dehydration: no urine for 8 or more hours, marked lethargy or reduced responsiveness, inability to drink or keep fluids down, sunken eyes, very dry mouth, and poor skin turgor. These mean oral rehydration at home is unsafe, because the child cannot replace losses and may deteriorate quickly. In hospital, give IV fluids, monitor electrolytes, and watch for shock.

cards.q: A 1-year-old is recovering from acute diarrhoea and the parents ask about diet. What should you advise about feeding during and after the illness?
cards.a: Continue breastfeeding and offer normal age-appropriate foods as soon as the child will eat, including starches, lean meat, yoghurt, and fruit. Do not starve the child or use a prolonged clear-fluid-only diet, because the gut needs nutrients to repair and the child needs energy to recover. Avoid very sugary drinks and juices, which worsen diarrhoea by drawing water into the bowel.

cards.q: A 12-year-old has bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus, and abdominal pain for 3 weeks, with disease limited to the colon on colonoscopy. What is the diagnosis, and what is first-line induction therapy for moderate disease?
cards.a: Ulcerative colitis, which affects only the colon in a continuous pattern starting from the rectum, with bloody diarrhoea and urgency. First-line induction for moderate disease is oral corticosteroids, such as prednisolone, plus mesalazine, because steroids rapidly control inflammation while mesalazine helps maintain remission. Severe disease needs hospital admission, IV steroids, and monitoring for toxic megacolon.

cards.q: A 14-year-old has chronic diarrhoea, right lower quadrant pain, weight loss, mouth ulcers, and perianal fistula. What diagnosis does this favour over ulcerative colitis, and why?
cards.a: Crohn disease, because it can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus, causes skip lesions and transmural inflammation, and produces perianal fistulae, strictures, and mouth ulcers. Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and does not cause fistulae or small-bowel disease. Crohn also commonly causes growth failure, so growth charts are part of monitoring.

cards.q: A 10-year-old with ulcerative colitis is started on steroids and improves, but relapses every time steroids are tapered. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Start a steroid-sparing maintenance drug, such as a thiopurine like azathioprine, or a biologic such as an anti-TNF agent, and involve paediatric gastroenterology. Repeated steroids cause growth suppression, bone loss, and adrenal suppression, so the goal is remission without long-term steroids. Check thiopurine methyltransferase activity before azathioprine, because low activity raises the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.

cards.q: A 15-year-old with Crohn disease has poor growth, delayed puberty, and low weight despite treatment. What is the most important monitoring measure, and what drives the growth failure?
cards.a: Plot height, weight, and pubertal stage at every visit, because growth failure in Crohn is caused by chronic inflammation, poor nutrient absorption, reduced appetite, and steroid use. Active inflammation suppresses growth hormone signalling, so controlling the disease is itself a growth treatment. Refer to dietetics, optimise nutrition, and minimise steroids; consider biologics if growth does not recover.

cards.q: A child with inflammatory bowel disease is about to start an anti-TNF biologic. What must be checked before the first dose?
cards.a: Screen for latent tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and varicella immunity, check full blood count, liver function, and vaccination status, and ensure no active infection. Anti-TNF drugs suppress immunity, so latent tuberculosis can reactivate and live vaccines are unsafe while on treatment. Give any needed inactivated vaccines before starting, and counsel the family about infection risk.

cards.q: A 13-year-old with ulcerative colitis presents with severe bloody diarrhoea 10 times a day, fever, tachycardia, and a distended abdomen. What is the feared complication, and what is the immediate management?
cards.a: Toxic megacolon with risk of perforation. Admit urgently, keep nil by mouth, give IV fluids and IV corticosteroids, stop anti-motility drugs and opioids, monitor abdominal examination and plain abdominal X-ray, and involve surgery early. If medical treatment fails or perforation is suspected, colectomy may be life-saving, so do not delay surgical review.

cards.q: A 9-year-old with Crohn disease has iron deficiency anaemia, low albumin, and vitamin B12 deficiency. Why do these deficiencies occur, and what is the management priority?
cards.a: Crohn affecting the ileum impairs absorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts, while chronic gut inflammation and blood loss cause iron deficiency and protein loss. Treat the underlying inflammation first, replace iron and B12, and monitor nutrition with a dietitian. Correcting deficiency without controlling the disease will fail, because absorption remains impaired.

cards.q: A 16-year-old with ulcerative colitis in remission on mesalazine asks about long-term cancer risk. What should you explain and arrange?
cards.a: Explain that long-standing extensive ulcerative colitis increases colorectal cancer risk, so surveillance colonoscopy starts about 8 to 10 years after diagnosis and is repeated regularly. The best protection is keeping the disease in remission, because ongoing inflammation drives the risk. Continue maintenance mesalazine, do not stop it when well, and attend gastroenterology follow-up.

cards.q: A 7-year-old has chronic diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss, and iron deficiency anaemia. Tissue transglutaminase IgA is strongly positive and total IgA is normal. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Refer for endoscopy with duodenal biopsy while the child is still eating gluten. Serology suggests coeliac disease, but biopsy showing villous atrophy confirms it and excludes other causes, so do not start a gluten-free diet before biopsy, because the gut heals and the biopsy becomes falsely normal. Also check for associated conditions such as type 1 diabetes and thyroid disease.

cards.q: A 5-year-old has positive coeliac serology but the parents started a gluten-free diet 2 months ago and the child feels better. What is the problem with proceeding to biopsy now?
cards.a: The biopsy may be normal because gluten withdrawal heals the villi, so a negative result would not exclude coeliac disease. The child needs a supervised gluten challenge, eating gluten daily for several weeks, before repeat serology and biopsy. Explain this clearly, because a false negative could lead to stopping the diet and ongoing gut damage.

cards.q: A child is diagnosed with coeliac disease. What is the lifelong treatment, and what must the family be taught about cross-contamination?
cards.a: A strict lifelong gluten-free diet, with no wheat, barley, or rye, including hidden gluten in sauces, processed foods, and shared cooking surfaces. Even small amounts damage the gut and increase the risk of poor growth, anaemia, and later malignancy. Refer to a dietitian, teach label reading, and arrange follow-up serology and growth monitoring to check adherence.

cards.q: A 10-year-old with coeliac disease on a gluten-free diet still has poor growth and positive tissue transglutaminase IgA after 12 months. What is the most likely cause, and what is the next step?
cards.a: Ongoing inadvertent gluten exposure is the most likely cause, so take a detailed dietary history with a dietitian, review labels and school meals, and check for cross-contamination. Persistent positive serology means the gut is still being exposed, so the diet, not the diagnosis, needs fixing first. If adherence is good, reconsider other causes such as refractory coeliac disease or an additional diagnosis.

cards.q: A 12-year-old with coeliac disease has low vitamin D, low calcium, and delayed puberty at diagnosis. Why does this happen, and what should be monitored at follow-up?
cards.a: Damaged villi impair absorption of calcium, vitamin D, iron, and other nutrients, so bone health and puberty suffer. At follow-up, monitor height and weight, tissue transglutaminase IgA, iron, calcium, vitamin D, and bone health, and replace deficiencies. Growth usually catches up once the gut heals on a strict gluten-free diet.

cards.q: A child with type 1 diabetes is screened and found to have positive coeliac serology but no gut symptoms. Why is screening done, and should a gluten-free diet be started if biopsy confirms coeliac disease?
cards.a: Coeliac disease is strongly associated with type 1 diabetes because both are autoimmune, and it is often silent, causing poor growth and unstable blood sugars without obvious gut symptoms. If biopsy confirms it, start a gluten-free diet even without symptoms, because ongoing gut damage worsens nutrition and glycaemic control. Screen also for thyroid disease in the same child.

cards.q: A 6-year-old passes hard stools twice a week, has abdominal pain, and soils his underwear daily. What is the diagnosis, and what is the first-line treatment?
cards.a: Functional constipation with overflow encopresis: retained hard stool stretches the rectum, reduces sensation, and liquid stool leaks around the blockage. First-line treatment is disimpaction with high-dose polyethylene glycol, followed by a daily maintenance laxative, plus toilet routine and dietary fibre. Reassure the family that soiling is not deliberate, because blame worsens withholding.

cards.q: A 4-year-old with chronic constipation is started on polyethylene glycol. The parents ask how long treatment should continue. What should you advise?
cards.a: Continue a daily maintenance laxative for months, often 6 to 12 months, and taper only after regular soft stools without pain for several weeks. Stopping too early causes relapse, because the stretched rectum needs time to regain tone and the child needs time to unlearn withholding. Combine with scheduled toilet sitting after meals and adequate fluids and fibre.

cards.q: A 3-year-old has constipation, withholding behaviour, and pain on passing stool, but no vomiting, blood, or neurological signs. What should NOT be done routinely, and what is the key history point?
cards.a: Do not order routine blood tests, abdominal X-ray, or referral for functional constipation when the history and examination are typical and red flags are absent. The key is the withholding cycle: a painful stool leads to fear, withholding, harder stool, and more pain. Break the cycle with laxatives that make stools soft and painless, plus a calm toilet routine.

cards.q: A 2-year-old has constipation since birth, a distended abdomen, and delayed passage of meconium in the newborn period. What diagnosis must be excluded, and what is the next step?
cards.a: Exclude Hirschsprung disease, where part of the bowel lacks nerve cells and cannot relax, causing obstruction from birth. The next step is referral for rectal suction biopsy, which shows absent ganglion cells, plus contrast enema and surgical review. This is not functional constipation, and laxatives alone will not fix it, so do not delay referral.

cards.q: An 8-year-old with encopresis is being punished at home for soiling. What is the most important counselling point, and what behavioural strategy helps?
cards.a: Explain that encopresis is involuntary overflow around impacted stool, not laziness or defiance, and punishment increases anxiety and withholding, making it worse. Use positive reinforcement, a star chart for sitting on the toilet after meals, and regular toilet time, alongside laxatives. Treat the constipation first, because behaviour alone cannot overcome a full rectum.

cards.q: A 5-year-old with constipation has a palpable faecal mass, anal fissure, and blood on the stool surface. What is the management sequence?
cards.a: First disimpact with high-dose oral polyethylene glycol, treat the fissure so passing stool stops hurting, then start maintenance laxatives and a toilet routine. The fissure matters because pain drives withholding, so pain relief and soft stools must come together. Check for red flags such as weight loss, vomiting, or neurological signs, which would need further investigation.

cards.q: A 3-month-old spits up after most feeds, is gaining weight well, and is otherwise happy. What is the diagnosis, and what is the management?
cards.a: Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux, which is common and normal in infants because the lower oesophageal sphincter is immature. No drug treatment is needed if the baby is thriving and has no red flags. Advise smaller frequent feeds, keeping the baby upright after feeds, and avoiding overfeeding. Reassure the parents and review growth, because most cases resolve by 12 to 18 months.

cards.q: A 6-month-old has frequent vomiting, poor weight gain, arching of the back during feeds, and recurrent wheeze. What diagnosis is now likely, and what is the first step?
cards.a: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, because reflux is now causing harm: faltering growth, pain, and possible aspiration with wheeze. Start with thickened feeds or a trial of acid suppression if feeds alone fail, and assess feeding, growth, and airway symptoms. Refer if there is faltering growth, haematemesis, or apnoea, because these need specialist review.

cards.q: A 9-month-old with suspected reflux disease does not improve with thickened feeds. Which drug is used next, and what should be avoided long term without review?
cards.a: A proton pump inhibitor is the next step when reflux disease causes pain, poor feeding, or oesophagitis, because it reduces acid and allows the oesophagus to heal. Do not continue acid suppression indefinitely without review, and do not use it for simple happy spitting in a thriving infant, because it does not help and carries risks such as gut infection and bone effects.

cards.q: A 2-year-old has vomiting, dysphagia, and food getting stuck, with eosinophils on oesophageal biopsy and no response to proton pump inhibitors. What is the diagnosis and the next management step?
cards.a: Eosinophilic oesophagitis, an allergic inflammation of the oesophagus, often linked to food allergy. The next step is allergy and gastroenterology referral, dietary elimination guided by allergy testing, and swallowed topical steroids if needed. Do not keep increasing acid suppression, because the problem is eosinophilic inflammation, not acid alone.

cards.q: An 8-year-old has heartburn, epigastric pain, and nocturnal cough. What lifestyle measures should be tried first, and when is endoscopy indicated?
cards.a: Advise avoiding late meals, large meals, fizzy drinks, chocolate, and spicy foods, raising the head of the bed, and weight management if overweight. Endoscopy is indicated if there is dysphagia, weight loss, haematemesis, anaemia, or symptoms that do not respond to treatment, because these may indicate oesophagitis, stricture, or Barrett change. Most children improve with lifestyle measures plus acid suppression.

cards.q: A 4-month-old has bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and constipation. Why is this a surgical emergency, and what is the next step?
cards.a: Bilious vomiting in an infant suggests intestinal obstruction, such as malrotation with volvulus, which can cut off blood supply to the gut. This is a surgical emergency: keep nil by mouth, give IV fluids, and get urgent surgical review and imaging. Do not attribute bilious vomiting to simple reflux, because delay risks bowel necrosis.

cards.q: A 4-week-old boy has forceful non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds, is hungry afterwards, and has lost weight. Examination shows a palpable olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen. What is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment?
cards.a: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, where the pylorus thickens and blocks the stomach outlet, causing projectile non-bilious vomiting and hunger. Definitive treatment is pyloromyotomy, a surgical cut through the thickened muscle. Before surgery, correct dehydration and the hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with IV fluids, because operating on a dehydrated, alkalotic infant is unsafe.

cards.q: A 5-week-old with pyloric stenosis has vomiting, dry mucous membranes, and blood gases showing metabolic alkalosis with low chloride and low potassium. Why does this pattern occur?
cards.a: Repeated vomiting loses stomach acid, which is hydrochloric acid, so chloride and hydrogen are lost and the blood becomes alkalotic. The kidneys then lose potassium while trying to retain hydrogen, causing hypokalaemia. This is why IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline and potassium replacement must come before surgery, to correct the electrolytes and volume.

cards.q: A 3-week-old has projectile vomiting and ultrasound shows a pyloric muscle thickness of 4 mm and a channel length of 18 mm. What does this confirm, and what should be checked before surgery?
cards.a: It confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, as the thickened muscle and elongated channel block gastric emptying. Before surgery, check hydration, electrolytes, acid-base status, and weight, and correct dehydration and alkalosis with IV fluids. Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice, and surgery is curative once the baby is stabilised.

cards.q: A 6-week-old has vomiting and poor feeding, but the vomit is not projectile and there is no palpable mass. What other causes should be considered before assuming pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Consider gastro-oesophageal reflux, overfeeding, cow milk protein allergy, infection, and raised intracranial pressure, because not all infant vomiting is pyloric stenosis. Pyloric stenosis typically appears at 3 to 6 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting, visible gastric waves, and a palpable olive mass. If the pattern does not fit, examine fully and use ultrasound rather than rushing to surgery.

cards.q: Parents ask whether pyloric stenosis can be treated with medicines instead of surgery. What should you explain?
cards.a: Surgery, pyloromyotomy, is the definitive treatment and is curative, with rapid recovery and resumption of feeds. Medical treatment with atropine is sometimes used when surgery is very high risk, but it is slower, less reliable, and needs prolonged hospital stay. Explain that the operation is routine, the muscle is split rather than removed, and the prognosis is excellent.

cards.q: A 2-week-old is lethargic, has poor feeding, and has not passed urine well since a pyloromyotomy. What is the most likely postoperative concern, and what should be checked?
cards.a: Check hydration, electrolytes, and feeding tolerance, because postoperative vomiting, poor intake, and electrolyte disturbance can persist for a short time after surgery. Also consider infection or incomplete relief of obstruction if vomiting continues. Most babies feed well within a day or two, so persistent vomiting or lethargy needs prompt review, not reassurance alone.

cards.q: An 18-month-old has episodic severe abdominal pain, draws up his legs, vomits, and passes redcurrant jelly stool. What is the diagnosis, and what is the first-line treatment if he is stable?
cards.a: Intussusception, where one segment of bowel telescopes into another, causing intermittent obstruction and ischaemia. First-line treatment in a stable child without peritonitis is air or contrast enema reduction under imaging, which often succeeds and avoids surgery. Do not delay, because prolonged intussusception causes bowel necrosis and perforation.

cards.q: A 2-year-old with suspected intussusception has peritonitis, shock, and free air on X-ray. What is the management, and why is enema reduction contraindicated?
cards.a: Go straight to emergency surgery, because peritonitis and perforation mean the bowel may already be dead or leaking, and enema reduction would worsen the leak and delay definitive treatment. Resuscitate with IV fluids and antibiotics first, then operate. Enema reduction is only safe in a stable child without signs of perforation or peritonitis.

cards.q: A 9-month-old has intussusception successfully reduced by air enema. What is the next step, and what should the parents be warned about?
